claims.statement: Among the 22 New York sub-borough areas with the lowest median gross rent in 2000, a minority (4 to 11) had both rent growth and growth in the share of college graduates above the city's by 2022-2024, and across all 55 areas rent growth and growth in the college share are positively associated.

graph_evidence.summary: The graph holds 33 findings in 15 studies with gentrification as a variable name; all concern health or injury outcomes and none concerns how often low-rent neighbourhoods gentrify. The studies' own counts, read in the abstracts, give a prevalence: Alroy 2023 classed 14 of 42 New York neighbourhoods as gentrifying or hypergentrifying (rent growth 2000 to 2017); Bhavsar 2022 found that 5 of 28 eligible block groups in Durham gentrified; Spitzer 2023 classed 23.8% of 59,379 urban tracts as gentrifying. Gao 2023 found opposite signs for severe maternal morbidity under two definitions (OR 0.89 and 1.18), and Bhavsar reports that results depend on the definition.

About 150 findings in about 60 studies (collection still running at registration; counts approximate). Lim 2017 followed 12,882 residents of gentrifying New York neighbourhoods who had hospital records: 23% were displaced between 2006 and 2014, and the displaced had 1.8 times (1.5 to 2.2) the rate of emergency visits and hospitalisations, mainly for mental health. Schwartz 2022: New York evictions in 2017 and loss of Medicaid coverage, OR 1.63 (1.38 to 1.92). Graetz 2024: an eviction judgment and 40% (36 to 43) higher mortality; the graph stores the percentages 40, 19, 16 and 12 as hazard ratios. The graph holds no finding that compares the rate at which low-income residents leave gentrifying and non-gentrifying neighbourhoods, which is the disputed question (Freeman and Braconi 2004; Ding, Hwang and Divringi 2016; Dragan, Ellen and Glied 2020).

prediction.magnitude: k between 6 and 10 of 22 (27% to 45%), best guess 8. k2 between 5 and 10. Spearman correlation of rent growth with change in college share across 55 areas between 0.3 and 0.7. Areas I expect in the gentrified set: Williamsburg/Greenpoint, Bedford Stuyvesant, Bushwick, Central Harlem, North Crown Heights/Prospect Heights, Brooklyn Heights/Fort Greene. I expect none of the eight Bronx low-start areas in it.
prediction.definitions: Unit: sub-borough area (SBA), 55 in the Furman Center file. Low start: the 22 SBAs (bottom 40%) by median gross rent in 2000 (Mott Haven/Hunts Point, Morrisania/Belmont, East Harlem, Central Harlem, Brownsville/Ocean Hill, Bedford Stuyvesant, Lower East Side/Chinatown, Coney Island, Rockaways, Williamsburg/Greenpoint, Highbridge/South Concourse, North Crown Heights/Prospect Heights, Bushwick, Morningside Heights/Hamilton Heights, Soundview/Parkchester, University Heights/Fordham, East New York/Starrett City, Washington Heights/Inwood, Throgs Neck/Co-op City, South Crown Heights, Brooklyn Heights/Fort Greene, Kingsbridge Heights/Mosholu). Rent growth: mean of the 2022, 2023 and 2024 values of rent_gross_med_adj divided by the 2000 value, minus 1. College change: mean of the 2022, 2023 and 2024 values of pop_edu_collp_pct minus the 2000 value, in points. Gentrified: both exceed the same quantities computed from the City row. k: gentrified SBAs among the 22. k2: the same count with growth measured from the mean of 2005, 2006 and 2007 to the mean of 2022 to 2024, the low-start group still chosen on 2000 rent (a baseline separate from the selection year, against regression to the mean). rho: Spearman correlation of rent growth and college change over all 55 SBAs, 95% interval by Fisher z with standard error sqrt(1.06/(n-3)).
prediction.readings: common: k >= 12 (Wilson 95% lower limit 0.34, above one third) and k2 >= 11 and the lower limit of rho above 0. myth: k <= 1 (Wilson upper limit 0.22), or the upper limit of rho below 0. real but a minority: k from 4 to 11 and k2 >= 3 and the lower limit of rho above 0. Anything else is undecided.
prediction.support_if: The reading is 'real but a minority'.
prediction.refute_if: The reading is 'common' or 'myth'; the outcome says which.
prediction.secondary_registered: Reported, not deciding: the count meeting both conditions among the other 33 SBAs; k with the low-start group defined on 2000 median household income; the counts meeting each condition alone; the low-start SBAs whose rent is in the top half (rank 29 or above of 55) in 2022-2024; the Spearman correlation of 2000 rent with 2022-2024 rent.

claims.plan: Script: analyses/affordability/gentrification_test.py, committed with this registration and run unchanged (PRECEDENCE rule 9). No resampling and no random numbers in the test. Data: data/derived/affordability/furman_panel.csv, built by analyses/affordability/build_panel.py from the NYU Furman Center CoreData workbook Neighorhood_Indicators_CoreDataDownload_2026-05-05.xlsx (sha256 in data/derived/affordability/furman_source.json). The Furman Center computes the SBA values from census 2000 and American Community Survey microdata and adjusts dollars for inflation. The Census API was not used because it requires a key.

can_it_fail.association: The count alone cannot separate a real pattern from two unrelated coin flips with p near 0.25, so the reading also requires the lower limit of rho above 0. With n = 55 that happens with probability 0.025 if rho = 0, 0.58 if rho = 0.3, 0.84 if rho = 0.4 and 0.97 if rho = 0.5.
can_it_fail.reading: The support condition fails with probability about 0.98 if rent growth and college growth are unrelated, and with probability about 0.9 if two thirds of low-rent areas gentrify. It can therefore fail in both directions. It is likely to pass (about 0.6) under my prediction, and the leak described under already_seen raises that.

claims.already_seen: Read before registration: the 2000 values of every indicator for the 55 sub-borough areas and the city (rent, income, college share, poverty, population), which fix the low-start group; the workbook's column names, data dictionary and the count of non-missing cells by year. Not read directly: any value after 2000 for rent, college share, poverty or population. One leak occurred. The code test (`gentrification_test.py --simulate`) was meant to replace later-year values with noise; it multiplied the real values by lognormal noise instead (sigma 0.3 on each annual value, seed 0), and I read its output: k = 6, k2 = 7, Spearman 0.38, and the list of areas it classed as gentrified (Brooklyn Heights/Fort Greene, Bushwick, Coney Island, Lower East Side/Chinatown, North Crown Heights/Prospect Heights, Williamsburg/Greenpoint). That output is a noisy view of the outcome: the noise is about as large as the real variation between areas. The thresholds (k of 12 or more, 4 to 11, 1 or fewer) and the script were written before that run and were not changed after it. Prior knowledge: the Furman Center's 2016 report classed 15 of 22 low-income sub-borough areas as gentrifying on rent growth above the median from 1990 to 2014, with one condition (rent) where this test has two; Alroy 2023 classed 14 of 42 neighbourhoods as gentrifying or hypergentrifying on rent growth from 2000 to 2017. Also seen before registration, none of them a deciding variable: executed evictions by community district and year (6z8x-wfk4), IRS county outflows, and the graph findings listed.
alternatives: Regression to the mean: an area with an unusually low rent estimate in 2000 would show fast growth without any change. The 2000 values come from the census long form (about one household in six), so sampling error is small, and k2 uses a later baseline.
Citywide rent growth: every area's rent rose; the definition compares with the city's growth for that reason.

Rent regulation and public housing hold the median rent of all tenants below the rent a newcomer pays, so median gross rent understates change where many tenants are regulated (Lower East Side, Harlem).
Boundary changes: the public-use microdata areas behind the SBAs were redrawn in 2012 and 2022; the Furman Center maps them to fixed SBAs, and any error is in its file.
College share can rise because long-term residents' children graduate or because older residents with less schooling die, without newcomers.
55 areas of 100,000 to 250,000 people hide change within them; a gentrifying corner of a large area may not move its median.
claims.prior_note: Probability of 'real but a minority'. About 0.2 for common, 0.02 for myth, the rest undecided.

outcome.notes:
Reading: real but a minority. 8 of 22 low-rent areas (36%, Wilson 20% to 57%) met both conditions: Bedford Stuyvesant, Brooklyn Heights/Fort Greene, Bushwick, Central Harlem, Morningside Heights/Hamilton Heights, North Crown Heights/Prospect Heights, Washington Heights/Inwood and Williamsburg/Greenpoint. City rent growth was 41% in constant dollars and the city's college share rose 14.7 points. Five of the eight (the Brooklyn areas) rose 32 to 38 rank places in rent; the three upper Manhattan areas passed the rent condition by 1 to 9 points of growth and moved 4 to 8 places. Secondary: 6 of the other 33 areas met both conditions; 8 of 22 with the low-start group defined on income; 9 of 22 met the rent condition and 12 of 22 the college condition; the Spearman correlation of 2000 rent with 2022-2024 rent is 0.71. Found after the outcome: the 2022 American Community Survey moved to 2020 public-use microdata areas, and in the Furman file the population of 28 of 55 areas changes by more than 8% between 2021 and 2022 (7 of 55 at the 2012 change, 13 in an ordinary year). The registered end period, 2022-2024, is therefore on different boundaries from 2000 for about half the areas. Exploratory check with the end period 2017-2019: k = 9 (South Crown Heights added), Spearman 0.53, 10 of the other 33. The reading does not change.

After the referee (13 Nov 2026): the verdict is kept under rule 1. The referee rebuilt the area table with separate code and reproduced k = 8 of 22, k2 = 8 and the correlation of 0.68 (0.50 to 0.80); all three registered conditions of the reading 'real but a minority' are met. The changes follow.
Not blind. The faulty --simulate run that the registrant read before registering was informative. Rebuilt with seed 0 it gives what the registration reports (k 6, k2 7, correlation 0.38). Over 400 other seeds the simulated k has mean 6.9 (95% range 2 to 15), the simulated correlation has mean 0.33 (0.08 to 0.53), an average of 5.4 of the areas in a simulated set are among the true eight, and the simulated k is between 4 and 11 in 79% of draws (referee). A registrant who had seen that output knew that the count and the correlation were probably inside the supporting window. The registration says the thresholds and the script were written before the simulated run. The repository cannot confirm this: no commit of the script or thresholds precedes the registration commit (07:47:16), the script's last save (07:43:44) is compatible with either order, and the file the simulated run wrote, gentrification_results_SIMULATED.json, is not in data/derived/affordability/. The referee judged tuning unlikely, because the window of 4 to 11 is wider than a window fitted to a leaked 6 would need to be and the six areas named in the prediction differ from the six leaked. The result is therefore a measurement under a definition fixed before the exact values were known, and not a blind prediction. The prediction is no longer scored as a hit.
Dependence on the rule. Over 35 combinations of seven rent rules and five college rules the count ranges from 5 to 12, and 34 of the 35 are between 5 and 11 (referee). With other end periods it is 6 to 10. Five Brooklyn areas (Williamsburg/Greenpoint, Bedford Stuyvesant, Bushwick, North Crown Heights/Prospect Heights and Brooklyn Heights/Fort Greene) are in the set under each of the eleven end periods tried and pass the rent condition by 42 to 96 points of growth. The three upper Manhattan areas pass it by 8.7, 7.9 and 0.8 points; Washington Heights/Inwood, at 0.8, leaves the set in five of the ten other end periods. East Harlem misses by 2.0 points. The supported statement is that five areas changed by a wide margin and that two to five more are near the threshold.
No difference from the other areas. Six of the other 33 areas also meet both conditions (18%), against 8 of 22 (36%); Fisher's exact test gives p = 0.21 (re-checked). The data show that about a third of low-rent areas had rent and college share rise faster than the city's. They do not show that this happened more often in low-rent areas than elsewhere.
The benchmark. The city's rent growth (41.1%) is above the median area's (35.6%) and its college change (14.7 points) above the median area's (12.3), so 18 of 55 areas exceed the city on rent and 21 on college share. The reading 'common' needed 12 of the 22 to pass both, which the benchmark made hard to reach; the registered binomial table did not allow for this. The correlation condition is the part that could fail and it is well supported (0.68 across 55 areas, 0.77 within the 22, 0.62 within the other 33).
The research range. The graph_effect of 0.24 (0.18 to 0.33) is the lowest and highest of three studies' shares, from different units, periods and definitions. It is not an interval, and agreement with it shows little, because the registered window of 18% to 50% would have accepted any of the three.
Not changed: regression to the mean in rent is not visible (rank correlation of 2000 rent with rent growth -0.14; k = 7 when selection and baseline both use 2005-2007), and rent and college share take little of the 2022 boundary change.
outcome.verdict_note: Confirmed on the registered conditions (k = 8 of 22, k2 = 8, correlation 0.68 with a lower limit of 0.50). The registration followed a noisy view of the deciding numbers, in which about 5 of the 8 areas appear in a typical draw. No commit shows that the thresholds existed before that view, and the simulated results file is not in the repository. The result is a measurement under a fixed definition and not a blind prediction. It does not show that low-rent areas gentrified more often than other areas (36% against 18%, Fisher p = 0.21).
outcome.stance_note: Null after the referee (rule 6): the city effect is a raw proportion with a null of 0, which does not express a research direction. The earlier value of 0.957 was the distance of 36% from zero.

can_it_fail.assumption: The spread of the log change in the poor count across SBAs is not known before the data are read; I assume a standard deviation between 0.20 and 0.35.
can_it_fail.standard_error: With 8 gentrified and 14 other areas the standard error of the difference is 0.09 (sd 0.20), 0.11 (sd 0.25) or 0.16 (sd 0.35); with 5 and 17 it is 0.10, 0.13 or 0.18.
can_it_fail.power: For a true difference of -0.30 the support condition is met with probability 0.90 (sd 0.20, 8 areas), 0.73 (sd 0.25, 8 areas), 0.60 (sd 0.25, 5 areas) or 0.34 to 0.43 (sd 0.35). With no true difference it is met with probability 0.025. The smallest difference detectable with 80% power is 0.26 to 0.52.
can_it_fail.reading: The test can fail. An unsettled verdict is likely if the true difference is under 0.25.

alternatives: A fall in the poor count is not displacement. Poor residents can leave, die, or stop being poor; the count cannot tell these apart.
The poverty line is national and takes no account of rent, so a household above it may still be unable to pay a higher rent.
Citywide poverty fell over the period; the comparison with other low-rent areas removes the common part.
New housing adds residents who are not poor and lowers the rate without changing the count; the test uses the count for that reason.
Public housing and regulated units keep poor residents in place in some gentrifying areas (Lower East Side, Harlem) and weaken the contrast.
The 2000 poverty count is from the census long form and the later ones from the ACS, which measure income over different reference periods; this affects both groups alike.

outcome.notes:
The number of residents below the poverty line fell 29% in the 8 gentrified areas (341,000 to 241,000), 10% in the 14 other low-rent areas and 3% in the other 33; the city total fell 11%. Secondary (b): the share of low-income renters paying 30% or more changed by -0.2 points in gentrified areas and -1.8 in the others, difference 1.6 (-0.7 to 4.0). Found after the outcome: the 2022 American Community Survey moved to 2020 public-use microdata areas, and in the Furman file the population of 28 of 55 areas changes by more than 8% between 2021 and 2022 (7 of 55 at the 2012 change, 13 in an ordinary year). The registered end period, 2022-2024, is therefore on different boundaries from 2000 for about half the areas. Exploratory repeat with the end period 2017-2019 and the registered groups: -0.24 (-0.35 to -0.14); the poverty rate fell 6.5 points more in gentrified areas (4.4 to 8.6). A fall in the count does not show displacement: the data cannot separate residents who left from residents who died or whose income rose.

After the referee (13 Nov 2026): the verdict is kept under rule 1: the registered condition, an upper limit of the Welch interval below 0, is met at -0.283 (-0.544 to -0.021; standard error 0.121, 13.4 degrees of freedom, p = 0.036), and the referee reproduced it with separate code. The referee's reason for keeping the verdict is the result on end periods before 2022. Those periods were chosen after the data and decide nothing under rule 4; the verdict stands because the registered condition is met, and for no other reason. The changes follow.
Fragility. Six of the 22 single removals of an area put the upper limit at or above 0 (without Washington Heights/Inwood +0.032, Brooklyn Heights/Fort Greene +0.030, North Crown Heights/Prospect Heights +0.030, Bushwick +0.020, Throgs Neck/Co-op City +0.017, Morningside Heights/Hamilton Heights +0.012). So do the end years 2023 and 2024 taken singly (-0.280, -0.579 to +0.018; -0.257, -0.519 to +0.005), Washington Heights/Inwood classed as not gentrified (-0.230, -0.523 to +0.063), East Harlem classed as gentrified (-0.234, -0.493 to +0.025) and groups by the k2 definition (-0.214, -0.498 to +0.071). Those two areas are 0.8 and 2.0 points of rent growth from the threshold. The point estimate is negative in every variant (referee).
Boundary change. A count is a rate multiplied by a population, so it takes the full 2022 change of survey areas. The standard error of the contrast is 0.050 with the end period 2017-2019, 0.062 with 2018, 2019 and 2021, and 0.121 with 2022-2024; the standard deviation of the log change within the groups rises from 0.11 and 0.12 to 0.28 and 0.26. Across the 22 areas the difference between the log change to 2022-2024 and the log change to 2017-2019 correlates 0.69 with the population jump between 2021 and 2022. The error does not favour either group: the contrast in log population change is +0.027 (-0.171 to +0.225). With end periods before the change the contrast is -0.243 (-0.350 to -0.137) and -0.250 (-0.380 to -0.119), and no single removal moves the 2017-2019 upper limit above -0.117. The log change of the poverty rate to 2022-2024 differs by -0.310 (-0.474 to -0.146) and the rate by -6.5 points (-10.3 to -2.7). All of these are post hoc. The interval of 4.4 to 8.6 points given above for the rate is for 2017-2019.
Borough. Seven of the 14 comparison areas are in the Bronx, where no area gentrified, so the contrast is partly Brooklyn and Manhattan against the Bronx. With borough terms the registered contrast is -0.173 (-0.479 to +0.132) and the 2017-2019 contrast is -0.165 (-0.294 to -0.037); without the seven Bronx areas they are -0.204 (-0.474 to +0.067) and -0.182 (-0.299 to -0.064). A different trend in Bronx poverty, for reasons unrelated to rent, is a rival the registration does not name.
Independence. The Welch interval treats the 22 areas as independent. Five of the eight gentrified areas adjoin one another in Brooklyn and the other three in upper Manhattan, so the effective number of areas is below 22 and the interval is too narrow by an amount these data cannot give.
Shared data. The groups are defined by a rise in the college share from the same survey samples and areas that give the poverty count, and graduates are seldom poor, so part of the association follows from the definition. Among the 22 the log change in the poor count follows the college change (-0.13 per 10 points, -0.23 to -0.04; rank correlation -0.61) more closely than rent growth (rank correlation -0.33).
Timing. The contrast in the change of the count by period is -0.002 (-0.068 to +0.065) from 2000 to 2005-2007, -0.087 (-0.186 to +0.011) from 2005-2007 to 2010-2012, -0.154 (-0.246 to -0.062) from 2010-2012 to 2017-2019 and -0.040 (-0.230 to +0.150) from 2017-2019 to 2022-2024. Most of the difference arose between 2010 and 2019, and these data say nothing reliable about the period since. (The referee's text labels these as changes 'to' each period; the script computes the change within each period.)
What the count cannot show. In the gentrified areas the number of residents above the poverty line rose 24.6% (728,000 to 907,000) while the number below it fell 29.2%; in the other low-rent areas the figures are +11.8% and -10.5%. The same contrast would result if poor residents moved out, if they died or aged and were replaced by residents who are not poor, if the incomes of residents who stayed rose past the national poverty line, or if poor households were counted in another area after the boundary change. The claim and the verdict concern the change of a count. They are not evidence on displacement.
The leak. By the referee's rebuild, the simulated run printed this claim's block from line 70 of 116, so the registrant's statement that the output was cut at 70 lines and the block not read is consistent with the output. The run also wrote the block to gentrification_results_SIMULATED.json, which is not in the repository, so the statement rests on the registrant's account. The simulated contrast was -0.520 (-1.053 to +0.014). The condition has no free threshold that such a view could tune; the predicted range could have been informed by it.
outcome.stance_note: Null after the referee: the graph holds no finding on counts of poor residents and the studies cited follow individuals, so there is no research direction for the city contrast to agree with. The earlier value of 0.786 was the distance of the contrast from zero (z = 2.12 on the stance scale, t = -2.33).

claims.statement: Across New York City census tracts, a larger gain in living street trees between the 2005 and 2015 street tree censuses is followed by a faster rise in median gross rent between ACS 2008-12 and ACS 2018-22, of the size that a Portland study of tree planting and house prices implies (green gentrification).

concepts: tree cover / tree canopy / street trees (variable names)
graph_evidence.summary: A search of the graph's variable names for tree canopy, street trees, tree cover and tree planting (30 shortest matching variables of 118, about 80 associations) returned no finding that links trees to rent, house prices, property values or gentrification. It returned findings on depression, distress, cardiovascular disease, mortality, sleep, dementia and one on shootings (IRR 0.91, PMID 36115422). The claimed harm of urban greening is absent from the graph as far as this search reached.

literature.citation: Donovan GH, Prestemon JP, Butry DT, Kaminski AR, Monleon VJ. The politics of urban trees: tree planting is associated with gentrification in Portland, Oregon. Forest Policy and Economics 2021;124:102387.
literature.finding: Abstract: each tree planted was associated with a 131 dollar (95% CI 53 to 210) increase in a tract's median single-family sale price six years later and 265 dollars (151 to 379) twelve years later; 141 tracts, 30 years. The authors call the association modest.

literature.citation: Troy A, Grove JM, O'Neil-Dunne J. The relationship between tree canopy and crime rates across an urban-rural gradient in the greater Baltimore region. Landscape and Urban Planning 2012;106:262-270.
literature.finding: A 10% increase in tree canopy was associated with about a 12% decrease in crime (cross-sectional). Used for the secondary measure only.

prediction.magnitude: Slope of the change in log median gross rent on the change in street trees: 0.044 log points per 100 trees (0.018 to 0.070). Derivation: 131 dollars (53 to 210) per tree at six years divided by an assumed Portland median sale price of 300,000 dollars gives 0.044% (0.018 to 0.070%) per tree per tract; assumed to carry over to rent and to New York tracts, which are of similar population. The hedonic alternative (about 2% of rent for a tree at the house, Donovan and Butry 2011) implies under 0.005 per 100 trees, which this test cannot tell from zero.
prediction.support_if: The 95% confidence interval of the primary slope (per 100 trees) lies wholly above 0.009, half the lower end of the predicted range.
prediction.refute_if: The 95% confidence interval of the primary slope lies wholly below 0.018, the lower end of the predicted range. Any other result is unsettled.

discrimination.method: analyses/all_boats/tree_test.py --dry: the registered model was fitted 200 times to simulated rent changes with the marginal standard deviation of the real rent change (0.199, read without reference to trees) and no relation to trees, on the real design matrix (n = 2,048 tracts, SD of exposure 1.03 hundred trees).
discrimination.secondary_crime: Predicted slope for violent crime: about -0.011 log points per 100 trees (100 young trees at 15 square metres of crown each add about 0.9 points of canopy to a median tract of 0.17 square km; Troy et al. give 1.2% less crime per point). Simulated standard error 0.0073, so z_null is 1.5 and D is 2.3, below 4. The crime measure therefore decides no verdict. It is computed by the same fixed script and reported as exploratory; a null on it is uninformative.

claims.plan: Script: analyses/all_boats/tree_test.py, committed with this registration; no resampling, so no seed. Unit: 2020 census tracts with ACS 2018-22 population of at least 500, both median gross rents present and neither top-coded (2008-12 below 2,000 dollars; 2018-22 below 3,500 dollars). Exposure: living street trees in the 2015 census (NYC Open Data uvpi-gqnh, status Alive) minus living trees in the 2005 census (29bw-z7pj, status not Dead), points joined to 2020 tracts, in hundreds of trees (data/derived/all_boats/tree_counts_tracts.csv). Outcome: d_logrent in data/derived/neighbourhood/tracts_acs.csv (log median gross rent, table B25064, ACS 2018-22 minus ACS 2008-12 area-weighted from 2010 tracts; built by analyses/neighbourhood/base.py). Primary model: OLS of d_logrent on the exposure, trees per square km in 2005, log median rent 2008-12, non-Hispanic white share 2008-12, log population density 2008-12 and borough, with standard errors clustered by 2020 NTA. Sensitivities fixed in the script: without baseline rent; adding the 2018-22 poverty rate; exposure as log ratio of tree counts; tracts with at least 50 trees in 2005. Distribution (exploratory): the slope within thirds of 2008-12 median rent. Secondary, exploratory: Poisson model of murders, robberies and felony assaults in 2016-18 (NYPD complaint data qgea-i56i, offence codes 101, 105, 106) on the exposure, log(1 + count in 2006-08) and the same covariates.
claims.data_seen: Seen before registration: tree counts by tract in both censuses and their correlation with the 2018-22 poverty rate (Spearman 0.30 to 0.35: gains were larger in poorer tracts); the marginal distribution of d_logrent (mean 0.377, SD 0.200, counts of top-coded tracts) and one row of tracts_acs.csv printed as a file header. Not seen: any relation between tree change and rent change, and any crime data by tract and period. d_logrent was used earlier in this project as a covariate in the 311 noise claim (analyses/neighbourhood/noise311.py), never with trees.
alternatives: MillionTreesNYC (2007-2015) directed planting to low-canopy, poorer neighbourhoods, several of which gentrified for other reasons. This would produce a positive slope without any effect of trees. Borough, baseline rent, baseline white share and density adjust for it in part.

The 2005 and 2015 censuses differ in method and completeness (1.5% of 2005 trees fall outside any tract by their coordinates against 0.01% in 2015), so the measured change contains error, which biases the slope toward zero.

ACS tract medians have large sampling error; with baseline rent as a covariate, regression to the mean affects the baseline coefficient and may leak into the tree coefficient. The sensitivity without baseline rent addresses this.
Rent stabilisation slows rent change in older multi-family tracts, where street trees are also dense.

city_effect.label: 2020 census tracts (n=2,048): change in log median gross rent, ACS 2008-12 to 2018-22, per 100 additional living street trees between the 2005 and 2015 censuses; OLS with baseline trees per km2, log rent, white share, log density and borough; SE clustered by NTA

outcome.prediction_scored: Predicted 0.044 (0.018 to 0.070) from the Portland study. Observed 0.0127 (0.0018 to 0.0235). support_if (interval wholly above 0.009) not met: lower bound 0.0018. refute_if (interval wholly below 0.018) not met: upper bound 0.0235. After the referee: on the registered model the estimate is 2.29 standard errors from zero, 5.67 below the central prediction and 0.96 below its lower end. Neither the exclusion of zero nor the ratio to the central prediction (29%) is robust to the form of the exposure or to the adjustments listed in the notes, so the prediction is scored as not decided in size or in sign. Standard error 0.0055 against 0.0049 computed before the data.

violent_crime_poisson_slope_per_100_tree.note: Registered as unable to decide a verdict (D 2.3 before the data). The sign is opposite to the literature: tracts that gained trees had more violent crime in 2016-18 relative to 2006-08. Planting was directed to poorer tracts, and the realised standard error (0.0144) is twice the simulated one, so this is not an estimate of an effect of trees.

outcome.notes:
Without baseline rent as a covariate the slope is 0.0084 (-0.0027 to 0.0196), so the exclusion of zero depends on that covariate. Rival explanations are in the registration: planting directed to poorer tracts that gentrified for other reasons, and measurement differences between the two censuses.

After the referee (13 Nov 2026): the verdict is kept. The referee rebuilt the tree counts from the downloaded points and the rents from the ACS summary files, matched the registrant's values in every tract, and refitted 0.0127 (0.0018 to 0.0235; standard error 0.0055; 2,048 tracts, 196 clusters). Neither registered condition is met and neither was missed narrowly (0.66 standard errors above the support threshold, 0.96 below the refutation threshold). The changes follow.
The exposure is only partly planting. The net change in living trees mixes new planting, loss of existing trees and differences between the two censuses. Across the sample tracts it correlates 0.31 with the count of trees of 3 inches or less in 2015, which must have been planted after 2005, and -0.35 with the 2005 count. The correlation with trees of 6 inches or less is 0.61 to 0.71 in Manhattan, the Bronx and Brooklyn, 0.29 in Queens and 0.10 on Staten Island, so in Queens and Staten Island (757 of 2,048 tracts, 37%) the exposure mostly measures losses or census differences. In the 2005 file 8,840 rows (1.5%) have a longitude of zero and fall in no tract, which is 12% of the counted citywide gain of 76,583 (re-checked); the 2005 counts are too low in unknown tracts and the gain is overstated there. The count of trees of 12 inches or more rose 48% in Manhattan, which planting cannot produce in ten years. In a model with both parts the slope is 0.0097 (-0.0032 to 0.0226) for the change in smaller trees and 0.0201 (0.0018 to 0.0385) for the change in trees of 12 inches or more, so the part that cannot be planting carries at least as much of the association as the part that can (referee).
The size is not stable. Over forms of the exposure and of the adjustment that can each be defended, the slope per 100 trees ranges from 0.0073 (-0.0044 to 0.0179; baseline rent corrected for sampling error at the mean error variance) to 0.0326 (0.0125 to 0.0527; tracts with a change under 200 trees), and the intervals reach 0.057 (0.0273, -0.0024 to 0.0570; net change instrumented by trees of 6 inches or less). Forty-seven tracts changed by 300 trees or more, twenty of them on Staten Island, with a median area of 0.74 square km against 0.18 for the sample; without them the slope is 0.0245 (0.0096 to 0.0395). Per square km the slope is 0.0818 (0.0445 to 0.1191) per thousand trees, which at the median tract area corresponds to 0.045 per 100 trees, the central Portland prediction. The statements that the estimate is 29% of the prediction and that its upper limit of 0.0235 is below 0.044 hold for the registered form only. These variants were chosen after the data and decide nothing under rule 4; three of them would meet the support condition and none meets the refutation condition.
The lower limit is not robust. The interval includes zero without baseline rent (0.0084, -0.0027 to 0.0196), with population change (0.0085, -0.0022 to 0.0193), with fixed effects for 60 districts (0.0095, -0.0005 to 0.0196) or for neighbourhoods (0.0098, -0.0008 to 0.0205), and with the correction for error in baseline rent at the mean error variance (0.0073, -0.0044 to 0.0179). With Conley standard errors to 10 km it is 0.0002 to 0.0251. No borough's interval excludes zero, and the Bronx, with the largest gain (40%), shows none (-0.0009, -0.0144 to 0.0125). The statement that the interval excludes zero is withdrawn from the prediction score.
The comparison with Portland is loose. The 300,000 dollar median price is an assumption; at 200,000 the prediction is 0.066 (0.026 to 0.105) and at 400,000 it is 0.033 (0.013 to 0.052), so the refutation threshold would lie between 0.013 and 0.026 and the observed upper limit of 0.0235 is inside that range. The Portland outcome is the sale price of single-family houses and the exposure is trees planted, at a lag of six years; the New York outcome is gross rent with much of the stock rent-stabilised, the exposure is a net change, and the baseline rent window (2008-12) lies inside the planting period (2005 to 2015). Each difference makes a smaller New York slope expected even if the Portland association carried over. The thresholds stay as registered.
Rivals not answered. New construction (street trees are required with new buildings, which carry higher rents) is not in the registration; the population-change adjustment addresses it in part. No pre-trend test was possible, because the files on disk hold no rent before 2008-12; whether trees went where rents were already rising is the main open rival for any positive reading. The sample drops 135 top-coded tracts, which selects on the outcome.
Blindness. The rent change had been on disk since 12 November and had been used in an earlier claim. The registration says only its marginal distribution was read. The repository cannot show this.
Reading. These data cannot say whether street trees raised rents. A sentence saying that New York shows less rent effect than Portland predicts is not supported and has been removed from docs/all_boats.md.

Moped and scooter crashes: driving speeds above 20 mph OR 2.02 (1.73 to 2.36) for severe or lethal injury. Abstract read.
Teschke et al. 2012 (Toronto and Vancouver cyclists, case-crossover): motor vehicle speeds below 30 km/h adjusted OR 0.52 (0.29 to 0.92) for injury. Abstract read.

literature.citation: Elvik R (2009). The Power Model of the relationship between speed and road safety: update and new analyses. TOI Report 1034/2009, Oslo.

The graph therefore supplies no link from a toll or from traffic speed to ambulance travel time. literature.finding: Toll began 00:00 on 5 January 2025; peak 05:00-21:00 weekdays and 09:00-21:00 weekends at $9 for cars, $2.25 overnight. Qualifying emergency vehicles are exempt.

prediction.magnitude: Composed log change -0.0178 (sd 0.0084): -1.68% (-3.59 to -0.38). Link 1: time per mile fell by the inverse of the speed ratio 1.0575 (1.0295 to 1.0862), CBD against Greater NYC, January to August 2025 against 2023-24 (mob-crz-traffic). Link 2: exponent 0.317 (sd 0.129), the slope of the monthly log ratio of zone to outside EMS peak travel time on the log ratio of CBD to Greater NYC taxi speed, October 2019 to December 2024, with calendar-month terms; the sd is widened to the spread of five specifications (-0.14 to -0.49). Proportional alternative: -5.4% (log -0.0559).
prediction.support_if: With e the primary estimate on the log scale and se its HAC standard error: z_chain = (e - composed mean) / sqrt(se^2 + composed sd^2) has |z_chain| < 1.96, AND D_prop = z_prop^2 - z_chain^2 >= 4 where z_prop = (e + 0.0559) / se. This says travel time moved by about a third of the speed change and not one for one.
prediction.refute_if: |z_chain| >= 1.96: the estimate is incompatible with the composed chain, in either direction.

claims.plan: Data: EMS Incident Dispatch Data (76xm-jjuj), incidents with valid_incident_rspns_time_indc = 'Y', aggregated by date, hour, area and severity group by analyses/congestion/ems_fetch.py. Outcome: incident_travel_tm_seconds_qy, mean per month. Areas by ZIP (analyses/congestion/common.py): zone = Manhattan ZIPs south of 60th Street; comparison = all other city ZIPs pooled. Peak hours: 05:00-20:59 weekdays, 09:00-20:59 weekends. Estimator (analyses/congestion/ems_lib.py, ems_bridge.py, both written before registration): d_t = log mean travel time zone - log mean travel time comparison, by month; OLS of d_t on post and calendar-month dummies, HAC 3 lags. Pre-period January 2023 to December 2024. Primary post-period 5 January to 31 August 2025, the months in which link 1 was measured (the MTA speed series 6p29-6xqn ends in August 2025). Composition: kit.bridge.compose, 200,000 draws, seed 20261113. Can the test fail (rule 8)? Expected endpoint se 0.0132 from the placebo of January-August 2024 against 2022-23. Against no effect the expected D is 1.8, below 4: the test CANNOT tell the chain from no effect, and a no-effect world would pass the chain band with probability 0.84. It is therefore not registered as a test of whether travel time improved. Against the proportional alternative the expected D is 8.3: the test can tell a one-third response from a one-for-one response, and that is the registered condition. The outcome reports z_null and says whether the interval excludes zero, but a verdict of confirmed does not by itself establish an improvement. Verdict by PRECEDENCE rules 1, 2 and 8: support_if met gives confirmed; refute_if met gives contested; otherwise unsettled (this includes |z_chain| < 1.96 with D_prop < 4). Secondary, reported and not deciding: the whole post-period to September 2026 (taxi speeds from trip records suggest the speed gain shrank after mid-2025, so the chain's link 1 may not apply to it); overnight hours; the triple difference of peak minus overnight; comparison areas Manhattan 60th-110th Street, downtown Brooklyn with Long Island City, and the rest of the city; life-threatening (initial severity 1-3) and lower-priority incidents separately; total response time and dispatch time; the same estimator on Fire Incident Dispatch Data (8m42-w767); the placebo with a false start in January 2024. Known pre-trend: the 2024-against-2023 placebo is +1.6% (-0.8 to +4.0), so the zone's relative travel time was rising before the toll, which biases the estimate against an improvement. Against Manhattan north the placebo is +5.4%, so that comparison is not used for the verdict.

outcome.notes:
Registered endpoint: mean ambulance travel time to incidents in the zone during peak toll hours, relative to all other city ZIPs, 5 January to 31 August 2025 against 2023-24: -0.9% (-3.0 to +1.4), standard error 0.0113 on the log scale, 32 months. Composed prediction -1.8%; z_chain 0.66; z against the proportional alternative (-5.4%) 4.18; D_prop 17.0. The registered support condition is met: travel time did not fall in proportion to the rise in speed. z against no effect is -0.76 and the interval includes zero, so an improvement is not shown; the registration stated in advance that this test could not tell the chain from no effect. Whole post-period to September 2026 (secondary): -0.2% (-1.9 to +1.6). The within-zone control does not support a toll effect. In overnight hours, when the toll is a quarter of the peak toll, the zone's relative travel time fell more: -4.0% (-6.3 to -1.7) to August 2025 and -2.1% (-4.1 to -0.2) to September 2026. The triple difference (peak minus overnight) is +3.3% (+1.4 to +5.2), with a 2024 placebo of +0.2% (-1.6 to +2.0). Life-threatening incidents (initial severity 1 to 3): +5.2% (+2.6 to +7.9), but the 2024 placebo is +6.0% (+3.3 to +8.8), so the zone's relative travel time for these calls was already rising before the toll. Lower-priority incidents: -2.4% (-5.2 to +0.5). Total response time (call to arrival), all incidents: +0.8% (-4.5 to +6.5). Against Manhattan 60th-110th Street: +1.8% (-0.9 to +4.6) (2024 placebo +5.4% (+3.7 to +7.0)). Against downtown Brooklyn and Long Island City: +4.1% (+1.9 to +6.3) (placebo +5.5% (+1.6 to +9.5)). The 2024 placebo of the primary comparison is +1.6% (-0.8 to +4.0). Fire Incident Dispatch Data, same estimator: travel time -0.6% (-1.8 to +0.6) to August 2025 and +0.4% (-0.6 to +1.4) to September 2026. Levels: mean EMS travel time in the zone at peak hours was 558 s in 2023, 617 s in 2024, 661 s in 2025 and 712 s in January to September 2026; in the rest of the city 591, 647, 696 and 772 s. Travel time rose everywhere by about 7% a year, which is several times any effect of the toll. Lives (composition, not a test and not a result): the number of lives a year among cardiac arrests in the zone at peak hours depends on which measured change is used, and its sign is not determined. The registered peak estimate gives +0.3 (-0.7 to +2.0), the difference of peak and overnight hours gives -1.4 (-4.1 to -0.2), total response time gives -0.3 (-4.6 to +2.9), and no effect gives 0.0 (-1.4 to +1.3).

After the referee (13 Nov 2026): the verdict is changed from confirmed to unsettled under rule 8. The claim is a bridge with an endpoint test. Rule 8 measures discrimination against no effect: D = z_null^2 - z_chain^2 = 0.76^2 - 0.66^2 = 0.14, below 4. The registration computed D against a fall in proportion to speed (-5.4%), which gave 17.0, and named rules 1, 2 and 8 for the verdict. A registration cannot replace the D that rule 8 defines, so rule 8 applies as written and the endpoint's agreement with the composed prediction does not decide. The registration said in advance that the test could not tell the chain from no effect. Round 4 changed graph-triad-cold-asthma-absence in the same way (D = 3.0). The referee simulated the registered rule at the observed standard error: it returns confirmed with probability 0.80 if the toll had no effect, 0.87 if the chain is true, 0.50 if travel time rose by 1% and 0.01 if it fell in proportion to speed. Any estimate from -3.04% to +0.99% met the support condition. What the registered estimate shows is narrower than the first label: with calendar-month terms it excludes a fall in proportion to speed (z = 4.18). That exclusion does not survive a linear trend in the pre-period: the estimate is then -3.13% (-7.47 to +1.42) and z against the proportional fall is 1.03. The trend term was chosen after the data and decides nothing under rule 4. The registered estimator run at 17 false start dates in 2023-24 gives estimates from -0.2% to +4.9% with a standard deviation of 0.016 on the log scale, against the HAC standard error of 0.011, so the registered interval is too narrow. No improvement is shown: the interval includes zero and a rise of 1.4%. The overnight control argues against the toll as the cause of the peak estimate. In overnight hours, when the toll is a quarter of the peak toll, the zone's relative travel time fell by 4.0% (1.7 to 6.3), and peak minus overnight is +3.3% (+1.4 to +5.2), which is 4.0 combined standard errors from the composed prediction and 3.5 from zero. The overnight series is not stable before the toll either (false starts in 2023-24 give +4.4% to +12.1%), so it is not a clean control. Incidents in the zone fell by 3.0% relative to the rest of the city at peak (-4.3 to -1.7) and overnight (-5.4 to -0.5), which would free units at all hours. Link 2 is not stable: the registered exponent 0.317 is fitted mostly on the pandemic months; without March 2020 to June 2021 the slope is -0.62 (se 0.10), for 2022-24 it is -0.49 (se 0.12) and for 2023-24 it is -1.13 (se 0.40), which is a proportional response. The overnight ratio has nearly the same slope on taxi speed (-0.29, se 0.06) as the peak ratio, so the monthly co-movement is not specific to congested hours. The composed prediction is quoted as -1.68%, the median of the draws; the notes above give -1.8%, the mean of the log (-0.0178), and the z values use the mean. ZIP 10044 (Roosevelt Island) is in the zone list in analyses/congestion/common.py and is outside the toll zone; with the zone defined by dispatch areas M1 to M3, which exclude it, the peak estimate is -0.79% (-3.10 to +1.59). The script was fixed with the registration and is not corrected. Citywide, mean travel time rose from 559 s in 2023 to 607 s in 2024, 651 s in 2025 and 724 s in January to September 2026, and the share of incidents with no valid response time, which the analysis drops, rose from 4.4% to 6.3% in 2025 and 9.5% in 2026. The closure of Mount Sinai Beth Israel was registered as an alternative and has not been examined.
outcome.verdict_note: Unsettled under rule 8: the endpoint test cannot tell the composed chain from no effect (D = 0.14 against no effect; the registered rule returns confirmed with probability 0.80 if the toll did nothing). Peak ambulance travel time in the zone changed by -0.9% (-3.0 to +1.4) relative to the rest of the city, so no improvement is shown. A fall in proportion to the 5.7% rise in taxi speed is excluded by the registered estimate and not when a trend term is added. Overnight, when the toll is a quarter as large, the zone's relative travel time fell by 4.0%, which argues against the toll as the cause. The number of lives is not a result: between about -1.5 and +2 a year, sign not determined, depending on the comparison used.
outcome.lives_note: Not a result. Lives a year among cardiac arrests in the zone at peak hours, by the measured change used: registered peak estimate +0.3 (-0.7 to +2.0); peak minus overnight -1.4 (-4.1 to -0.2); total response time -0.3 (-4.6 to +2.9); composed prediction +0.7 (0.0 to +2.5). The count of 1,331 attended arrests includes the 43% pronounced dead on scene, the all-incident estimate is applied to calls whose own travel time rose by 5.2%, and odds ratios per minute are applied to about 3 seconds.

prediction.magnitude: Composed: -2.2% (-9.2 to +5.5). The registrant does not make a directional bet beyond the composition. Knowing the v1 result, the registrant expects the v2 estimate to lie near zero and the verdict to be unsettled under rule 8.
prediction.support_if: Verdict bridged if, in the primary estimate and at both bias bounds (B_up and B_down below): |z_chain| < 1.96, D = z_null^2 - z_chain^2 >= 4 (PRECEDENCE rule 8), and the 2024 placebo interval includes zero. z_chain = (b - mean_log_composed) / sqrt(se_b^2 + sd_log_composed^2); z_null = b / se_b; b is the zone-by-2025 coefficient on the log scale.
prediction.refute_if: Verdict contested if |z_chain| >= 1.96 with the same sign in the primary estimate and at both bias bounds, and the 2024 placebo interval includes zero. This would say the endpoint is incompatible with the composed chain, whatever its distance from zero.
prediction.unsettled_if: Any other case: compatible with the chain but D < 4 at any of the three points; incompatible at one point but not at all three; or the 2024 placebo interval excludes zero.
prediction.no_test_if: The crash rows cannot be fetched, or Manhattan north of 60th St has fewer than 1,000 geocoded injury crashes in any year 2022-2025.

pre_data_power.note: Computed before data from the composed prediction alone. The bridged condition can be met only by an observed change of roughly -6% to -13%, and its probability is low even if the chain is true. An unsettled verdict is the expected result. The test can still refute the chain.

prediction.stance: Report z_chain and z_null side by side, at the primary estimate and at both bias bounds. The dashboard stance is concord.claims.endpoint_stance(z_chain, z_null) at the primary estimate (rules 7 and 8).

claims.plan: Endpoint data: NYPD Motor Vehicle Collisions - Crashes (h9gi-nx95), queried through concord/socrata.py so that each source record keeps rowsUpdatedAt, the SoQL and the fetch time. Q1 (rows): collision_id, crash_date, latitude, longitude, borough, on_street_name, cross_street_name, off_street_name, number_of_persons_injured, number_of_persons_killed, where crash_date 2022-01-01 to 2026-08-31 and (persons injured > 0 or persons killed > 0) and latitude 40.68-40.89 and longitude -74.03 to -73.90, paged by collision_id. Q2 (coverage by record class, citywide, injury crashes): by year 2022-2025 and class, count and count without coordinates (latitude null or 0). Classes: intersection (on_street_name and cross_street_name both present), address (off_street_name present, not intersection), other. Q3 (coverage by month, citywide, injury crashes): count and count without coordinates by month, 2022-2025. Q2 and Q3 have no area split. Areas. Zone: the largest polygon of the MTA CBD geofence (srxy-5nxn, the cached copy fetched 12 Nov 16:01, as in v1). Manhattan: the union of UHF42 neighbourhoods 301-310 (data/raw/ehdp/UHF42.geojson) buffered by 0.0005 degrees, excluding points inside any non-Manhattan UHF polygon. North of 60th: Manhattan points outside every geofence polygon and north of 60th Street, using the avenue-axis projection in analyses/mobility/crz_air.py (south_of_60th). Primary comparison area: all of Manhattan north of 60th St. Secondary comparison area: Manhattan from 60th to 96th St (the projection value at 5th Ave and 96th St), a stand-in for the MTA's CBD Adjacent area, whose boundary is not published. Injury crash = persons injured > 0 or persons killed > 0. Primary model, unchanged from v1 apart from the comparison area: OLS of log monthly injury crashes on area, calendar month, year and zone x post (post from January 2025), HAC standard errors with 3 lags, 2022-01 to 2025-12, 96 area-months. Placebo: false start January 2024 on 2022-2024. Bias bounds. Let w be the zone's share of geocoded injury crashes in zone plus north area in 2022-2024 (from Q1), D_new the citywide fall in the share of injury crashes without coordinates from 2022-2024 pooled to 2025 (from Q2 totals), and e the rise in the share without coordinates among injury crashes coded MANHATTAN, 2022-2024 pooled to 2025 (from the cached v1 counts: 441 of 13,893 to 266 of 6,060, 1.22 points). Assumptions on the missing records: B0, missing records fall in zone and north area in proportion to geocoded ones (bias 0; the primary estimate). B1, records newly geocoded in 2025 are twice as frequent per crash in the zone as in the north area: r_N = D_new/(1+w), r_Z = 2 r_N, bias = log(1+r_Z) - log(1+r_N). B2, twice as frequent in the north area: r_Z = D_new/(2-w), r_N = 2 r_Z, same formula. B3, the rise e in Manhattan-coded records without coordinates falls wholly in the zone: bias = log(1 - e/w). B4, wholly in the north area: bias = -log(1 - e/(1-w)). Corrected estimate = b - bias, with se_b unchanged. B_up = B2 and B3 together (the largest upward correction); B_down = B1 and B4 together (the largest downward correction). Reported, not deciding: the extreme case in which every newly geocoded Manhattan record falls in one area (r_Z = D_new/w, r_N = 0, and the reverse). Stable-coverage restriction (secondary, not deciding). Records: a class from Q2 is stable if its share with coordinates varies by less than 2 percentage points across 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025; the primary model is re-run on Q1 rows of the stable classes only. If no class is stable, this analysis is not run and that is reported. Months: pre-period months whose citywide coverage (Q3) is within 2 points of the 2025 mean coverage; if at least 12 such months exist, the primary model is re-run with only those pre-period months; otherwise it is not run and that is reported. Other secondary results, reported and not deciding: the secondary comparison area; Poisson GLM with area x calendar month terms (quasi-Poisson scale); the composed prediction with correlated links; the v1 composed prediction (-0.4%) against the v2 endpoint; January-August 2026 added as a second post year. Outcome: claims/outcomes/bridge-crz-injury-crashes-v2.json with the Q1-Q3 source records; figure in figures/bridges/ in the style of the v1 figure. The v1 outcome is then revised through concord.claims.revise, keeping its history.
alternatives: Differential geocoding between the zone and the north area (bounded by B1-B4).
Spillover: traffic diverted from the zone onto streets north of 60th St would raise crashes there and make the zone look better; the composition does not model the comparison area's volume.
Pre-existing differential trend between the zone and the north area (2024 placebo).
Other 2025 changes that differ between lower and upper Manhattan (street redesigns, enforcement, the citywide daylighting work).
No effect of pricing on injury crashes, which the composed prediction lies close to (rule 8).

outcome.prediction_scored: uninformative. The registered test cannot decide: the 2024 placebo, +15.2% (+4.8 to +26.6), excludes zero, so the zone and Manhattan north of 60th St were already moving apart before pricing, and under the registered rule the verdict is unsettled whatever the 2025 estimate. The 2025 estimate, +4.5% (-2.7 to +12.2), lies about as far from the composed -2.2% (z_chain 1.25) as from no effect (z_null 1.21); D = -0.11, far below the 4 that rule 8 requires. At the upward bias bound it is +11.6% (+3.9 to +19.8), incompatible with the chain (z_chain 2.50); at the downward bound it is -2.0% (-8.8 to +5.2). The registrant expected an unsettled verdict; the reason is the pre-trend more than the lack of discrimination.
outcome.settle: Two things would settle it. First, the crash records without coordinates in 2022-2024 (about 3,000 injury crashes a year with no borough and no coordinates) would need to be geocoded from their street names, so that the zone, the rest of Manhattan and the rest of the city are counted the same way in every year; this removes the bias bounds. Second, the 2024 divergence between the zone and upper Manhattan needs an explanation (a fall in injury crashes north of 60th St in 2024, from 3,181 to 2,795, while the zone rose slightly) before any comparison area can be trusted. Even then, a composed prediction of about -2% cannot be told from zero with monthly area counts; segment-level speeds, volumes and crashes inside the zone would test the two link terms separately.

Annual geocoded injury crashes (zone / Manhattan north of 60th St): 2022 2,581 / 2,955, 2023 2,710 / 3,181, 2024 2,763 / 2,795, 2025 2,726 / 2,891; January-August 2026 1,837 / 1,920. Bias bound inputs: the zone's share of geocoded injury crashes in the two areas, 2022-2024, w = 0.474; citywide share of injury crashes without coordinates 9.07% (2022-24) and 2.60% (2025), a fall of 6.47 points; rise among Manhattan-coded injury crashes 1.22 points. Estimates by assumption: B0: +4.5%, z_chain +1.25, z_null +1.21, D -0.11 (unsettled). B1: +0.3%, z_chain +0.47, z_null +0.08, D -0.21 (unsettled). B2: +8.7%, z_chain +2.01, z_null +2.30, D 1.26 (contested_above). B3: +7.2%, z_chain +1.75, z_null +1.92, D 0.64 (unsettled). B4: +2.1%, z_chain +0.81, z_null +0.56, D -0.33 (unsettled). B_up: +11.6%, z_chain +2.50, z_null +3.02, D 2.83 (contested_above). B_down: -2.0%, z_chain +0.02, z_null -0.57, D 0.32 (unsettled). Reported, not deciding: if every newly geocoded Manhattan record fell in the zone the estimate would be -8.1%, and if every one fell north of 60th St it would be +17.3%. Secondary results (registered, not deciding): zone against the 60th-96th St band +5.0% (-2.5 to +13.1), with its own 2024 placebo +14.8% (+4.1 to +26.5); Poisson GLM with area-by-month terms +4.6% (-3.6 to +13.4); with January-August 2026 added +5.3% (-0.9 to +11.9) (z_chain 1.50, z_null 1.66); against the correlated composition z_chain 1.34; against the v1 composition (-0.4%) z_chain 0.84. Stable-coverage restrictions: not run: no class has coverage varying by less than 2 points across 2022-2025. Coverage of injury crashes by record class, 2022 to 2025: intersection records 90.1% / 93.3% / 95.0% / 98.9%, address records 93.4% / 95.7% / 95.3% / 91.5%, other records 85.2% / 86.7% / 77.4% / 99.0%. Month restriction: not run: 2 pre-period months within 2 points of the 2025 mean coverage (12 needed) (2025 mean coverage 97.4%; the months within 2 points are 2024-11-01, 2024-12-01). Monthly coverage (share of injury crashes with coordinates, citywide) was 82 to 95 percent from January 2022 to October 2024, with a dip to 82-89 percent from July to October 2024, and 96.5 to 98.0 percent in every month from November 2024 on. The change in geocoding came in November 2024, two months before pricing. Exploratory, not registered: the July-October 2024 dip falls inside the placebo's post period, and if it removed more records north of 60th St than in the zone it would produce part of the placebo difference. The MTA does not publish the boundary of its CBD Adjacent area, so the speed link of the composition (CBD vs CBD Adjacent, +4.2%) is only a stand-in for the contrast with Manhattan north of 60th St. Data seen before registration are listed in the registration (data_seen_before_registration). The registration was committed in ce3586a and pushed to GitHub at about 00:32 UTC on 13 November 2026; the crash queries for v2 were made from 00:35 UTC.

After the referee (13 Nov 2026): the referee reproduced the deciding numbers and every variant leaves the verdict unsettled. The two areas are not the same kind of road network: the north area includes limited-access highways that hold 12% to 14% of its injury crashes, against almost none in the zone; without them the estimate is +6.1% (-0.8 to +13.5) and the placebo +16.4%. The way crash locations are recorded changed, and differently in the two areas: records with an on-street name only (about 750 a year in the north area in 2022 and 2023) are gone by 2025, and the 2024 placebo difference sits in that class. The registration treated geocoding as a matter of coverage only. The estimate depends on the pre-period: -4.9% against 2024 alone, +9.5% against 2022-2023 alone. Recovering records without coordinates by matching street names gives +4.1% (-3.2 to +12.0), so missing coordinates do not explain the 2024 divergence. The verdict 'bridged' could not have been reached: the rule required it at three bias points that are 0.13 apart on the log scale, and the window in which it holds at one point is 0.04 wide. The registration attributes PMID 23411678 to Teschke et al. 2012; it is Harris et al., Injury Prevention 2013, and its odds ratio applies to intersections only. There is no prereg branch for this claim, so the evidence that it was public before the query is weaker than for claims that have one.

claims.statement: Composed from faster speeds (mob-crz-traffic) and fewer vehicles in the Congestion Relief Zone, with the research link between speed, volume and crashes (bridge-crz-crash-link), the predicted change in injury crashes in the zone relative to the rest of the city in 2025 against 2022-2024 is the endpoint observed in the NYPD crash records.

graph_evidence.summary: Rothman et al. 2016 (Toronto, child pedestrian-motor vehicle collisions): higher speed roads IRR 1.27 (1.13 to 1.44). Abstract read.
Moped and scooter crashes: driving speeds above 20 mph OR 2.02 (1.73 to 2.36) for severe or lethal injury. Abstract read.
Teschke et al. 2012 (Toronto and Vancouver cyclists, case-crossover): motor vehicle speeds below 30 km/h adjusted OR 0.52 (0.29 to 0.92) for injury. Abstract read.

No finding in the graph links traffic volume, vehicle-miles or congestion to crashes or injuries. The graph holds no power-model (Nilsson, Elvik) findings and no road-pricing findings (see docs/mobility.md).

literature.citation: Elvik R (2009). The Power Model of the relationship between speed and road safety: update and new analyses. TOI Report 1034/2009, Oslo.
literature.finding: Exponents for urban and residential roads: 1.2 for injury accidents, 1.4 for injured persons, 2.6 for fatal accidents, 3.0 for persons killed (rural: 1.6, 2.2, 4.1, 4.6). The urban estimates rest on few studies (summary by ONISR, 14 May 2014).

literature.citation: Nilsson G (2004). Traffic safety dimensions and the Power Model to describe the effect of speed on safety. Lund Bulletin 221.
literature.finding: Exponent 2 for injury accidents, 3 for fatal and serious, 4 for fatal accidents.

literature.citation: Elvik R (2013). A re-parameterisation of the Power Model of the relationship between the speed of traffic and the number of accidents and accident victims. Accident Analysis and Prevention 50:854-860.
literature.finding: Exponential form; the effective exponent depends on the initial speed and is lower at low speeds.

literature.citation: Green CP, Heywood JS, Navarro M (2016). Traffic accidents and the London congestion charge. Journal of Public Economics 133:11-22.
literature.finding: London's charge (2003), with network speeds of 8.6 mph before it and vehicle-km in the zone down about 12 to 34 percent, reduced accidents in the zone by roughly 38 to 40 percent and serious-and-fatal accidents by 46 a year, against 20 British cities. The authors note that higher speeds could raise severity in theory; they found declines in serious and fatal accidents.

composed_prediction.scale: percent change in monthly injury crashes, zone vs rest of city, 2025 vs 2022-2024

prediction.magnitude: Composed: -0.4% (-8.2 to +8.7). The speed term (+6.7%) and the volume term (-6.7%) nearly cancel. The registrant's directional bet is negative, between -2% and -15%. Reasons: (1) the power model was fitted to speed changes on roads that are not congested, and Elvik (2013) finds lower effective exponents at low initial speeds, so the speed term is probably overstated at 8 to 9 mph; (2) London's charge, with the same pre-charge network speed (8.6 mph), reduced accidents far more than its volume change alone predicts; (3) the registrant recalls, without having checked them, statements by the MTA and the city in 2025 that traffic injuries in the zone fell. Persons killed: composed +7% (-4 to +23), too few deaths in the zone to test.
prediction.support_if: Endpoint compatible with the chain: with D = log(observed ratio) - mean_log(composed) and SE = sqrt(se_observed^2 + sd_log(composed)^2), |D| < 1.96 SE, and the 2024 placebo interval includes zero. Verdict confirmed.
prediction.refute_if: |D| >= 1.96 SE with the 2024 placebo interval including zero: the endpoint is incompatible with the composed chain. Verdict contested.
prediction.unsettled_if: The 2024 placebo (false start January 2024, data 2022-2024) has an interval that excludes zero, so the zone had a pre-existing differential trend that the design cannot separate.
prediction.directional_bet: Scored separately in prediction_scored: hit if the observed interval lies below zero, miss if above zero, partial otherwise.

claims.plan: Endpoint: NYPD Motor Vehicle Collisions - Crashes (h9gi-nx95), crash_date 2022-01-01 to 2025-12-31. Zone: the largest polygon of the MTA CBD geofence (data.ny.gov srxy-5nxn), which is the tolled zone without the FDR Drive and West Side Highway strips (the other six polygons). Crash rows with coordinates inside the bounding box lat 40.69-40.78, lon -74.03 to -73.95 are fetched and assigned by point in polygon; citywide monthly totals are fetched for crashes with valid coordinates (lat 40.45-40.95, lon -74.30 to -73.65); rest of city = city minus zone. Injury crash = persons injured > 0 or persons killed > 0. Model as in mob-crz-traffic: OLS of log monthly count on area, calendar month, year and zone x post (post from January 2025), HAC standard errors with 3 lags, 96 area-months. Placebo: false start January 2024 on 2022-2024. Secondary, reported but not deciding: Poisson GLM of the same; persons injured; pedestrians plus cyclists injured; all crashes; persons killed (Poisson, zone vs rest); zone including the excluded highway polygons; January-August 2026 added as a second post year.
alternatives: Pre-existing differential trend in the zone (tested by the 2024 placebo).
Changes in crash reporting or geocoding that differ between Manhattan and the rest of the city (share of crashes without coordinates is reported by year).
Changes in pedestrian and cyclist volumes in the zone after pricing (more walking and cycling would raise exposure).
Spillover of traffic to streets just outside the zone, which would bias the rest-of-city comparison only slightly because the rest of the city is large.
Other 2025 changes specific to Manhattan below 60th Street (enforcement, street redesigns, the 2025 citywide speed-limit and daylighting work).

If the missing records are distributed like the geocoded ones within each borough, this biases the zone-vs-rest estimate downward by roughly 2 to 3 points, which would move it to about +4 percent, still compatible with the composed prediction. Stance: rule 5 gives the weakest link's stance (mob-crz-traffic; the research link has none). The endpoint's own stance against the registered negative direction is kept as endpoint_stance. A compatible endpoint supports the chain as a whole; it does not show that each link is right, since a larger speed exponent and a larger volume elasticity would compose to the same result.

After the bridge referee: the composed prediction (-0.4%) is near zero because the speed and volume terms cancel, so the endpoint (z 0.32 from the chain, 0.43 from no effect) cannot separate the chain from no effect; a contentless chain would have passed with probability above 0.99. Re-estimating against a comparison area that avoids the geocoding change (Manhattan north of 60th St) is exploratory now that the endpoint has been seen, and is listed as research needed.

After the re-analysis (bridge-crz-injury-crashes-v2, registered and pushed to GitHub before its data were queried): against Manhattan north of 60th St, which shares the zone's geocoding regime, injury crashes in the zone changed by +4.5% (-2.7 to +12.2) in 2025, with z 1.25 from the v2 composed prediction (-2.2%) and z 1.21 from no effect. Under the registered bias bounds for the geocoding change the v2 estimate ranges from -2.0% to +11.6%. Neither comparison area gives a test that separates the chain from no effect. The v1 verdict stays unsettled. The geocoding bias in v1 (zone against the rest of the city) is not resolved by v2: v2 changes the comparison area and so cannot correct the v1 estimate.

outcome.notes:
Sample: 174 taxi zones in the Bronx, Brooklyn, Queens and Staten Island (175 met the population rule; Rikers Island dropped because it has no household income). In 2024 TLC recorded 239.5 million app pickups, 40.6 million yellow taxi pickups and 0.66 million green taxi pickups (c5iv-bn4s). The median zone outside Manhattan had 17.2 app pickups per resident and a population-weighted distance of 0.61 km to a station. Registered sensitivities: unadjusted -0.40 (-0.54 to -0.26); borough fixed effects -0.17 (-0.26 to -0.08); drop-offs -0.31 (-0.39 to -0.24); all boroughs -0.34 (-0.41 to -0.27); yellow and green taxis -0.65 (-0.88 to -0.42). Adding the share of households with no vehicle reverses the sign: +0.14 (+0.04 to +0.25), with each point of no-vehicle share adding 2.8% (log points x 100) to pickups per resident. Distance and no-vehicle share are correlated at -0.76 across zones, so this model rests on the zones where the two diverge. Within boroughs: Bronx -0.08 (-0.20 to +0.04), Brooklyn -0.16 (-0.40 to +0.09), Queens -0.19 (-0.32 to -0.06), Staten Island +0.18 (+0.00 to +0.35). A first run treated Census annotation codes (negative income values) as numbers; they are now set to missing, which changed the primary estimate from -0.29 to -0.30 and restored 11 zones.

After the referee: 'contested' follows the registered rule, but it contradicts the registrant's prediction, not the published research. The one peer-reviewed source (Barajas and Brown 2021) also finds more ride-hail use near transit, and the city data agree with it. The stance is therefore drawn against the research direction. The reversal after adding car-free households is not decisive: car ownership is plausibly a mediator, the reversed estimate is +0.09 with an interval including zero when Staten Island is dropped, and it was registered as report-only.

stance.note: Sign taken against the research direction (Barajas and Brown 2021), not the registrant's prediction.

outcome.notes: Method: 48 NB jobs drawn at random (seed 20261112) from jobs with a first NB permit in 2018-2020 (all in the legacy system, since DOB NOW NB filings begin in 2021). NAIP New York flights of Aug-Sep 2017 (1.0 m) and Jul-Oct 2022 (0.6 m) were resampled to 0.5 m. I judged each pair on sheets that showed only an index number, and committed the judgements (commit 7755daf) before joining CO status. Of the 5 sampled jobs with no CO in November 2026, three show a new building by 2022, one is unclear and one unchanged. Graph evidence check (12 Nov 2026, after the coordinator's audit): association aFGrNWb1i5 (vacant housing demolitions and 'change in crime', PMID 36228876), cited in the registration, is NOT in the Dataverse v2.1 CSV. The abstract (Kvik et al., Prev Med 2022) shows it is mis-extracted: the -0.068 (95% CI -0.119 to -0.018) is the change in total emergency-department visits per 1,000 people, and demolitions showed no significant change in crime. claims.plan: Data: Storefronts Reported Vacant or Not (92iy-9c3n). Script analyses/congestion/vacancy.py, written and run in design mode (years to 2024) before registration; design output data/derived/congestion/vacancy_design.json. Each reporting year gives vacant_on_12_31 for that 31 December; only the main annual filing (the filing_due_date with most rows) is used; rows answering neither YES nor NO are dropped. Areas by ZIP (analyses/congestion/common.py): zone = Manhattan south of 60th Street (about 15,100 storefronts in 2024, 12.3% vacant); comparison = all other city ZIPs (about 47,000, 7.3% vacant). Estimator: change in the vacancy share 2024 to 2025 in the zone minus the same change outside, in points. Interval: bootstrap over tax lots within each group, 2,000 draws, seed 20261113, percentiles. Can the test fail? The bootstrap se was 0.34 to 0.44 points in each earlier year and the DiD itself moved between -1.40 and -0.45 over 2022-24 (sd 0.49), so the uncertainty about the no-toll value is about 0.6 points around -0.5. A toll effect of +1.2 points (about 180 more vacant storefronts, a tenth more than now) would put the estimate near +0.7, two such standard errors from the no-effect expectation (D about 4); it would miss support_if (point estimate above +0.5, upper bound near +1.4) and would meet refute_if about half the time. A rise smaller than 1.2 points cannot be told from the trend, and the outcome will say so. Verdict by PRECEDENCE rules 1 and 2. Secondary, not deciding: the same DiD against Manhattan 60th-110th Street, against downtown Brooklyn with Long Island City, and against the rest of the city; the 2025 DiD minus the mean of the 2022-24 DiDs (a trend-adjusted figure). Limits known in advance: there is one observation after the toll; leases turn over slowly, so a year may be too soon; filings are by owners and coverage changed after 2020 (17,000 zone storefronts then, 15,100 now).
alternatives: Continued recovery of Manhattan retail from the pandemic peak in vacancy, which lowers zone vacancy whatever the toll does.
Office attendance and tourism in the zone, which changed in the same period.
Changes in which owners file, or in how vacancy is reported.
Commercial rents adjusting instead of vacancy.

No value of vacant_on_12_31 for reporting year 2025 or 2026 has been queried or seen. The registrant recalls press statements by the Governor's office in 2025-26 that retail activity in the zone rose, and none about the storefront registry.

outcome.notes:
Vacancy in the zone was 12.33% of 15083 storefronts on 31 December 2024 and 12.50% of 15442 on 31 December 2025, a change of +0.18 points. Outside the zone it changed by +0.65 points. The difference is -0.47 (-1.08 to +0.17) points; both registered conditions for support are met (estimate at most +0.5, upper bound below +1.2). The same difference was -0.45 in 2024, the one earlier year under the present filing structure, so the 2025 value equals the 2024 value. The values for 2022 and 2023 (-0.74 and -1.40) are not used as a trend, for the reason given in the referee note below. Vacancy rose slightly in the zone and rose more elsewhere. Against Manhattan 60th-110th Street: -0.23 (-1.33 to +0.88). Against downtown Brooklyn and Long Island City: +1.09 (-0.60 to +2.85) (about 2,100 storefronts; vacancy there fell). Against the rest of the city: -0.56 (-1.18 to +0.08). The test excludes a rise of 1.2 points (about 180 storefronts) in the zone's vacancy relative to the whole rest of the city, counting sampling error only. It cannot detect a smaller rise, and one year may be too soon for leases to show an effect.

After the referee (13 Nov 2026): the verdict stays confirmed under rule 1. Both registered support conditions are met on the registered comparison, and they remain met in the referee's four variants: with the February filing added, -0.76 (-1.70 to +0.16); on tax lots present in both years, -0.36 (-0.95 to +0.25); with a bootstrap over ZIP codes, -0.47 (-1.19 to +0.24); without ZIP 10044 (Roosevelt Island, which is in the zone list and outside the toll zone), -0.46. The label covers less than its wording suggests, and the verdict_note now says what it covers. The negative difference comes from a rise elsewhere: zone vacancy rose by 0.18 points and vacancy outside rose by 0.65. Against downtown Brooklyn and Long Island City, where vacancy fell by 0.91 points, the zone did worse by 1.09 points (-0.60 to +2.85), an interval that includes zero and twice the threshold; that area has four ZIPs and about 2,100 storefronts. The registered interval covers the sampling of tax lots only. With the year-to-year standard deviation of the difference (0.48, from three values) added, the upper bound against zero is +0.67, and against the mean of 2022-24 the 2025 value is +0.39 with a standard error of 0.64 and an upper bound of +1.66, which does not exclude 1.2. The registry was restructured between reporting years '2022 and 2023' and 2023: one filing due in August became a main filing due in June and a separate February filing in which every row is vacant, and the coding of business activity changed. The 2023 difference of -1.40 compares a filing under the old structure with one under the new; with the February rows added it is +1.14. Only 2024 (-0.45) is a clean pre-toll year, so the registration's expectation of about -0.5 without a toll rests on one year, and the mean of three earlier years (-0.86) is withdrawn from the notes. Between the filings for 31 December 2020 and 2021 the registry lost 18% of its rows outside the zone and 9% inside. The threshold of 1.2 points is the resolution of the test: the plan chose it as the effect at which the design reaches a discrimination of about 4, before the 2025 values were seen. It is not an effect size from the retail literature. The two papers in the registration (London and Stockholm) concern retail sales, were cited from memory, have not been checked against their texts, and supply no number to the test. Within the zone the change runs from -4.0 points (ZIP 10038) to +2.1 (10036) among ZIPs with 300 or more storefronts. Commercial leases commonly run five to ten years, so one filing after the toll cannot tell no effect from a delayed one.
outcome.verdict_note: Confirmed on the registered comparison only. Zone vacancy itself rose by 0.2 points in the first year, and vacancy in the rest of the city rose by 0.65. A rise of 1.2 points relative to the whole rest of the city is ruled out, with sampling error only, and nothing smaller is. It is not excluded against the zone's earlier trend (upper bound +1.66) or against downtown Brooklyn and Long Island City (upper bound +2.85). The 2023 pre-trend value spans a change in the registry's filing, so 2024 is the only clean pre-toll year. The 1.2 threshold is the resolution of the test, and the two cited papers are unverified. Sales, rents and effects that take more than one lease cycle are not tested.
outcome.literature_note: The two citations in the registration (Quddus, Carmel and Bell 2007; Daunfeldt, Rudholm and Ramme 2009) were written from memory and have not been checked against the papers. Nothing in the test depends on them.

critique.answer: accepted; verdict kept under rule 1 with a verdict_note; the mean of three earlier years withdrawn; the two citations marked unverified
