claims.plan: Script analyses/health_gaps/ems_model.py and fetch analyses/health_gaps/ems_fetch.py, committed in 6278c85 before this registration and before the daily data are fetched. Data: NYC Open Data 76xm-jjuj, daily citywide aggregates 2017-01-01 to the last complete month, excluding 2020-03-01 to 2020-06-30. Outcome: log daily mean dispatch_response_seconds_qy (incident creation to first unit assigned) among incidents with valid dispatch time. Exposure: log daily mean of incident_close_datetime minus first_hosp_arrival_datetime among transported incidents (disposition 82), trimmed to 0-4 h and to close and arrival in the same calendar month. Controls: log daily incident count, day-of-week dummies, year-month fixed effects (which absorb staffing, fleet and definition changes that move slowly). OLS, Newey-West standard errors with 7 lags. No resampling and no seed. Secondary, not deciding: severity 1-3 and 4-8 separately; previous-day turnaround; annual means; attribution of the 2019-2025 change. A technical test of the SoQL date arithmetic was run on one hour of 3 January 2017 (counts of 98 rows and three histogram bins) before registration.
alternatives: Common daily shock: heat, flu or other surges crowd emergency departments and raise ambulance demand together, beyond what the call count captures; the previous-day model and the severity split partly separate this.
Reverse direction: when the system is busy crews may shorten time at hospital, which would bias the elasticity down.
Staffing: fewer ambulance tours lengthen waits; year-month effects absorb slow change but not day-to-day staffing gaps.
Data artefact: incident close may be recorded late on busy days, inflating measured turnaround when waits are long.

outcome.notes: Primary elasticity 4.55 (3.21 to 5.88); call-count elasticity 5.28 (4.95 to 5.61). Previous-day turnaround 1.06 (0.13 to 1.99). Life-threatening calls (severity 1-3) 2.11 (0.95 to 3.27); other calls 4.94 (3.53 to 6.35). Annual means (all calls; wait = creation to first assignment, travel, time at hospital, seconds; calls per day): 2019 wait 100, travel 536, hospital 2168, calls 4201; 2022 101, 516, 2291, 4338; 2025 329, 649, 2437, 4417; 2026 to September 630, 722, 2517, 4412. From 2019 to 2025 log mean wait rose by 1.19 (a factor of 3.3); hospital time rose 12% and calls 5%. Applied to the annual changes, the same-day elasticities attribute 0.53 log points to hospital time and 0.27 to calls, about two thirds of the rise; with the previous-day elasticity hospital time accounts for 0.12. This extrapolation from daily variation to the trend is secondary and exploratory in strength. In 2026 wait almost doubled again while hospital time rose 3% and calls did not rise; the MMR attributes the year to a 5% fall in ambulance in-service hours (8,572 to 8,109 a day) and 11 hospital ambulances leaving the 911 system. Units in service are not in the open data, so staffing could not enter the model; year-month effects absorb it only as slow change. The MMR annual figures were read before registration; the daily data were not.
outcome.notes_referee: Referee reproduced 4.54 (3.20 to 5.88); year-week FE 3.49 (2.22 to 4.75). Verdict stands under rule 1. Placebo fails: next-day turnaround predicts today's wait at 2.40 (1.20 to 3.60); with year-week FE lag and lead near zero; afternoon turnaround predicts same morning's wait. Not evidence that offload time is a lever.

D = change in log mean EMS travel; pace term = EMS-incident-weighted (post-period area-hour shares) change in log taxi hours per mile by area and hour. S1 = pace term / D (deciding). S = beta x pace term / D with beta and its se from the deciding T1 fit (x only, sev hi) is reported. Interval: day-block bootstrap within each period, 400 draws, then 20,000 draws combining beta, seed 20261113. Discrimination: the predicted S1 near 0.2 is far from 0.5 if the bootstrap half-width is below 0.15, which a 9-month comparison with about 60,000 incidents a period gives. Secondary: other periods (2019 vs 2025), all severities, the overnight hours 01-05 as a check (traffic is light, so a rise there is distance or supply).
alternatives: Fewer ambulance unit-hours (MMR: in-service hours per day 8,891 in FY22 to 8,109 in FY26), so the nearest free unit is farther away (a distance effect, not traffic)

claims.plan: Script analyses/health_gaps/food_access.py, committed in d787695 before this registration and before any outcome is read; it is the procedure (no resampling, no seed). Unit: NYC ZCTAs (2020) assigned to a NYC county by largest land overlap, adult population >= 5,000. Outcome: SPARCS adult PQIs by patient ZIP (health.data.ny.gov 5q8c-d6xq), PQI 01, 03, 14, 16, three latest years, log(sum observed / sum expected). Exposure: NY State Retail Food Stores (data.ny.gov 9a8c-vfzj), type A, >= 6,000 sq ft, per 10,000 residents, log2 with 0.5 added to counts. Covariates: log2 residential density (ACS 2019-23 population / 2020 Gazetteer land area), percent poor, log2 median household income, median age. Weighted least squares by population, HC3. Secondaries listed in the script are reported and do not decide. The store list is the current one (October 2026) and the outcome years are earlier, so stores that closed or opened in between add noise. FRESH store locations are not published; only FRESH zoning boundaries (cgn7-aehz) are, and they are not used.
alternatives: Reverse placement: supermarket chains locate by purchasing power, so supply follows income and density rather than causing health; adjustment for income and density addresses this only in part.
ZIP boundaries: people shop outside their ZIP; a per-resident count within the ZIP misstates access near boundaries and biases towards the null.
Admissions measure access to and quality of primary care as well as disease prevalence.
Residual confounding by race and ethnicity, which predict diabetes and store placement; reported as a secondary model.

Secondary models: adding percent Black and percent Hispanic 0.993 (0.943 to 1.046); adding households without a car 0.987 (0.931 to 1.047); stores of 10,000 sq ft or more 0.978 (0.940 to 1.017); all retail food stores 0.994 (0.923 to 1.070). Chicken-and-egg check: supermarkets per km2 alone give 0.951 (0.905 to 0.999); adding log residential density gives 0.895 (0.822 to 0.975), which is algebraically the per-resident unadjusted estimate, so density explains the per-area pattern and per-resident supply then carries the crude association; that association disappears when poverty and income are added. In the primary model a 10-point rise in poverty goes with 1.22 (1.09 to 1.35) times the admission ratio; R2 0.67. Deviation from the committed script, before any outcome was read: the Census API now requires a key, so the same ACS 2019-2023 variables were read from the Census table-based summary files; the county filter for the store list was corrected to upper case after the first query returned no rows. Stores are counted by their address ZIP from the current list (October 2026), so openings and closings after 2023 add noise; two ZCTAs have no supermarket. Admissions measure access to primary care as well as disease. The cross-section cannot show what a new store would do; it shows that in New York the places with fewer supermarkets per resident do not have more diabetes admissions than their income and density predict.
outcome.notes_referee: Referee reproduced 0.995 (0.946 to 1.046); clustered and spatial-error models still meet support_if; Moran's I 0.35; lower bound 0.88 unweighted or with 2.5 km supply. Outcome tracks poverty and access to care: pneumonia and UTI admissions show the same crude gradient (0.885).

claims.plan:
WHAT WAS SEEN BEFORE REGISTRATION. Published text only: the AALDEF report, the AAF 2021 and 2025 briefs (text read, quotes above). Lookup and boundary tables, with no population values read: DCP 2010 census-tract to NTA equivalency 8ius-dhrr (rowsUpdatedAt 2015-02-17), Census Gazetteer internal points for 2010 and 2020 tracts (the 2010 file also carries a POP10 column, which was not printed or used), Census 2010-to-2020 tract relationship file tab20_tract20_tract10_natl.txt (downloaded, not opened beyond its header), NYC centerline inkn-q76z (street geometry for 8 AVE in Brooklyn and MAIN ST/ROOSEVELT AVE in Queens), and Census API variable and geography listings. The repository holds no earlier query of Census population counts, of any NYC Open Data population table, or of any dataset on this subject (checked: data/cache/socrata, analyses/, claims/). The scouting note (notes/scouting/enclave-shift.md) read no outcome values. The tract sets below are fixed by data/derived/further/chinatown_sets.json (sha256 228e965434863f646c548c643a15549ae058475a671e546f02f37bd529c4ce82), written by analyses/further/chinatown_sets.py, and are part of this registration.
UNITS AND SETS (2010 census tracts, 11-digit GEOID without the leading 36, county code first). Chinatown B1 (primary): all 2010 tracts of NTAs MN27 Chinatown and MN28 Lower East Side, 23 tracts: 061000201 061000202 061000600 061000800 061001001 061001002 061001200 061001401 061001402 061001600 061001800 061002000 061002201 061002202 061002400 061002500 061002601 061002602 061002700 061002800 061002900 061003001 061003601. B2: MN27 only, 8 tracts. B3: MN27, MN28 and MN22 East Village, 30 tracts. B1 is primary because the AALDEF boundary runs from the City Hall courthouse area to Houston Street and the East River and (in words) up the NYCHA riverfront to East 14th Street; B1 is the closest NTA union and B3 brackets it from above. Sunset Park: all 31 tracts of NTAs BK32 Sunset Park West and BK34 Sunset Park East. Core (8 tracts) = tracts whose Gazetteer internal point is within 400 m of a centreline segment of 8 AVE in Brooklyn between 40.620 and 40.648 N (approximately 40th to 65th Street): 047009000 047009200 047009400 047010400 047010600 047010800 047011800 047012000. Periphery = the other 23 tracts. Flushing: 38 tracts of NTAs QN22 Flushing, QN51 Murray Hill and QN52 East Flushing; core (7 tracts) = internal point within 700 m of the Main Street and Roosevelt Avenue intersection (40.75958 N, -73.83014 E): 081084900 081085300 081085500 081085700 081086500 081086900 081087100; periphery = the other 31.
MEASURES AND SOURCES. 2010: Census API 2010/dec/sf1 tract tables P003 (race), P005 (Hispanic origin by race: P005006 non-Hispanic Asian alone, P005007 non-Hispanic Native Hawaiian and Other Pacific Islander alone, P005004 non-Hispanic Black alone, P005003 non-Hispanic White alone, P004003 Hispanic), PCT005 (Chinese except Taiwanese alone, with one Asian category). 2020: Census API 2020/dec/dhc tract tables P1 (race), P9 (P9_008N non-Hispanic Asian alone, P9_009N non-Hispanic NHPI alone, P9_002N Hispanic), and ACS 2018-2022 5-year (2022 vintage) B03002 (B03002_006E, _007E, _012E and margins of error). Chinese alone in 2020 from DDHC-A (2020/dec/ddhca) if it returns a Chinese-alone tract total, otherwise from ACS 2022 5-year B02015; if neither gives it for the Chinatown, Sunset Park and Flushing tracts, the Chinese-alone secondary is reported as not obtained.
DATA READINGS. D1 (primary): 2010 SF1 non-Hispanic Asian alone plus non-Hispanic NHPI alone; 2020 ACS 2018-2022 B03002_006E+007E (the AALDEF construction). D2: same 2010; 2020 decennial DHC P9_008N+P9_009N. D3: non-Hispanic Asian alone only (no NHPI), 2010 SF1 and 2020 ACS. D4: as D3, 2020 decennial DHC. D5: Asian alone any Hispanic origin (P003005 / P1_006N). Boundary readings B1 (primary), B2, B3.
MAPPING 2010 to 2020 TRACTS. M1 (primary): the 2020 set for a 2010 set S10 = 2020 tracts for which the summed AREALAND_PART over S10 tracts, divided by AREALAND_TRACT_20, is at least 0.5, from the Census relationship file. 2010 counts are summed over S10 as published. M2 (sensitivity): 2020 counts apportioned to 2010 tracts by AREALAND_PART / AREALAND_TRACT_20 and summed over S10. Because land area is not population, M2 is a check on M1, not a better estimate. All Manhattan, Brooklyn and Queens 2020 tracts in the sets are listed in the outcome with their 2010 parents.
REPRODUCTION (Part A). For each reading report the 2010 count, the 2020 count (with the ACS margin of error, aggregated as the square root of the sum of squared tract margins, for ACS readings), the percentage change, the signed gap to AALDEF's 52,613, 41,024 and -22%, and whether each is in tolerance. Also report total population and non-Hispanic white, Black and Hispanic counts for the primary boundary as diagnostics against AALDEF's table (this is the only place total population is compared and it is not used to choose a boundary). The primary reading is fixed; a reading that fits better is not promoted to primary after the data are seen.
SUNSET PARK AND FLUSHING (Parts B and C). Asian alone (any origin), 2010 SF1 P003005 to 2020 DHC P1_006N, tract level, M1. Percentage change = (sum 2020 - sum 2010)/sum 2010 within each set. Core minus periphery difference in percentage points for Sunset Park and for Flushing. Intervals: 95% percentile interval from 5,000 tract-cluster bootstrap resamples (resampling the parent 2010 tracts with replacement within each of core and periphery, with their mapped 2020 counts carried with the parent via M2 apportionment; seed 20261112). The bootstrap describes spatial heterogeneity between tracts, not sampling error of the census, which is a full count. The Chinatown figures are reported with the same bootstrap.
PRE-SPECIFIED SENSITIVITY CHECKS. (1) Decennial to decennial (D2, D4, D5) against decennial to ACS (D1, D3). (2) Boundary B1, B2, B3. (3) Mapping M1 and M2. (4) 2020 disclosure-avoidance noise: add independent normal noise with standard deviation 5 persons and then 20 persons to each 2020 tract cell and report the change in the primary-set percentage (the standard deviations are assumptions, not Census figures; with 8 to 31 tracts the aggregate noise is small against sets of thousands, and this check shows how small). (5) 2020 undercount: recompute the Asian change after raising 2020 Asian counts by 3% and by 5%; this shows what size of Asian undercount would be needed to move the change out of the tolerance band; no published undercount rate is asserted. (6) Chinese-alone version of Parts A-C if the data are obtainable.
CENTROID AND NORTHERN EDGE (secondary, descriptive, no verdict). Using Gazetteer internal points for the tracts of each year: (i) the Asian-alone-weighted centroid of all Manhattan tracts south of 14th Street (internal point latitude below 40.7365 N), 2010 and 2020, and its displacement in metres; (ii) the northern edge of the majority-Asian area = the highest latitude of any Manhattan tract south of 14th Street whose Asian-alone share (any origin) is at least 50% of its total population, 2010 and 2020 with that year's own tracts; (iii) the same Asian-alone-weighted centroid for Sunset Park (31 tracts) and Flushing (38 tracts). Displacements are given without intervals because tract boundaries differ between years; they are descriptive.
QUESTION 2 (secondary, only if free of registration walls). 2000 SF1 tract counts of Asian alone for Manhattan are on the Census API (2000/dec/sf1). If the 2000 tract Gazetteer and counts are retrievable without an account, report the northern edge (ii) for 2000 with 2000 tracts. 1990 data need NHGIS or another registration and are not attempted. If 2000 data cannot be obtained, the outcome says so.
PLACEBOS. (a) Sunset Park: the same core-minus-periphery difference for Hispanic or Latino residents (2010 P004003 to 2020 P2_002N). If the Hispanic difference is within 10 percentage points of zero while the Asian difference is at most -5, the Asian gap is not a general property of core tracts (for example housing loss or undercount affecting all residents of the corridor); if the Hispanic difference is of similar size and sign to the Asian one, the Asian result is not specific to Asian residents. (b) Chinatown: the distribution of the Asian-alone percentage change across 2,000 random sets of 23 Manhattan tracts south of 96th Street (seed 20261112), to show how unusual the B1 change is for a Manhattan tract set of that size.
FIGURE. One map of tract-level change in Asian-alone population 2010 to 2020 (apportioned by M2 to 2010 tracts) for the three areas with the sets outlined, saved to figures/further/ with an embedded sRGB profile. Tract polygons from the Census cartographic boundary files (2010), a boundary dataset not used for any count.
Everything not listed here is labelled exploratory in the outcome and decides nothing.
alternatives: Boundary: AALDEF's Chinatown is not an NTA union, so a different boundary (B2 narrower, B3 wider, or an unlisted line) changes the counts and the percentage change.

Measure: AALDEF's 2020 value is an ACS five-year estimate (2018-2022), a pooled sample with sampling error at tract level, not the decennial count; a decennial-to-decennial change may differ from -22% either way.
Undercount: the 2020 census may have undercounted Asian residents or residents of dense, multi-unit and immigrant tracts, so part of the measured decline could be a count error.
Disclosure avoidance: 2020 tract counts carry injected noise, small at set level.

Housing change: new market-rate construction adds non-Asian residents and does not by itself displace Asian residents, so the Asian share can fall while the Asian count is stable; the Asian count and the share have to be read separately.
Out-migration by age and life stage (AAF: adult children leave, older parents stay) with household counts stable, which is displacement of the next generation and not eviction.
Chinese movement to other places (Sunset Park, Flushing) versus movement within the same neighbourhood to periphery tracts; the sets can separate the second only if tract boundaries are fine enough.
Boundary change between 2010 and 2020 tracts (splits and merges) mapped by land area.

outcome.notes:
Deviations from the registration. The Census API returned 'Missing Key' for all queries, so no key was requested and keyless bulk files were used: 2010 and 2020 PL 94-171 tract tables in place of SF1 P5 and DHC P9 (the 2010 values equal SF1; the 2020 PL values come from a different disclosure-avoidance run than DHC and can differ slightly), and the ACS 2018-22 table-based summary file in place of the API. The registered Chinese-alone secondary was not obtained: 2010 needs the 535 MB SF1 state file and the 2020 detailed tables were not located in time; the ACS 2018-22 Chinese-alone count (B02015) is in data/derived/further/acs2022_tracts.csv but gives one time point. The mapping grid was run for M1 and M2 for all 15 boundary and data readings (30 rows), a superset of the registered 16; none reproduces under either mapping. Diagnostics for B1 against AALDEF's table: total population 2010 120,801 (AALDEF 116,722), white 24,270 (23,314), Black 10,216 (8,457), Hispanic 35,290 (30,227), Asian+PI 48,749 (52,613). An exploratory comparison of NTA unions (data/derived/further/chinatown_exploratory_unions.csv, not registered, decides nothing) found none that matches. The reason is given in the referee's finding below: the published table uses a different tract set in each year. The decennial-to-decennial change in the B1 set is -10.3% (95% tract bootstrap -17.1 to -0.7), about half of AALDEF's 22%; the larger figure arises from comparing the 2010 census with ACS 2018-22, whose 2020-vintage tract estimate of Asian+PI residents in the same 24 tracts (38,279, margin 2,551) is below the census count (43,715). Total population in the set was 120801 in 2010 and 119699 in 2020 (census), a change of -0.9%, not AALDEF's +3%. Undercount: raising the 2020 Asian counts by 3% or 5% makes the decennial change -7.6% or -5.8%, so an Asian undercount would reduce the decline, not remove the gap with 22%. Disclosure-avoidance noise of 5 or 20 persons per tract changes the set estimate by under 0.5 points (assumed standard deviations). Manhattan south of 14th Street: Asian-alone-weighted centroid moved 22 m east and 0 m north between 2010 and 2020 and about 120 m south between 2000 and 2010; the northern edge of the majority-Asian tracts was tract 36061004100 (latitude 40.7202 in 2000, 40.7192 in 2010 and 2020) in all three years, so no shift is visible at tract resolution; the number of majority-Asian tracts was 7 (2000), 8 (2010), 6 (2020). Sunset Park and Flushing Asian-alone centroids moved 28 m and 14 m. Placebo (b): 2,000 random sets of 23 Manhattan tracts south of 96th Street had a mean Asian-alone change of +23.5% (5th to 95th percentile +4.3 to +44.6); none was as low as the Chinatown set. Manhattan Asian alone rose 23.6% and the city 33.4%. Flushing core minus periphery is +1.4 points (95% -19.8 to 57.4), not distinguishable from zero. Sunset Park core had 8 tracts and the 2020 tracts split the 2010 ones, so M1 and M2 agree exactly. Intervals from the tract bootstrap describe variation between tracts, not census sampling error. 1990 tract data were not attempted (registration wall).

After the referee (13 Nov 2026): the earlier diagnosis of the mismatch was wrong and has been removed. The referee searched tract sets near B1 and found one that matches AALDEF's 2010 table exactly on all five rows, and a different one that matches its 2020 column exactly on all five rows (re-checked from the tract tables in data/derived/further). The 2010 set is B1 without tracts 22.02, 26.01, 26.02 and 28 and with tracts 41, 43 and 45 (22 tracts: total 116,722, white 23,314, Black 8,457, Hispanic 30,227, Asian 52,613). The 2020 set is the 24 tracts of B1 plus tract 41 (25 tracts, ACS 2018-22: 120,173; 30,520; 11,094; 32,840; 41,024). None of the seven tracts that differ changed boundary between the censuses, so the published table compares two different areas. On AALDEF's 2010 set in both years the total fell 7.7%, Asian residents fell 25.7% against the ACS (90% margin -30.5 to -20.9) and 12.9% against the 2020 census, white residents rose 15.8%, Black residents 15.1% and Hispanic residents fell 7.4%. On its 2020 set the figures are -6.6%, -23.6% (-28.5 to -18.8), -11.6%, +15.0%, +8.1% and -7.8%. The published +3% total, +31% white, +31% Black, +9% Hispanic and the gain of about 12,000 white, Black and Hispanic residents come from the change of area; on the 2010 set the three groups together gained about 2,700. The Asian decline of 22% to 26% against the ACS does not depend on the change of area. The search was made after the data were seen and decides nothing under rule 4; the verdict rests on the registered readings. The row labelled 'Asian or Pacific Islander' is Asian alone (23 Pacific Islanders in the set). The gap between the ACS and the 2020 census can come from a census count that is too high, an ACS estimate that is too low, or real change within the 2018-22 window; the undercount check ran in one direction only, and the Post-Enumeration Survey estimated a net overcount of the Asian population nationally. Group quarters and student housing in tracts 41, 43 and 45 were not examined.

stance.note: Agreement with the direction of change (a decline in Asian residents), not with the published counts; the contested verdict concerns the counts. The interval in city_effect is a 90% ACS margin and is converted to 95% here.

plan.treated_unit: Manhattan Community District 9 (311 community_board '09 MANHATTAN'; DOHMH community_board '9' with borough 'Manhattan'). Treatment date: full containerised service 2 June 2025, so June 2025 is the first post month. Verified in DSNY and Mayor's releases above. The pilot-zone map and bin list are not public; CD9 boundaries stand in.
plan.comparison: Manhattan CD7, CD10, CD11, CD12, fixed by rule from published characteristics (adjacent northern Manhattan districts not fully containerised in the window). Fixed before any rat count was read. No match on pre-period level or trend was done, because that would require looking at the outcome.
plan.datasets: 311 Service Requests erm2-nwe9 via concord/socrata.py; DOHMH Rodent Inspection p937-wjvj via concord/socrata.py. Both queried on the server with count(*) grouped by community board and month.
plan.outcome_311: complaint_type = 'Rodent' and descriptor = 'Rat Sighting' (the city's apparent definition of a rat sighting), counted by created_date month and community_board, no de-duplication.
plan.outcome_dohmh: Share of inspection_type = 'Initial' with result in ('Failed for Rat Activity', 'Failed for Rat Activity and Other Reason'), by inspection_date month and community board; the number of Initial inspections per cell is reported as effort.
plan.primary_estimator: R = (N9_post / N9_pre) / (NC_post / NC_pre), where N are summed monthly counts over the 12 months June 2025-May 2026 (post) and June 2024-May 2025 (pre), and C is the pooled comparison districts. The interval is the 2.5 and 97.5 percentiles of 4000 month-pair bootstrap replicates (resample the 12 calendar-month pairs with replacement, same pairs for all districts, numpy seed 20261112), with counts taken as observed. A quasi-Poisson GLM (district and period effects plus CD9 x post) is reported as a check. DOHMH odds ratio: same construction on shares, ratio of odds.
plan.placebo: (1) Placebo year: the same estimator on June 2023-May 2024 (pseudo-post) against June 2022-May 2023 (pseudo-pre), all before any citywide containerisation of homes. Decides under support_if (b). (2) Placebo complaint type Noise - Residential in the real window; reported.
plan.sensitivity: As listed under prediction.secondary. The comparison set and windows are fixed here and are not changed after the data are seen.
plan.window_note: Citywide residential containerisation (buildings with 1-9 units) began 12 Nov 2024 and falls inside the pre window; it affects CD9 and the comparison districts alike and is absorbed by the difference. If the rule affected CD9 differently (more small buildings), the estimate is biased and this is reported as a limit.
plan.what_311_can_show: 311 counts record complaints by residents, not rats. A fall in CD9 relative to neighbours shows that complaints fell relative to neighbours; it supports fewer rats only if reporting behaviour did not change differently in CD9. The DOHMH measure does not depend on residents calling but depends on inspection effort and targeting. Neither separates bins from other concurrent changes in CD9 (the 2023 Harlem pilot, NYCHA sites, bin-related tidiness that lowers 'sighting' calls). The design cannot show that rats fell, nor that bins caused any change.
plan.prior_data_seen: Earlier project work (analyses/neighbourhood/fetch311.py, rodents_asthma.py, claim nbhd-rodents-asthma) queried 311 'Rodent' complaints by latitude/longitude for 2022-2024 and p937-wjvj results aggregated to census tracts, for a neighbourhood-asthma question. No monthly, community-district or 2025-2026 rat figures from those were seen by the registrant, and none were consulted for this design. Metadata, column names and distinct lists of descriptor, community_board, inspection_type and result values (without counts) were read before registering.

alternatives: Citywide 311 reporting fell for reasons unrelated to bins (attention, app changes, weather); a CD9 fall no larger than elsewhere counts against the causal sentence.
Spillover: rats displaced from CD9 into adjacent comparison districts would inflate the contrast; reduced harbourage in CD9 could instead lower neighbours' counts.
Differential reporting: new bins and DSNY presence in CD9 change who reports and what is reported.
CD9 differs in building stock (more large buildings, NYCHA) so the citywide 12 Nov 2024 rule affected it differently.
Other concurrent actions in northern Manhattan (rat mitigation zones, the 2023 Harlem pilot, construction, weather).
Regression to the mean if CD9 had an unusual high before the window (cannot be checked before registering).

outcome.notes:
311 counts measure complaints. The data show that CD9 complaints fell about as much as in neighbouring districts after June 2025 (and that all of them fell by roughly a quarter against the year before), which is consistent with a citywide change in reporting or rats and gives no evidence of an extra effect of containers in CD9. They do not show that bins had no effect: the interval allows an additional fall of 14% or a rise of 23%. The DOHMH active-sign share fell in CD9 (15.3% to 14.8% of initial inspections) but fell more in the comparison districts (19.7% to 17.7%); inspection counts in the comparison districts fell 6% while CD9's were flat, so effort differs. Several of the single-district comparisons point either way (CD11 0.85, CD12 1.19). Comparison districts were fixed in advance, not matched on pre-period level; CD9 started the placebo period lower than the comparison and was higher later (event series), so pre-trends are not parallel. Data fetched 12 Nov 2026; the table's last month (Nov 2026) is incomplete and was not used.

After the referee (13 Nov 2026): the registered interval (0.86 to 1.23) is too narrow. The same rate ratio computed for each of the other eleven Manhattan districts, none of which had containers, runs from 0.77 to 1.56, a spread about twice what the month-pair bootstrap reports; with that spread the interval for CD9 is roughly 0.69 to 1.49. The quasi-Poisson check that the registration said would be reported was not fitted; the referee's fit gives 1.018 (0.832 to 1.245) with district and month effects. The answer depends on the pre-trend and on repeat calls: CD9's share of the comparison districts' sightings rose in each of the three years before the bins (0.133, 0.144, 0.153, 0.156), a model with a linear trend gives 0.92 (0.80 to 1.07) and one without gives 1.08 (0.99 to 1.17). Counting distinct addresses gives 1.11 (0.95 to 1.29); on that unregistered measure the refutation condition would be met, and it decides nothing. The bins were installed in April and May 2025, inside the pre-period, and July 2024 holds 17% of CD9's pre-period sightings (without the July pair the ratio is 1.06). District boundaries stand in for the treated blocks, so a district ratio near 1 is compatible with a fall on the streets that have bins. Support needed a ratio below about 0.83, so most of the predicted range could not have been confirmed.

critique.answer: accepted; verdict kept, wider interval recorded

claims.plan:
SCOPE AND DATA. Manhattan rows (borough MANHATTAN) of NYC Local Law 84 'Energy and Water Data Disclosure for Local Law 84 2023 to Present (Data for Calendar Year 2022-Present)', Socrata 5zyy-y8am on data.cityofnewyork.us, rowsUpdatedAt 2025-11-25 (checked 12 Nov 2026 in the Socrata catalog: it is the current dataset; the 2022 and earlier calendar years are in 7x5e-2fxh, usc3-8zwd and older ids; monthly data are fvp3-gcb2; no calendar-year 2025 file exists). report_year 2024 is primary and report_year 2023 is a sensitivity year; the cached file data/derived/further/ll84_mn_bx.csv (query logged in datacentre_sources.json) is reused, so no new LL84 query is made. Fields: electricity_use_grid_purchase_1 (kWh), property_gfa_calculated (fallback property_gfa_self_reported), data_center_gross_floor_area, data_center_it_site_energy (kWh), data_center_pue, largest_property_use_type, nyc_borough_block_and_lot, parent_property_id, alert and estimated flags.
DENOMINATORS. D1 = sum of grid electricity over all Manhattan LL84 rows with usable electricity, built as in the first registration (listed buildings without a 2024 row taken from the latest earlier year). D2 = Utility Energy Registry g2x3-izm4 (data.ny.gov), Con Edison, non-residential consumption (2_nat_consumption), Manhattan ZIP codes 100, 101, 102, 2024; the cached file uer_mn.csv is reused. Borough total D3 (sensitivity, not decisive) = NYISO Zone J (N.Y.C.) 2024 energy summed from the cached data/derived/further/zonej_daily.csv, multiplied by Manhattan's share of Con Edison delivered electricity, which is UER total consumption (3_nat_consumption) in Manhattan ZIP codes over UER total consumption in all New York City ZIP codes (prefixes 100 to 104 and 110 to 116; one new data.ny.gov query for the non-Manhattan ZIP codes, a denominator query that contains no data-centre field). The Zone J load includes losses and so exceeds delivered electricity; D3 is therefore the largest denominator and gives the smallest shares.
ESTIMATOR A (IT times PUE). For each Manhattan building in 2024 with data_center_it_site_energy greater than 0: A_low = min(IT x 1.4, building grid kWh), A_high = min(IT x 2.0, building grid kWh). The cap is stated because IT meters may record tenant-metered or on-site energy that the landlord's grid figure does not contain; the uncapped sums are reported as well. Reported PUE (2 values in the whole file as seen in the first run) is not used except as a sensitivity.
ESTIMATOR B (carrier-hotel excess). Median office intensity m = median of grid kWh per square foot over Manhattan 2024 rows with largest_property_use_type 'Office', property GFA of at least 50,000 square feet, positive electricity, parent_property_id not applicable, data_center_gross_floor_area not positive, not on the list, and not flagged for estimated values or a data-centre alert. For each listed building with a usable row (latest earlier year if none in 2024, as before): B = max(0, intensity - m) x GFA. B is an upper figure for the carrier-hotel load because it counts all excess over a typical office as data-centre use (cooling, telecom equipment, but also any non-data-centre excess).
LIST (fixed here, unchanged from the first registration; the rows were selected from public sources before any electricity value was read in the first run): 60 Hudson Street (Western Union Building, BBL 1001440040), 111 Eighth Avenue (1007390001), 32 Sixth Avenue / 32 Avenue of the Americas (1001920001), 325 Hudson Street (1005970062), 375 Pearl Street (1001137501), 85 Tenth Avenue (1006870029), 75 Broad Street (1000290070), 33 Whitehall Street (1000100014), 32 Old Slip (1000350001), 150 Varick Street (1005050001). This is the list of the first registration, unchanged; no building was added, because the web search made for this registration confirmed 60 Hudson, 111 Eighth, 32 Avenue of the Americas, 85 Tenth and 75 Broad only and did not confirm 25 Broadway, 55 Broad Street or 799 Broadway.
COMBINATION. Per building, S_low = A_low. S_high = max(A_high, B) for listed buildings and A_high for other buildings, so IT and excess are not added twice for the same building. S_low and S_high are summed over buildings and divided by D1, D2 and D3. A building can be both listed and IT-reporting.
INTERVAL. 2000 bootstrap resamples of the non-listed, non-IT buildings in the denominator (numerator buildings fixed), 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles, as in the first run; a separate range over PUE 1.4 to 2.0 is the S_low to S_high range itself. The intervals do not include reporting error.
PLACEBO P_B. 2000 draws, from the Manhattan office pool defined for m (excluding the median-defining restrictions' complement, i.e. the same pool), of one building within 25 percent of GFA for each listed building that has a usable row; compute the same summed excess over m; the 97.5th percentile is the threshold in (d). Also reported: the percentile of the listed set among the draws. P_A: the same A estimator for the Bronx (expected near zero; first run saw zero IT energy there).
SENSITIVITY (reported, not decisive). 2023 report_year; uncapped A; use of building-reported PUE where present; median over all Manhattan offices at least 25,000 square feet; dropping rows with estimated-value or alert flags from D1; D3; flagged buildings (data-centre floor area positive, not listed, not reporting IT) allocated area-proportional electricity as in L2 of the first run; and the reverse bound R = 4.4 / S_high, the factor by which unreported data-centre load would have to exceed the allocated load for the share to reach 4.4 percent.
MINIMUM DETECTABLE EFFECT AND WHETHER THE TEST CAN FAIL. The refute condition (S_high at or above 4.4 percent) can fail the national comparison only if S_high exceeds the sum of the two first-run numbers already seen: IT energy 0.83 percent of D1 times 2.0 is 1.66 percent, and the whole-building electricity of the whole listed set is 2.23 percent, which bounds B from above; their sum is 3.9 percent, below 4.4. The registrant therefore judges the probability that refute_if is met at about 0.03, and says that condition (a) alone is close to uninformative, which is the defect of the first test in the other direction. The informative conditions are (b), (c) and (d): (b) and (c) fail if the cap binds, if the median office intensity is high relative to the hotels, or if IT-reporting buildings differ from what the first run's totals suggest (registrant's probability that (b) fails 0.25, that (c) fails 0.4); (d) fails if the listed hotels are not distinguishable from ordinary large offices on intensity, which the landlord-reporting caveat makes plausible (probability 0.25). Each of (b), (c), (d) is a range or threshold with a stated alternative outcome, so the test can return unsettled. The bootstrap interval for D1 shares in the first run was about 0.1 to 0.2 percentage points wide for the IT share; this is much narrower than the 0.5 point gap between the ranges, so sampling error does not blur the ranges; reporting error does, and is not in the interval.
CONTEXT NOT TESTED. The comparison with Northern Virginia (EPRI: a quarter of Virginia's load in 2023) is stated for the public perception only; a Manhattan figure far below it is expected and is not a registered condition.
VERDICT. As in prediction. Anything not named here is exploratory and cannot decide the verdict.
alternatives: Tenants of carrier hotels meter their own electricity, so the landlord-reported figures (A cap and B) understate the data-centre load; the allocated share would then be a lower bound and a larger true share is compatible with the result.
The IT meter, where present, may belong to enterprise data rooms in offices and hospitals, not to colocation; A then measures server rooms, not carrier hotels.
A median-office baseline is too low for buildings whose telecom and trading tenants use more electricity per square foot than a typical office, so B overstates data-centre use for them.
The 4.4 percent national figure and the Manhattan figure have different denominators (all US electricity versus a dense office and apartment district), so the two are not expected to be equal.
Manhattan data centres draw from Con Edison networks not captured by LL84, such as buildings under 25,000 or 50,000 square feet.

outcome.notes:
Primary 2024. D1 17.06 TWh (matches the first run), D2 16.03 TWh, D3 22.61 TWh (Zone J 49.76 TWh times Manhattan's 45.4 percent of Con Edison New York City deliveries, 208 ZIP codes). Allocated electricity: low 173 GWh, high 386 GWh. Shares: D1 1.01 to 2.26 percent (bootstrap 0.96 to 1.06, 2.15 to 2.38); D2 1.08 to 2.41; D3 0.76 to 1.71. Median office intensity 9.6 kWh per square foot (538 offices); this is low, probably because landlord figures omit tenant meters, which raises B. The cap binds: the 56 Hudson Street property (Western Union Building) reports IT energy equal to 90 percent of its grid electricity, so IT x 1.4 exceeds the building total, and it supplies half of the low figure. 19 buildings report positive IT energy (the first run's 26 included zero values), 3 of them listed. The BBL for 60 Hudson Street again joins to 56 Hudson Street. B alone is 1.70 percent of D1; 111 Eighth Avenue (53 kWh per square foot) contributes 107 GWh of it. Sensitivity (D1 high figure): uncapped 2.72; 2023 1.05 to 2.47; adding area-proportional electricity for 150 other buildings with data-centre floor area gives 3.00. Dropping estimated or alert rows leaves a 6.6 TWh D1 and gives 2.3 to 3.5 percent, a different and smaller population. Reverse bound: unreported data-centre load would have to be 1.9 times the allocated high figure for the D1 share to reach 4.4 percent. Bronx placebo: no IT-reporting building. Condition (a) was judged before the test to be almost incapable of failing (registered probability 0.03); the verdict rests on (b), (c) and (d). The placebo for (d) uses a median baseline, so its draws sit near zero by construction.

After the referee (13 Nov 2026): the stance is set to null. Its interval resampled only the buildings outside the numerator, so the z of 36 measured nothing about reporting error or tenant metering, and the comparison with the national 4.4% is not like for like. The result describes the share visible in landlord-reported Local Law 84 electricity, not metered data-centre load: the unreported load would need to be 1.9 times the allocated load for the share to reach 4.4%, which is not a large factor for tenant-metered colocation. Condition (b) passes by 0.011 points on a point estimate whose bootstrap interval (0.96 to 1.06) includes the limit, and a PUE of 1.3 gives 0.98 and fails it (rule 10 asks that this be said). D1 counts campuses twice: 468 parent rows (2.16 TWh) and 685 child rows (1.68 TWh) are both summed. Without child rows the figures are 1.12 and 2.51 percent, and without parent rows 1.16 and 2.59; all four conditions remain met. The high figure is not an upper figure: fifteen other Manhattan rows whose largest use type is 'Data Center', mostly telephone central offices, hold 99 GWh, and with them the share is 2.84 percent. Each of conditions (b) and (c) rests on one building: the Western Union Building supplies 86 of the 173 GWh in the low figure and 111 Eighth Avenue 107 of the 289 GWh of excess; without the largest contributor the figures are 0.51 and 1.64. The join of 60 Hudson Street to 56 Hudson Street is correct, since both are addresses of the same building. The registrant had seen the first run's totals, which bounded the high figure between 1.66 and 3.9 before registration.

outcome.verdict_note: The registered conditions are met for landlord-reported electricity. Condition (b) passes by 0.01 points, and the result is an allocation, not a measurement of data-centre load.

claims.plan:
SCOPE AND YEAR. Manhattan (borough = MANHATTAN) rows of NYC Local Law 84 'Energy and Water Data Disclosure 2023 to Present' (Socrata 5zyy-y8am, data.cityofnewyork.us), report_year 2024 (calendar year 2024 by the dataset title; 2023 and 2022 are sensitivity years). UER denominator from the Utility Energy Registry monthly ZIP code file g2x3-izm4 (data.ny.gov; set concord.socrata.DOMAIN accordingly and record it), year 2024; if 2024 lacks twelve months for Con Edison in Manhattan ZIP codes, use 2023 for both numerator and denominators and say so. Coverage limits to state in the outcome: LL84 covers buildings above 25,000 or 50,000 sq ft (the two dataset descriptions differ), only large buildings; tenant-metered electricity may be absent from landlord-reported figures; UER is Con Edison deliveries by ZIP and privacy screens may blank cells.
BUILDING LIST (fixed here from public sources and addresses, not from electricity values). Identifiers were looked up before registration (address, property_id, BBL only): 60 Hudson Street (Western Union Building) [property_id 2614608; BBL 1001440040; source: DCF Tours, Digital Realty 60 Hudson; baxtel.com/data-center/60-hudson-street]; 111 Eighth Avenue [property_id 7536925; BBL 1007390001; source: datacenterdynamics.com NYC carrier hotel microcosm; datacenters.com 111 8th Ave]; 32 Sixth Avenue (32 Avenue of the Americas) [property_id 6284230; BBL 1001920001; source: baxtel.com/data-center/32-avenue-of-the-americas]; 325 Hudson Street [property_id 33987950 (2022: 3306897); BBL 1005970062; source: datacenterfrontier.com H5 Data Centers 325 Hudson]; 375 Pearl Street [property_id 33966445 and 14697585 (2022: 2688590); BBL 1001137501; source: Sabey Intergate.Manhattan; scouting note; not independently sourced by this agent]; 85 Tenth Avenue [property_id 3114292; BBL 1006870029; source: baxtel.com Lumen New York Gateway 2 (85 10th)]; 75 Broad Street [property_id 2682108; BBL 1000290070; source: baxtel/web search: historic ITT building, Verizon colocation]; 33 Whitehall Street [property_id 2591905 and 48547894; BBL 1000100014; source: web search: Cogent colocation]; 32 Old Slip [property_id 6794379; BBL 1000350001; source: web search: Lumen]; 150 Varick Street [property_id 4412459; BBL 1005050001; source: web search: Level 3]. Join key: nyc_borough_block_and_lot after stripping hyphens (formats vary between years), with property_id and address as cross-checks. Flagged set: every Manhattan property in report_year 2024 with data_center_gross_floor_area greater than 0 (text field; 'Not Available' and blanks are zero). A listed building with no 2024 row (60 Hudson Street has rows only for 2022 and 2023 in the identifier lookup) is taken from its latest earlier year and added to both the numerator and the D1 denominator, and reported as such.
MEASURES. Electricity = 'Electricity Use - Grid Purchase (kWh)' (electricity_use_grid_purchase_1), parsed from text; non-numeric and negative values are excluded and counted. Floor area = property_gfa_calculated (buildings and parking), falling back to property_gfa_self_reported. Denominator D1 = sum of grid electricity (kWh) over all Manhattan LL84 rows in the year (children and parents of campus properties are not de-duplicated; a sensitivity drops rows whose parent_property_id is not 'Not Applicable'). D2 = UER electricity 'Non-Residential Consumption (C+I)' (data_field 2_nat_consumption, MWh, Con Edison) summed over months and over Manhattan ZIP codes (zip_code beginning 100, 101 or 102); total consumption (3_nat_consumption) is the secondary denominator. Units MWh/MWH are both used.
ESTIMATES. U (upper bound, decides the verdict) = whole-building grid kWh of the listed and flagged buildings, over D1 and over D2 (kWh converted to MWh). L1 (strict lower bound) = sum of reported data_center_it_site_energy (kWh) over buildings reporting it, over D1 and D2. L2 = data-centre floor area / property GFA times building grid kWh (area-proportional; likely understates because data-centre intensity exceeds the building average), over D1 and D2. L3 = L1 times reported PUE where both are present. Area share = sum of data_center_gross_floor_area over total Manhattan reported floor area. Interval for each share: 2000 bootstrap resamples of the denominator buildings (listed and flagged buildings held fixed, so the numerator is a fixed set and the interval reflects the composition of the rest of Manhattan), 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles; the D2 interval is not computed because UER is a census of deliveries, and instead a range is given from using the monthly series with and without the privacy-blanked ZIP cells (cells counted by month).
SENSITIVITY CHECKS (pre-specified, reported, not decisive). (a) Year: 2023 and 2022. (b) Drop flagged buildings that are not on the fixed list from U (the list alone). (c) Drop rows with alert_data_center_issue_with, estimated_values_energy or estimated_data_flag set from D1 and U. (d) D1 with campus child rows removed. (e) Drop 60 Hudson Street, whose reporting is incomplete, from U. (f) Net electricity: grid purchase plus on-site generated used on site (electricity_use_grid_purchase_2) in place of grid purchase.
PLACEBOS. P1: the same area share, L1/L2 and the ratio of listed-set U to D1 computed for the Bronx (no carrier hotels are known there; expected near zero for the data-centre fields). P2: size-matched placebo set: 2000 random draws, from Manhattan LL84 buildings with largest_property_use_type 'Office' that are not listed or flagged, of ten buildings (ten listed buildings, or the number of listed buildings with a 2024 row) each within 25 percent of a listed building's floor area; the share of D1 they hold is the baseline for what ten large buildings hold with no data centre, and U is reported relative to that distribution (percentile of U among draws). P3: laboratory floor area (laboratory_gross_floor_area > 0) share of Manhattan reported floor area and electricity, using the same whole-building rule, as a use type of similar rarity; it tests whether the whole-building rule inflates the share of any rare use. Placebo results do not decide the verdict.
VERDICT. As in prediction.support_if and refute_if. Anything not named here (for example other buildings added to the list after viewing values) is exploratory and cannot decide the verdict.
alternatives: Colocation floors are reported under Office or Other rather than Data Center, so the use-type route (L1, L2, area share) understates and the whole-building route (U) overstates; U is therefore the conservative bound for a 'below 4.4 percent' claim.

Landlords of carrier hotels may report only base-building electricity, because tenants (carriers, colocation operators) hold their own meters, so U understates true data-centre electricity in those buildings.
Buildings omitted from the list (small or unlisted colocation rooms inside financial and media offices, below the LL84 size threshold) are missing from every estimate.

Manhattan has little data-centre load because the land and power are expensive and large facilities sit in New Jersey, upstate and Queens; the national share of 4.4 percent is therefore not the relevant comparison, and a share below 4.4 percent is expected on location grounds alone.
The national denominator includes industry and transport-heavy regions, while the Manhattan denominator is dominated by offices and multifamily buildings, so the two shares are not like-for-like.

outcome.notes:
Verdict follows the registration, which listed R1 to R6 and called the complaint-based ratio secondary. It is contested because no registered reading reproduces both numbers. The yeek-jhmu NYCT rows for January to November 2025 hold 1,755 felonies, all from NYPD, compared with 1,940 NYPD felony complaints with the subway premise in the same months, and the table's implied rider count is 1,578 million against 1,186 million subway entries in the ridership table. The table's rates are therefore on a larger denominator and a smaller count than the State's number implies (the denominator is subway plus bus ridership; see the referee's check below). The secondary check, computed after the registered readings, gives 1,940 complaints over 1,186.3 million entries, 1.64 per million for January to November 2025 and 2.33 for the same months of 2021, a fall of 29.9%. That matches the published 1.65 and 30% within the registered tolerance, but it is a reading that the registration did not include among R1 to R6, so by the register's rules (PRECEDENCE 4) it decides nothing; it is a candidate for a new registration. R5 and R6 were registered with a riders formula that adds rates across agencies, which is not valid for more than one agency; a per-agency version gives 1.17 for all four agencies and 1.12 for NYCT and SIR, still far from 1.65.

After the referee (13 Nov 2026): contested here means that the registered source was the wrong one. It does not mean that the State's figure fails. The State's 1.65 per million does reproduce: 2,028 NYPD felony complaints of the seven major types with the subway premise, 1 January to 14 December 2025, over 1,226.8 million subway rides in the MTA daily ridership table (sayj-mze2) give 1.653, and 1,695 complaints over 722.4 million rides in the same days of 2021 (vxuj-8kew) give 2.346, a fall of 29.5% (referee; re-checked by a fresh query on 13 November). This reading was found after the data were seen, so under rule 4 it decides nothing and the verdict stays. The registered table (yeek-jhmu) fails because its NYCT rate is per subway and bus rider: the riders implied by its NYCT rows equal subway plus NYCT Bus plus MTA Bus ridership in the MTA monthly table (xfre-bxip; median ratio 0.998 over 93 months), 1,578 million for January to November 2025, of which the subway is 1,171 million. The sentence that the table's counts are consistent with arrests has been removed: the counts are 90% of the complaint counts and the column description reads 'the count of Major Felonies committed'. Whether the 1,755 includes crimes on buses was not tested. R1's fall of 26.96% is just below the 27 to 33 percent band, not at its edge. With four of the six registered readings equal or close to R1, the registration tested one reading of one table.

prediction.definitions: Numerator N[b,p]: NYPD complaints (qgea-i56i for cmplnt_fr_dt through 2025-12-31, 5uac-w243 for 2026-01-01 to 2026-09-30, the last complete quarter) with law_cat_cd = 'FELONY', ky_cd in {101 murder, 104 rape, 105 robbery, 106 felony assault, 107 burglary, 109 grand larceny, 110 grand larceny of motor vehicle} (the seven MTA major felony types), prem_typ_desc = 'TRANSIT - NYC SUBWAY', assigned to the hour of cmplnt_fr_tm and the date of cmplnt_fr_dt. Complaints with a missing time or date are dropped and their share reported. Denominator E[b,p]: sum of `ridership` (estimated fare entries, in millions) over transit_mode = 'subway' for the same hours (t69i-h2me for 2019, 5wq4-mkjj for 2025-2026). Hour h of the ridership table covers h:00-h:59. Bands: 0-5 = hours 0-4, 5-10 = 5-9, 10-16 = 10-15, 16-20 = 16-19, 20-24 = 20-23. Periods: 2019 = 1 Jan-31 Dec 2019; L12 = 1 Oct 2025-30 Sep 2026. Rate r[b,p] = N/E per million entries. Intervals: exact (Garwood) Poisson interval for a count, divided by the fixed exposure; for a ratio of two rates, the exact conditional binomial interval for N1/(N1+N2) given the exposures; for a ratio of ratios, a Wald interval on the log scale with variance equal to the sum of 1/N over the four counts. Ridership is treated as known; its estimation error is not propagated and is named as a limit. Quantities: A = r[0-5, L12] / r[10-16, L12]. G[b] = r[b, L12] / r[b, 2019]. G_all = the same ratio for all bands pooled. B = G[0-5] / G_all.
prediction.magnitude: A (0-5 against 10-16 rate, L12) 3 to 8, point guess 4.5. G[0-5] (L12 against 2019) 1.2 to 2.2. G_all 1.1 to 1.6, that is, the all-day rate per entry is also expected to be above its 2019 level because entries are well below 2019 while complaint counts are at or somewhat below the 2019 count; the premise that the all-day rate per ride has returned to 2019 is expected to be false. B 1.0 to 1.5. The 20-24 band rate is expected at 1.3 to 2.5 times the 10-16 rate and is reported but does not decide the verdict.
prediction.support_if: A >= 3.0 with the lower 95% bound of A >= 2.0, AND the lower 95% bound of G[0-5] > 1, AND B >= 1.10.
prediction.refute_if: The upper 95% bound of A < 3.0, OR the upper 95% bound of G[0-5] < 1 (the 0-5 rate per entry is below its 2019 level). Anything else is unsettled.
prediction.placebo: Placebo (reported, not part of the verdict): the same seven felony types at non-subway premises (all prem_typ_desc except subway, transit facility other, tunnel and bridge), counted by the same bands and periods without a ridership denominator. D_placebo = [N(0-5,L12)/N(0-5,2019)] / [N(all,L12)/N(all,2019)]. If D_placebo >= 1.10 with its 95% interval excluding 1, a citywide shift of reported crime toward the night, not the subway, explains a B >= 1.10, and the outcome says so.

claims.plan: Question: is the State's fall in crime per rider true at every hour, or only on average? Part 1 (the reproduction of the State's number) is registered separately as further-subway-crime-per-million-repro. Part 2 (this claim) uses NYPD complaint data over MTA hourly ridership, with the definitions in prediction.definitions fixed here. Primary numerator premise: 'TRANSIT - NYC SUBWAY'. Datasets: qgea-i56i, 5uac-w243 (data.cityofnewyork.us), t69i-h2me, 5wq4-mkjj (data.ny.gov; wujg-7c2s for 2020-2024 descriptive years only). Aggregation on the server by date and hour; no row downloads. Unit: citywide subway system by hour band and period (no station crosswalk is attempted, because the complaint file's station_name is incomplete and the rate is a system rate). Model: the rates and ratios in the definitions; a descriptive year series 2019 to 2025 by band is plotted (2020 to 2024 ridership from wujg-7c2s). Pre-specified sensitivity checks, each reported with A, G[0-5] and B: S1 numerator premise also includes 'TRANSIT FACILITY (OTHER)'; S2 numerator is every felony in the seven types with transit_district not null; S3 drop complaints whose time is exactly 00:00:00 or 12:00:00 (default or rounded entries); S4 violent types only (101, 104, 105, 106); S5 calendar 2025 in place of L12; S6 bands shifted to 22-4 against 10-16. Placebo as in prediction.placebo. Limits named in advance: the denominator counts fare entries, not riders present or train-hours, so a transfer within the system, a rider staying aboard overnight, or free exits are not counted and the per-ride rate is per entry; a complaint's time is the reported time of occurrence and many are estimates; hourly ridership after 2020 is a modelled estimate; the 0-5 band holds few entries, so intervals are wide; complaints are reports and reporting may differ by hour and year; the complaint tables record only crimes reported, and subway-premise assignment depends on officers' coding.
alternatives: Reporting and coding: a change in how subway crimes are coded (premise) or reported by hour produces the pattern without a change in risk (placebo and S1, S2).
Composition of riders: the night rider mix changed after 2020, so a higher per-entry rate reflects who is present and exposure per entry, not unsafe conditions.
Denominator: entries per hour understate the people present on platforms and trains late at night, who include people sheltering, so per-entry rates overstate risk per person-hour at night.
Offense mix: a rise confined to grand larceny or robbery of sleepers differs from a rise in violent crime (S4).
Citywide: crime at all premises shifted toward the night (placebo).
claims.disclosure_prior_looks: Before registration this session read only metadata, column lists, the distinct values of prem_typ_desc, juris_desc, jurisdiction_code, law_cat_cd, transit_district and ky_cd/ofns_desc, and the date coverage of qgea-i56i (to 2025-12-31) and 5uac-w243 (to 2026-09-30), and the distinct agency, police_force and felony_type values and the month range of yeek-jhmu. No complaint count, felony count or ridership total was read. The repo's cache already holds hourly ridership aggregates fetched by other agents: t69i-h2me subway entries by day and hour for 2018 (all complexes, CBD complexes, and by borough), by station and night/day split for the week of 14 January 2019, and the 2025-2026 station list; these were not opened for this claim and are not used. No NYPD complaint or yeek-jhmu query had been made in the repo. The prior comes from general knowledge that entries are well below 2019 and that the State reports complaint counts below 2019.

outcome.notes:
Primary numerator: NYPD felony complaints of the seven MTA major types with premise 'TRANSIT - NYC SUBWAY'; counts 2,501 in 2019 and 2,103 in the 12 months to 30 September 2026. Denominator: MTA estimated subway entries, 1,695 million in 2019 and 1,323 million in the 12 months, so the all-day rate per million entries was 1.48 (1.42 to 1.53) in 2019 and 1.59 (1.52 to 1.66) in the latest 12 months. Rates per million entries in the latest 12 months were 17.7 (16.2 to 19.2) at 0-5, 1.04 (0.93 to 1.15) at 5-10, 1.18 (1.07 to 1.29) at 10-16, 1.02 (0.93 to 1.13) at 16-20 and 2.11 (1.88 to 2.35) at 20-24. The 2019 rates were 18.3, 0.83, 1.14, 0.98 and 2.01. The 0-5 band holds 2.4% of entries and 26% of complaints. The 5-10 band has the clearest rise, 1.26 (1.08 to 1.46) times its 2019 rate; the other bands are near 1.0. The result therefore agrees with the first half of the hypothesis (a late-night rate many times the daytime rate) and does not agree with the second half: the late-night rate per entry is at its 2019 level, not above it, and the all-day rate is also above its 2019 level, so the premise that the all-day rate had returned was false. The State's all-day fall is a fall in counts and in entries together; per entry, the rate in every band except 5-10 is within the intervals of its 2019 value. Calendar 2025 in place of the latest 12 months gives A 17.3, G[0-5] 1.06 (0.95 to 1.19) and B 0.96 (0.84 to 1.09), and the 20-24 band at 1.27 (1.10 to 1.48) times 2019. None of the six sensitivity checks changes the verdict. Placebo: non-subway felonies of the same types rose in the 0-5 band relative to all hours by D = 1.05 (1.02 to 1.07), which excludes 1 but is under the registered 1.10, so a citywide shift toward the night is small. Limits: the denominator is fare entries, which understate people present on trains and platforms at night, so the per-entry night rate overstates per-person-hour risk if night riders stay longer; ridership is a modelled estimate and its error is not in the intervals; the interval on a ratio treats the denominators as fixed; complaint times are reported times and 1.9% (2019) and 3.8% (latest 12 months) of 0-5 complaints sit at exactly 00:00; no complaint was missing a time. The CBC survey of perceived safety was not read at the source. Registration was pushed to prereg/further-subway-crime-per-ride-by-hour before any complaint or ridership count was queried.

After the referee (13 Nov 2026): the State's fall is measured from 2021 and the registered test measures the late-night rate from 2019, so the statement about 'the State's all-day fall' needs that qualification. On the State's baseline (calendar 2025 against 2021, same numerator and denominator) the all-day rate fell by 30% (ratio 0.70, 0.66 to 0.75), the 0-5 rate by about 19% (0.81, 0.71 to 0.92) and the rate for hours 5 to 24 by about 35% (0.65, 0.61 to 0.70). The late-night fall since 2021 is smaller than the daytime fall, while against 2019 the late-night rate is level. This comparison was made after the data were seen and decides nothing; it is the natural second registration. The pooled late-night ratio near 1 hides opposite movements by offence: within the 0-5 band, felony assaults per entry are 1.95 (1.44 to 2.64) times their 2019 level, robbery 0.73 (0.55 to 0.95) and grand larceny 0.88 (0.77 to 1.02). 'At its 2019 level' is therefore not a statement about personal safety. Changes in how assaults are charged and recorded after 2020, and the overnight police patrols that began in 2025, are rivals for the rise in assaults and were not examined. The 2019 monthly counts in the band are overdispersed (dispersion 2.6); a bootstrap over months gives 0.97 (0.85 to 1.10). The predicted rise of 1.2 to 2.2 is rejected (z = -3.8 from its lower edge), and a rate at its 2019 level is unsettled only because the refutation rule was written as an upper bound below 1.

critique.answer: accepted; verdict kept

claims.plan:
DATA AND WHAT HAS BEEN SEEN. Before registering I read only metadata: the column lists of erm2-nwe9 (311 Service Requests from 2020 to Present), kb2e-tjy3 (FloodNet sensor deployment table: ZIP, tidally_influenced flag; a lookup table of sensor sites, not events), aq7i-eu5q (FloodNet events; columns only), 5xsi-dfpx; the CO-OPS flood levels and datums for 8518750; and the 2023 hourly Battery series, solely to confirm the unit and datum of the thresholds (12 days in 2023 reached the threshold below, consistent with the roughly ten a year in the State assessment). No 311 flooding complaint counts were read for this claim. The project's cache holds 29 earlier queries of erm2-nwe9, all for noise and rodent complaints (nbhd-noise311-exposure, nbhd-rodents-asthma) or address look-ups in Red Hook for the Red Hook case study; none concerns flooding, sewer or catch-basin complaints, FloodNet events, or any time series by tide. Scouting note flooding-sea-level.md read no outcome values. The descriptor strings of the 311 flooding complaints were not enumerated; they are specified below by text patterns.
SAMPLE. Calendar days 1 Jan 2020 to 31 Oct 2026 (311 file from 2020 only; extension to the 2010-2019 file is not part of this claim). RAIN-FREE DAY: GHCN-Daily PRCP under 1.0 mm at both Central Park (USW00094728) and JFK (USW00094789) on the day and on the previous day, both values non-missing. All other days are dropped.
EXPOSURE. NOAA CO-OPS station 8518750 The Battery, product hourly_height (verified where available, else preliminary), datum MLLW, metric, local clock time; calendar day = local date. Daily maximum H. Threshold: NOS minor flood level 10.19 (the flood-levels endpoint reports it in feet above station datum; the station datum is 1.002 m below MLLW per the datums table), i.e. 2.104 m above MLLW. E1 (primary) = 1 if H >= 2.104 m. E2 (secondary) = H in units of 10 cm, continuous, using all rain-free days. E1 lagged one day (flood day yesterday) is a secondary.
ZIP SETS (fixed now). TIDAL (primary), named from the neighbourhoods listed in the scouting note: Howard Beach 11414; Broad Channel and the Rockaways 11693, 11691, 11692, 11694, 11697; Red Hook 11231; Coney Island 11224. TIDAL-BROAD (secondary): the primary set plus every ZIP that holds a FloodNet sensor flagged tidally_influenced = Yes in kb2e-tjy3 as read on 12 Nov 2026 (10464, 11413, 11422, 10305, 10306, 10301, 10310, 10312, 10034). PLACEBO: every other ZIP code with at least one 311 record, excluding TIDAL-BROAD. Known weakness: the placebo set contains some other waterfront ZIPs and 11231 contains inland blocks.
COMPLAINTS. Created date in the sample. C1 (primary): records where upper(complaint_type) or upper(descriptor) contains 'STREET FLOOD'. C2 (secondary): C1 plus records whose descriptor contains 'CATCH BASIN' or 'SEWER BACKUP' (case-insensitive). If C1 gives fewer than 100 records in the TIDAL set on rain-free days over the whole sample, C2 becomes the primary complaint set (the same decision rule applies to it), and this is reported.
MINIMUM-DATA RULE. The test is run only if the sample has at least 30 rain-free days with E1 = 1 and at least 100 primary-set complaints from the TIDAL set on rain-free days. Otherwise the verdict is no_test.
UNIT. ZIP-set-day: the count of complaints per day for the TIDAL set and for the PLACEBO set (aggregated on the server with SoQL group by date and incident_zip, then summed in Python).
MODEL (primary). Negative binomial (NB2, log link) of the daily count on E1, with year fixed effects, month-of-year fixed effects and day-of-week fixed effects, fitted separately to the TIDAL and PLACEBO series. A stacked version with a group indicator and group interactions with all the same terms gives the TIDAL-over-PLACEBO ratio of rate ratios. Intervals: moving-block bootstrap over dates (blocks of 14 consecutive calendar days, 1000 replicates, TIDAL and PLACEBO resampled together, percentile 95 percent interval), which allows for serial correlation. The point estimate is exp(coefficient).
PRE-SPECIFIED SENSITIVITY CHECKS (reported, none decides the verdict): (1) E2 continuous tide in place of E1, per 10 cm; (2) E1 lagged one day; (3) C2 in place of C1; (4) TIDAL-BROAD in place of TIDAL; (5) rain-free defined as under 0.1 mm instead of under 1 mm; (6) Poisson with the same terms and the same bootstrap; (7) leave-one-year-out for the TIDAL rate ratio; (8) the same model on rainy days (PRCP >= 10 mm at either station) as a reference slope: reports are expected to follow rain far more than tide.
PLACEBOS. (a) PLACEBO ZIP set, as above. (b) Tide shifted: E1 assigned from the calendar day 7 days later, and separately from the day 100 days later, within the same rain-free sample, expected rate ratio about 1. (The shift is 7 and not 15 days because the spring-neap cycle repeats every about 14.8 days and a 15-day shift would reproduce the tidal phase.)
SECONDARY B (FloodNet, descriptive, never decides). Sensor-days from kb2e-tjy3 (date_installed to date_removed or 31 Oct 2026) for sensors flagged tidally_influenced = Yes and No; an event is a row of aq7i-eu5q with flood_start_time converted to local date; compute events per sensor-day on rain-free E1 = 1 days and rain-free E1 = 0 days for each group, with exact Poisson intervals treating sensors as independent, and the ratio of the two groups' rate ratios. Reported only if the event table loads; otherwise listed under what could not be done.
OUTCOME. Primary estimate and interval, placebo estimates, all checks, the count of rain-free flood days and of complaints, a figure in figures/further/, a section in docs/further.md. Verdict by the precedence rules in concord.claims.PRECEDENCE: support_if or refute_if decides; otherwise unsettled.
alternatives: Reports follow rainfall and sewer failure, not tide, so the true response to tide-only flooding is near zero because tidal nuisance flooding is brief, localised, expected by residents, and not reported to 311 (the flat-slope reading: 311 does not register the tidal hazard the city plans around).
Residents of the tidal ZIPs use other channels or do not report (reporting rates differ by tract: Agostini et al.), so a flat slope reflects reporting behaviour, not absence of flooding.

Tide height at the Battery is a poor proxy for water in Jamaica Bay and the Rockaways, which respond to wind set-up and have a different tidal range, so a flat slope reflects exposure misclassification.

Days at or above the threshold coincide with storms, nor'easters or wind events that bring rain locally but not at the two airport gauges, or that raise sewer backups, so any positive slope reflects weather, not tide (the rain-free restriction reduces but does not remove this).
Residual rain from the previous night or sewer surcharge after earlier rain keeps complaint counts high on days that happen to coincide with spring tides.
Seasonal confounding: perigean spring tides cluster in autumn and complaint rates vary by season (month terms address this only partly).

Part 2a is scored in prediction_scored as hit (95 percent t-interval of the OLS slope excludes 0 and contains 0.55), partial (contains both 0 and 0.55), or miss (excludes 0.55).
