claims.plan:
WHAT HAS BEEN SEEN. The first run (further-tidal-flooding-311) read 311 erm2-nwe9 for 1 Jan 2020 to 31 Oct 2026 for ALL ZIP codes (aggregated by day and ZIP; the tidal set, a FloodNet-based broad set and every other ZIP as placebo), with complaint sets C1 (street flooding) and C2 (C1 plus catch basin and sewer backup patterns), the descriptor counts for 2020 onward, daily Battery maxima 2020-2026 in MLLW, GHCN precipitation, and FloodNet events and sensors. Its results (listed in the literature field) were seen. No ZIP code is therefore unseen for 2020 onward, so the HELD-OUT unit is the PERIOD: 1 Jan 2010 to 31 Dec 2019 in the separate file 311 Service Requests from 2010 to 2019 (76ig-c548). The project's cache holds one query of that file (noise complaints, 'Noise - Street/Sidewalk' and 'Drinking', daily counts 2010-2019, from other claims); no flooding, sewer or catch-basin count of 2010-2019 has been queried, and the descriptor strings of that file have not been listed. The ZIP sets were fixed in the first registration from neighbourhood names and FloodNet sensor metadata, not from complaint counts, and are reused unchanged. Before registering I read the Battery daily maxima (hourly_height, datum MHHW, verified) and GHCN-Daily precipitation for 2010-2025, which are exposure data, and looked only at aggregate counts of dry days above water levels (by period 2010-2019 and 2020-2025, and for 2010-2025 in total, plus the number in a band of +/- 2.5 cm around 0.35 m). I did not look at counts by year, and I read no 311 flooding count for 2010-2019. For part 2 the 2020-2025 complaint counts are partly seen (daily C1 and C2 panel and yearly means from the first run; C3 below was not computed). The 2010-2025 tide-day counts by year were not seen.
THE KNOT. In the 2010-2019 dry sample (1,882 days after exclusions) the number of days with H at or above 0.563 m (the NOS minor flood level, 2.104 m above MLLW with MHHW 1.541 m above MLLW per CO-OPS datums, epoch 1983-2001) is 7, too few for the first claim's threshold. The knot is the highest 5 cm level at which the held-out dry sample holds at least 150 days: 0.35 m above MHHW (1.892 m above MLLW) gives 173 days (0.40 m gives 102, 0.45 m gives 55). The knot was chosen from the tide record alone and is not an estimate of where complaints begin; sensitivity checks move it.
SAMPLE. Calendar days 1 Jan 2010 to 31 Dec 2019. DRY DAY: GHCN-Daily PRCP under 1.0 mm at both Central Park (USW00094728) and JFK (USW00094789) on the day and the previous day, all four values non-missing. Days from 29 Oct 2012 to 30 Nov 2012 are dropped (Hurricane Sandy and its aftermath, when complaints reflect storm damage); the model with them kept is a sensitivity check. Days with fewer than 20 hourly Battery values are dropped (none in 2010-2025).
EXPOSURE. NOAA CO-OPS 8518750 The Battery, hourly_height, verified where available, datum MHHW, metric, local time (lst_ldt); calendar day is the local date; H is the daily maximum. x = max(0, (H - 0.35)/0.10).
ZIP SETS. TIDAL (primary): 11414; 11693, 11691, 11692, 11694, 11697; 11231; 11224. TIDAL-BROAD (secondary): TIDAL plus 10464, 11413, 11422, 10305, 10306, 10301, 10310, 10312, 10034. PLACEBO: every other ZIP with at least one 311 record in the sample, excluding TIDAL-BROAD.
COMPLAINTS. C3 (primary, 'street-flooding and catch-basin'): created_date in the sample and (upper(descriptor) like 'STREET FLOODING%' or upper(descriptor) like 'CATCH BASIN CLOGGED%' or upper(complaint_type) like '%STREET FLOOD%'). This matches, in the 2020 file, 'Street Flooding (SJ)', 'Catch Basin Clogged/Flooding (Use Comments) (SC)' and 'Catch Basin Clogged' and excludes sunken, grating, search, industrial-waste and sewer-backup descriptors. Patterns are fixed now; the 2010-2019 descriptor list is read only after this registration and any surprise is reported, not changed. C1 (secondary): street flooding only (descriptor like 'STREET FLOODING%' or complaint_type like '%STREET FLOOD%'). C4 (secondary): C3 plus descriptor like 'SEWER BACKUP%'.
MINIMUM-DATA RULE. The test is run only if the sample has at least 150 dry days with H at or above 0.35 m (exposure count already 173) and at least 1,500 C3 complaints from the TIDAL set on dry days (a mean of about 0.8 a day; below that the standard error exceeds 0.11 and the refute condition cannot be reached). Otherwise the verdict is no_test and C4 is not substituted.
CAN IT FAIL. Simulations on the actual 2010-2019 dry-day tide values (knot 0.35 m, NB2, dispersion 0.5 from the 2020-2026 C2 tidal series, year, month and weekday terms, 150 replicates per cell) give a model-based standard error of the log rate ratio per 10 cm of 0.11 at a baseline of 0.5 complaints a day, 0.084 at 1.0 and 0.07 at 2.0. Allowing 1.4 times that for serial correlation (block bootstrap), the standard error is 0.12 to 0.15 at a baseline of 0.5 to 1.0 and the minimum detectable effect at 80 percent power (2.8 standard errors) is a rate ratio of about 1.4 per 10 cm. If the true rate ratio is 1.00, the upper 95 percent limit is about 1.26 at a baseline of 1.0, so the refute condition (below 1.30) is reached in a little over half of such samples; if it is 1.2 (the first run's continuous figure), the lower limit is above 1.00 in about 45 percent of samples. The test can therefore fail in both directions but will often be unsettled; this is stated before the data are seen. Part 2a: with 329 dry days at or above 0.35 m in 16 years (mean 20.6 a year) the Poisson standard error of an OLS slope of annual counts on year is 0.25 days per year per year, against an implied slope of 0.55 (0.47 to 0.64 from the band count of 150 days within 2.5 cm of the knot, times 2.95 mm a year); a 95 percent t-interval (14 degrees of freedom) has half-width at least 0.53. Part 2b: the effect expected from part 1 at the registrant's centre (a rate ratio of 1.3 per 10 cm) is about 0.2 to 0.4 extra complaints per tide day on a baseline of about 190 dry-day complaints a year, a change in the annual total of 1 to 3 percent over the period, against year-to-year changes in 311 volume of tens of percent; at 16 years only a correlation of about 0.66 or more is detectable, so 2b is registered as descriptive and cannot support or refute anything.
MODEL (PART 1, primary). Negative binomial (NB2, log link) of the daily TIDAL count on x with year, month-of-year and day-of-week fixed effects; no linear term in H below the knot (the registered shape is flat below the knot and log-linear above it). The same model on the PLACEBO series. A stacked model with a group indicator and group interactions with all terms gives the tidal-over-placebo ratio of rate ratios. Intervals: moving-block bootstrap over dates (blocks of 14 consecutive days, 1,000 replicates, TIDAL and PLACEBO resampled together, percentile 95 percent interval). The point estimate is exp(coefficient).
PRE-SPECIFIED SENSITIVITY CHECKS (none decides): (1) knots at 0.30, 0.40 and 0.45 m; (2) log-linear in H over all dry days (per 10 cm), the shape of the first run; (3) binned dose-response, bands of H <0.30 (reference), 0.30-0.35, 0.35-0.40, 0.40-0.45 and 0.45 m or more, with a trend test across the bands; (4) C1 and C4 in place of C3; (5) TIDAL-BROAD in place of TIDAL; (6) Sandy window kept; (7) Poisson with the same terms and bootstrap; (8) leave-one-year-out; (9) the indicator for H at or above 0.563 m (NOS minor) reported with its day count; (10) dry defined as under 0.1 mm; (11) the same model on rainy days (PRCP at least 10 mm at either station) as a reference slope; (12) the 2020-2025 period, which is not held out, with the same model, reported only as a comparison of the held-out estimate with an in-sample estimate.
PLACEBOS. (a) PLACEBO ZIP set. (b) Tide shifted: x assigned from the calendar day 7 days later, and separately 100 days later, within the same dry sample.
PART 2a (TREND IN TIDE DAYS, exposure only). N_y = number of dry days in calendar year y with H at or above 0.35 m, y = 2010 to 2025 (dry days as defined above, all days of the year, Sandy window not dropped). OLS of N_y on y with a 95 percent t-interval on the slope (14 df). Checks: Poisson regression with log link and quasi-Poisson interval, Theil-Sen slope with a bootstrap over years, all days (not only dry) at or above 0.35 m, and the same count with H detrended by removing 2.95 mm a year (a null in which the trend has been taken out, to show what the slope would be without sea-level rise). The implied value 0.55 is fixed above; the registrant makes no other claim about the observed slope. Known alternatives: the 18.6-year nodal cycle and decadal wind and storm variability change annual counts by more than Poisson noise, and the local relative sea-level trend in 2010-2025 may differ from the 1856-2025 trend.
PART 2b (DESCRIPTIVE). For 2010-2025 (2010-2019 from 76ig-c548, 2020-2025 from erm2-nwe9), the annual TIDAL-set C3 complaints on dry days divided by the annual PLACEBO-set C3 complaints on dry days (a volume-normalised series), reported against N_y with a Spearman correlation and a Poisson regression with offset. The seen portion (2020-2025 C1 and C2) is disclosed above. It decides nothing.
OUTCOME. Estimates and intervals for part 1, all checks, the day and complaint counts, the part 2a slope and interval against 0.55, the 2b series, a figure in figures/round2/, a section in docs/round2.md. Verdict by concord.claims.PRECEDENCE with part 1 deciding.
alternatives: Reports follow rain that falls locally but not at the two airport gauges, and sewer surcharge after earlier rain, so a positive slope reflects weather and not tide.
Perigean spring tides cluster in autumn and complaint rates vary by season; month terms address this only partly.
The Battery is a poor proxy for water in Jamaica Bay and the Rockaways (wind set-up, a different range), so a flat slope reflects exposure misclassification.

311 reporting behaviour differs by tract and changed between 2010 and 2019 (the 311 app and web channels grew), so a flat slope may reflect low reporting of tidal nuisance flooding and a year-to-year trend in volume enters through the year terms only.
In 2010-2019 the tidal ZIPs had Hurricane Sandy repairs and Superstorm aftermath, and Sandy-driven changes in sewer use or reporting after 2012; the Sandy window is dropped but later effects are not.
The annual tide-day count varies with the 18.6-year nodal cycle, so a slope over 16 years need not equal the sea-level trend times the density of the distribution.

outcome.notes:
Held-out sample: 1882 dry days in 2010-2019 (Sandy window 29 Oct to 30 Nov 2012 dropped), 173 with maximum at or above 0.35 m MHHW, 2042 C3 complaints in the 8 coastal ZIPs and 28899 in the other ZIPs; minimum-data rule met. Only 7 dry days reached the NOS minor level (0.563 m), so the first claim's threshold could not be used. Registered 311 queries were run with agency = 'DEP' added and in one-year chunks because the unrestricted upper() LIKE query timed out; all matching records in 2010-2019 for the case-sensitive patterns belong to DEP (249,360 records including sewer backups). Checks, tidal rate ratio per 10 cm: knot 0.30 1.73, 0.40 2.38, 0.45 2.88; street flooding only 3.02 (2.36 to 4.22); with sewer backups 1.53; log-linear over all dry days 1.11 (1.06 to 1.15); 2020-2025 in-sample 2.13; shifted-tide placebos 0.99 and 0.97. The registered shape was flat below the knot, but the band model shows the complaint rate already above the reference in 0.30 to 0.35 m (rate ratio 1.34), so the rise is smooth, not a threshold. Part 2a: annual counts 2010-2025 range from 11 to 41 (2024); detrending the tide by 2.95 mm/yr gives a slope of 0.01 (-0.79 to 0.81); the gauge's own annual-mean slope over 2010-2025 is 4.0 mm/yr, above the long-term 2.95. The verdict is decided by part 1 alone as registered.

After the referee (13 Nov 2026): the referee reproduced the result with an independent bootstrap (2.00, 1.64 to 2.34) and it survives stricter dry-day rules, wind, season and influence checks. Three qualifications are added. The figure of 2.00 per 10 cm depends on the knot (1.73, 2.00, 2.38 and 2.88 at 0.30 to 0.45 m; 1.11 per 10 cm log-linear over all dry days) and should not be quoted as a general dose-response; the direction and the coastal specificity do not depend on it. The effect is concentrated in the Rockaway ZIP codes (2.01 to 2.52); Howard Beach, which supplies 625 of the 2,042 complaints, shows 1.25 (0.98 to 1.59) and Red Hook 1.10 (0.70 to 1.73). Several of the busiest dry days follow Hurricane Irene, and without the ten busiest days the estimate is 1.82 (1.60 to 2.17). The other-ZIP series also rises, so some common factor moves complaints citywide on high-water days. The referee added the strongest evidence against the weather rival: complaints in the coastal set follow the part of the water level that is predictable from lunar and seasonal periods (1.083 per 10 cm, SE 0.020) as well as the remainder (1.136, SE 0.022). In data/derived/round2/tidal_trend/graph_flood_findings.json the records under 'flooding -> post-traumatic stress disorder' with PMIDs 29344631, 32758312 and 24368465 are trials of a psychotherapy technique called flooding and are not flood evidence; docs/round2.md already says that the concept 'flooding' is mis-grounded, and no outcome cites those records.
outcome.verdict_note: Direction and coastal specificity are confirmed. The size (2.00 per 10 cm) depends on the knot and the effect is concentrated in the Rockaway ZIP codes.

prediction.magnitude: The claim's direction is +. The registrant's expected value for the weather-normalised Zone J energy trend (primary model, 2015-2025 excluding 2020-03-15 to 2021-06-30) is about 0.0 percent a year, with a plausible range of -0.6 to +0.6. For the weather-normalised summer daily-peak trend the expected value is about 0.0 percent a year, range -0.8 to +0.8. Zone K is expected in the same range, slightly lower.
prediction.support_if: Primary model (below): the energy trend point estimate is greater than +0.5 percent a year AND its 95 percent HAC confidence interval has a lower limit greater than 0 AND the summer-peak trend point estimate is greater than 0. All three must hold.
prediction.refute_if: The upper limit of the 95 percent HAC confidence interval for the energy trend is below +0.5 percent a year (growth, if any, is smaller than the registered threshold). The peak trend does not rescue the claim.
prediction.neither: Anything else (for example the interval straddles +0.5, or energy supports but the peak estimate is not positive) is unsettled.
prediction.secondary_gold_book: Reported and scored separately; it does not decide the verdict. If Zone J tables can be read from at least five editions, forecast growth error = F_e(t)/F_e(b) - R(t)/R(b), where e is the edition, b = e-1 is its last historical year, t is a target year up to 2025, F is the edition's Zone J baseline energy (GWh) and R is the realised weather-normalised energy from the primary model. Forecasts are called biased high if the mean growth error over editions at a three-year horizon is above +1 percentage point with a 95 percent bootstrap interval (over editions) excluding zero, and biased low if below -1 with interval excluding zero. With fewer than five readable editions this part is reported as not done.

data.name: NOAA GHCN-Daily, Central Park USW00094728 (TMAX, TMIN), via concord/noaa.py

plan.unit: Zone-day, 1 January 2015 to 31 December 2025. Daily energy (MWh) = sum of 5-minute load x 5/60. Daily peak (MW) = maximum 5-minute load. Days with fewer than 90 percent of the expected 5-minute readings are dropped and counted. Duplicate timestamps (daylight-saving fall-back) are averaged.
plan.weather: Daily mean temperature T = (TMAX+TMIN)/2 at Central Park. HDD = max(65-T,0); CDD = max(T-65,0) (degrees F). The temperature is converted from deg C to deg F.
plan.primary_model: OLS on days: ln(E_d) = a + b*t + g1*HDD + g2*HDD^2 + g3*CDD + g4*CDD^2 + g5*CDD_{d-1} + g6*CDD_{d-2 to d-3 mean} + day-of-week effects + US federal holiday indicator + month effects. t is years since 2015-01-01 (continuous). b is the trend; the reported trend is 100*(exp(b)-1) percent a year. 95 percent interval from Newey-West HAC standard errors with 14 lags. Days from 2020-03-15 to 2021-06-30 inclusive are excluded (the pre-specified pandemic rule, chosen as the period of stay-at-home orders and the staged reopening before the 1 July 2021 full reopening).
plan.peak_model: Summer days (1 June to 30 September): ln(P_d) = a + b*t + CDD, CDD^2, CDD_{d-1}, CDD mean of d-2..d-3 + day-of-week + holiday + month effects, same exclusion and HAC rules. Weather-normalised summer peak for a year = the model's predicted peak on a design day, defined as the weekday in July with CDD at the 90th percentile of July weekday CDD over 2015-2025 (CDD lags set to the same percentile values), for the year's own t. Trend of that series is reported as percent a year.
plan.annual_normalised_energy: Descriptive: the same energy model with year indicators in place of t; each year's weather-normalised energy is the sum over that year's calendar days of the predicted energy with HDD and CDD (and lags) set to the 2015-2025 mean for the same calendar day (15-day centred window). Years 2020 and 2021 are shown but flagged (pandemic days excluded from the fit, so those years are predicted from their non-excluded days only and marked as less reliable).
sensitivity_checks: S1 Include all days with a pandemic indicator for 2020-03-15 to 2021-06-30 instead of excluding them.
S3 Fit 2015-2019 only; and S4 fit 2022-2025 only (post-pandemic).
S5 Cooling base temperature 70 F and heating base 60 F.
S6 LaGuardia (USW00014732) weather in place of Central Park.
S7 Month x CDD interactions added.
S8 Annual moving-block bootstrap (resampling whole years is not feasible with 9 usable years, so 30-day blocks, 2000 draws) as an alternative interval.
plan.placebo: Zone K (Long Island, LONGIL) through the identical pipeline. Zone K has a different utility, building stock and tariff structure. The comparison is the difference J minus K in trend with a 30-day block bootstrap interval. It is a contrast, not a null: if K shows a trend of similar size, the Zone J result is not specific to New York City. A second placebo: re-run the primary Zone J model with the weather series from the calendar-shifted year (each date's weather taken from the same date three years earlier); the weather coefficients should lose most of their explanatory power (R-squared falls by more than half of the weather-attributable R-squared), which checks that the weather model is doing what is claimed.

confounders.behind_the_meter_solar: NYISO load is net of rooftop solar that offsets utility supply, so growth in solar lowers measured load and especially daytime and summer-peak load. Not corrected. Direction of bias: toward lower measured demand. Reported as a limitation; no correction is applied.
confounders.efficiency: Building and appliance efficiency lowers load; it is part of what the claim's 'demand' includes, so not corrected.
confounders.pandemic_occupancy: Office occupancy in Manhattan stayed below 2019 levels after 2021. Handled by the pandemic exclusion window and S1 to S4; the post-2021 baseline may still be lower than 2015-2019, which would put a level shift into the trend. S3 and S4 separate the two halves.
confounders.population_and_building_stock: Population, floor area and electrified heating change over time and are not separated from 'demand'.
confounders.data_quality: PAL real-time data are not settlement-quality and can contain gaps or spikes. Days failing the coverage rule are dropped; daily values above 3 x the zone's median daily value or below 0.3 x are flagged and the model is re-fit without them as a check.
confounders.weather_model: One station, no humidity or cloud cover, so heat-wave response is approximated. Residual weather variation inflates the interval, not necessarily the trend.
confounders.load_pocket_definition: Zone J is NYISO's N.Y.C. zone, which is Con Edison's city load; it does not include Westchester (Zone I).

plan.gold_book: For each edition from 2019 to 2026 that can be downloaded and parsed, extract the Zone J baseline energy (GWh) and summer coincident peak (MW) forecast tables with pdftotext; check each extracted row against the page text. Editions where extraction cannot be verified are dropped and listed.

alternatives: Flat demand: efficiency, rooftop solar and weaker office occupancy offset electrification, so the weather-normalised trend is within about +-0.5 percent a year of zero.
Growth confined to the post-pandemic recovery: a positive trend from 2021 to 2025 is a rebound to the pre-2020 level, not a new growth path (separated by S3 and S4).
Growth in peak but not energy, or the reverse, caused by changes in solar penetration and load shape.
Growth that is real but is mostly outside Zone J (upstate large loads, data centres), so the system-wide statement does not describe New York City.

Those data would separate a lasting drop in commercial load from a recovery.

outcome.notes:
Verdict follows PRECEDENCE rule 1: the registered refute_if (upper 95 percent limit of the energy trend below +0.5 percent a year) is met in the primary model and in every sensitivity check that uses the whole period (S1, S2, S5, S6, S7, S8). Zone K shows a similar decline (-0.86), so the Zone J result is not specific to New York City; Zone J is 0.11 points a year higher than Zone K (0.02 to 0.19). The shifted-weather placebo removed almost all of the weather-attributable R-squared (0.238 to 0.004), so the weather model captures real temperature dependence. PAL annual totals match the Gold Book's own historical Zone J energy within 1 percent in every year 2016 to 2025. Measured load is net of behind-the-meter solar, which rises over the period and lowers measured load; it is not corrected. Gold Book comparison used editions 2021 to 2025 (the 2026 edition has no past target years); at a three-year horizon only three editions apply (2021, 2022, 2023), with forecast-growth errors +3.0, -1.9 and -4.0 points, mean -1.0 (bootstrap -4.0 to +3.0), so neither registered bias condition is met. The 2021 edition's base year, 2020, is a pandemic year, and the normalised value for 2020 and 2021 is less reliable because most of those years' days were excluded from the fit. Exploratory and unregistered: against the Gold Book's own later historical values, forecast growth at three years was 2.6 points too low on average (-1.5, -3.1, -3.3). The HAC intervals are narrow because the daily model has thousands of days, but the trend rests on 9 to 11 years; the unregistered annual-level interval is wider but also excludes zero.

After the referee (13 Nov 2026): the registered interval is about three times too narrow. The trend is identified by nine to eleven years and residuals are correlated over much longer than 14 days. With standard errors clustered by year the trend is -0.752 (-1.027 to -0.475) percent a year; a bootstrap of whole calendar years gives -1.176 to -0.517. The upper limit is below +0.5 under every method, so the verdict does not depend on the interval. The result is a step and not a steady decline: a single step of -5.7% (-7.1 to -4.2) across the excluded pandemic window accounts for the whole negative trend, and with the step in the model the trend is +0.03 (-0.22 to +0.29) percent a year. The refutation condition is still met in the step model. After June 2021 the slope is +0.36 (about -0.02 to +0.75), so whether Zone J demand is growing now is open. The verdict means that the registered claim about Zone J over 2015 to 2025 was refuted. It does not contradict NYISO's statement, which concerns the whole state and forecasts. Measured load is net of behind-the-meter solar. The PAL series has no data for 1 to 24 April 2017 and 1 to 7 April 2021, which the outcome did not report. With three applicable Gold Book editions the registration called for that part to be reported as not done; the mean and interval given should be read that way. The `last_modified_range` in the source record is the alphabetical minimum and maximum of date strings and not a range of dates. The design-day peak series is a straight line by construction.
outcome.verdict_note: The registered claim of growth above 0.5 percent a year in Zone J over 2015 to 2025 is refuted. The decline is a step of about -5.7% across 2020 to 2021 and not a steady trend, and the result does not test NYISO's statewide forecast.

claims.plan: Unit: UHF42 neighbourhood (n = 42). Indicators: the 56 in analyses/graph_concordance/indicators.py, fixed before this registration; EHDP measures use the latest period with at least 40 areas reported, and an indicator with no such period is dropped. Project tables (shootings, vacant land, modelled noise, population density) are aggregated from tracts to UHF42 by the tract's representative point. Literature sign: for each pair, all API associations linking any concept of one indicator to any concept of the other, in either order; a finding is signed when tools/graph_evidence.normalise gives a direction, the statistic is not a group difference and it has no data-check flag; the sign is multiplied by the two polarities and flipped for each variable name carrying a negation word (analyses/graph_concordance/graph_signs.py). A pair qualifies with signed findings from at least 3 studies and at least 80% of signed findings on one side. City sign: Spearman correlation across neighbourhoods, raw, and partialled for poverty (correlation of the residuals of each indicator's ranks on poverty's ranks). The poverty-partialled correlation decides; for pairs that include poverty the raw correlation decides. Reported: agreement rate raw and deciding; the area-shuffle null; a 95% bootstrap interval from resampling neighbourhoods (2,000 draws); a second null that shuffles literature signs among qualifying pairs; the agreement a rule of 'always positive' would reach, since almost all qualifying literature signs are positive; agreement among pairs with |rho| of at least 0.2 and 0.3; and the rate with the five previously analysed pairs removed. Individual pairs, including the strongest disagreements and agreements (ranked by |deciding rho| among qualifying pairs), are exploratory leads and not tests. Pairs with a concept at both ends and no findings, and indicators with no concept, are listed as gaps. Disclosure: no city correlation for this matrix was computed before registration and no EHDP value was loaded in this study; only EHDP metadata (measure names, periods, geographies) was read to choose indicators. The project has already analysed, at UHF42, NO2 and PM2.5 against asthma ED visits (mob-asthma-pollution: positive after poverty adjustment, interval includes no effect), walking and cycling to work against obesity (mob-active-commute-obesity, graph-confounders-commute-obesity: negative), commute time against depression with exercise, obesity and subway access as covariates (commute-time-depression), and rodents, cockroaches and housing problems against child asthma ED visits (nbhd-rodents-asthma: positive); at tract level vacant land against shootings (nbhd-vacant-shootings: positive) and modelled noise against 311 complaints; at NTA and community district level green space, surface temperature, air conditioning and heat illness (heat claims). Of the 109 qualifying pairs, five overlap pairs whose direction the project has seen: [('asthma_adult', 'no2'), ('asthma_adult', 'pm25'), ('asthma_adult', 'cockroaches'), ('asthma_adult', 'poverty'), ('asthma_adult', 'asthma_child')]. The registrant also knows from general knowledge that NO2 and traffic are highest in Manhattan's wealthy core and that most adverse health outcomes in New York follow poverty.
alternatives: Ecological confounding: neighbourhood correlations reflect who lives where (poverty, age, race, migration), not the individual-level relation in the literature.

Common valence: nearly all qualifying literature signs are positive between two adverse conditions, so agreement may show only that adverse conditions cluster in the same neighbourhoods; the 'always positive' benchmark and the sign-shuffle null measure this.
Extraction and grounding error in the graph (about a fifth of API findings; negations in variable names) biases the literature sign.
Measurement: survey estimates for 42 areas are noisy, and self-reported diagnosis depends on access to care.
Dependence: pairs share indicators, so the effective number of independent pairs is much smaller than the count.

outcome.notes:
Raw agreement 79.8% (bootstrap 67.0% to 89.0%); deciding 66.1% (59.6% to 78.0%); area-shuffle null 95% range 40.4% to 58.7%. Agreement by kind of pair (deciding): {'air, traffic or noise with anything': {'n': 27, 'agree_deciding': 10, 'agree_raw': 10}, 'behaviour with anything else': {'n': 26, 'agree_deciding': 14, 'agree_raw': 21}, 'health outcome with health outcome': {'n': 41, 'agree_deciding': 34, 'agree_raw': 41}, 'social or housing condition with anything else': {'n': 15, 'agree_deciding': 14, 'agree_raw': 15}}. Without the five previously analysed pairs: 66.3%. Exploratory: without the negation rule 66.4% of 125 pairs; partialling population density as well as poverty 65.3% of 101. Correction to the registration text: 50 of the 56 indicators have a concept, not 48. The bootstrap interval is not centred on the estimate because resampling neighbourhoods with replacement creates ties. Several EHDP measures have no recent UHF42 release (pedestrian injuries and heat ED visits 2014, infant deaths 2013, housing conditions 2017, tree shade 2014, walkability 2011). Traffic volume is published as vehicle miles without an area denominator. The negation rule has false positives ('non-cystic fibrosis', 'compared to lowest quartile'). Individual pairs are exploratory.

After the referee (13 Nov 2026): the referee recommended unsettled. The verdict is kept as confirmed, because the registered support condition is written on the agreement rate itself (at least 60% and above the 97.5th percentile of the area-shuffle null, 58.7%), the rate is 66.1%, and rule 1 binds. What is confirmed is narrower than the registered statement reads. The test shows that these indicators, coded so that higher means more of an adverse condition, are positively correlated across neighbourhoods after partialling poverty. It does not show that the graph's signs carry information about the city. Of the 109 literature signs 105 are positive, and a rule that ignores the literature and always answers 'positive' scores 70 of 109 (64.2%) against the literature's 72 (66.1%). The four pairs with a negative literature sign split three to one (Fisher exact p = 0.13), and the registered sign-shuffle null gives p = 0.14. The exposure-with-outcome pairs, where the literature's sign says something about a cause, agree at 29 of 56 (51.8%), which is chance; the 41 pairs of two health outcomes agree at 82.9%, the same as always-positive. The lower bootstrap bound (59.6%) is below the 60% threshold and 5% of resamples fall below it, so the condition is met on a point estimate about 1.3 standard errors above its threshold (rule 10). An always-positive rule passes the 60% threshold in 78% of resamples, so a literature with no information beyond valence would usually have been confirmed. Seven indicators each appear in 12 to 19 pairs; leaving one indicator out moves the rate between 63.5% and 70.0%. A pair qualifies only with three studies and 80% consistency, and published associations between two adverse conditions are almost all positive, so the qualifying set holds almost no negative signs by construction. The stance is now measured against the always-positive rate and not against 50%.

stance.note: Measured against the always-positive rate of 64.2%, not against 50%: the stance is the agreement the literature's signs add beyond common valence.

outcome.verdict_note: Confirmed only in this sense: adverse indicators are positively correlated across neighbourhoods after partialling poverty. The literature's signs add two pairs in 109 to a rule that always answers 'positive' (66.1% against 64.2%; sign-shuffle p = 0.14), and exposure-with-outcome pairs agree at 29 of 56.

claims.plan: Unit: 42 UHF neighbourhoods. Data: EHDP at commit 547482b9df589006543e13e8cdf6546e00ed9998 through analyses/mobility/ehdp.py. Outcome, exposure and poverty exactly as in mob-active-commute-obesity (indicator 2063 measure 506, mean of 2017-2019; indicator 2415 measures 1304 + 1307, 2015-19; indicator 103 measure 221, 2015-19). New covariates, chosen from the graph's shared neighbours and matched to EHDP measures by reading only the EHDP metadata file (no values): education = indicator 2334 measure 1025, percent graduated high school, ACS 2015-19; race and ethnicity = indicator 2325 measures 988, 989, 987 (percent Black, Hispanic, Asian; White is the reference), ACS 2015-19; built environment and population density = indicator 2133 measure 673, walkability index, 2011 (the only period); crime and safety = indicator 2073 measure 1058, percent who perceive the neighbourhood as safe, mean of 2015 and 2016 (the only periods). Primary model: OLS of obesity on active share, poverty, high-school graduation, percent Black, percent Hispanic, percent Asian, walkability and perceived safety; HC3 standard errors; slope per 10 points. Secondary, reported and not deciding: (a) the same plus park access (indicator 2388 measure 1224, 2017) and unemployment (indicator 2337 measure 1032, 2015-19); (b) leave-one-covariate-out, to see which graph-named variable moves the estimate; (c) the analyst's own alternatives for comparison (poverty only; poverty and borough); (d) the model with the graph's mediator added (recent exercise, indicator 2060 measure 500, mean of 2017-2019), labelled as over-adjustment; (e) R2 of the active share on the covariates, as a collinearity check. Age structure and sex, which the graph also names, have no UHF42 measure in EHDP and are left out; this is stated as a limit. Missing values: complete cases, with n reported.
alternatives: Collinearity: walkability and the walk-to-work share measure nearly the same thing across 42 areas, so the adjusted slope may shrink only because its variance is inflated. The half-width condition and the leave-one-out table address this.

Over-adjustment: walkability may be a cause of walking to work only, with no other route to obesity, in which case adjusting for it removes real exposure variation. The leave-one-out result without walkability is reported.

Any eight covariates would attenuate a slope across 42 units. The comparison with the analyst's borough adjustment (-6.62, no attenuation) is the available check; a random-covariate comparison is not registered.
Residual composition: income above the poverty line, age and selection into walkable neighbourhoods remain unmeasured.

outcome.notes:
All 42 UHFs had every covariate. Secondary results, none deciding: with park access and unemployment added the slope is -3.25 (-5.63 to -0.87), inside the registered support range; without walkability it is -5.09 (-6.59 to -3.59); poverty with race and ethnicity alone gives -5.07 (-6.75 to -3.40); poverty with education alone -6.39 (-8.26 to -4.53); poverty with perceived safety -5.49 (-6.96 to -4.03). Race and ethnicity move the estimate most among the graph-named variables; education, which the graph ranks highest among them, moves it away from zero. Adding the graph's top-ranked shared concept, physical activity (recent exercise), which is a mediator, gives -2.61 (-4.69 to -0.54); an analyst who took the graph's ranked list without reading roles would have reported that figure. Every adjusted estimate remains several times the size individual studies imply. Age structure and sex, which the graph also names, were not available at UHF42 and were left out as registered.

After the referee (13 Nov 2026): the stance is set to null. It was computed from the sign of the adjusted slope (+0.876), but the claim is about attenuation of that slope and its prediction was a miss, so the value presented a missed prediction as strong agreement. A paired bootstrap over neighbourhoods gives an attenuation of 28% with a 95% interval from -14% to +64%; 0.42 of resamples fall in the support range and 0.30 in the refutation range, so the data cannot tell an attenuation of one third from none. The registered thresholds were applied to a point estimate (rule 10 now asks that the interval be reported beside such a threshold). Leaving out UHF 305 puts the estimate in the support range and leaving out UHF 307 puts it in the refutation range. Without Manhattan the slope is -7.60 (-12.98 to -2.22); with borough terms it is -4.16 (-8.43 to +0.11), so the HC3 interval is likely too narrow for contiguous neighbourhoods. The random-covariate comparison that the registration named and did not run was run by the referee: six noise covariates give slopes from -6.59 to -5.36 and none of 2,000 draws reaches -4.40, so the attenuation is not what any eight covariates produce. Derivation from the graph's sizes: if a share p of older adults lives alone and living alone multiplies their heat-illness risk by the odds ratio (8.1 or 42.3, treated as risk ratios for a rare outcome), the rate among older adults is proportional to 1 + p(OR - 1); raising p from 25% to 35% raises it by 26% (OR 8.1) or 36% (OR 42.3), about 0.023 to 0.031 in log rate per point. Older adults are assumed to carry 15% to 25% of an age-adjusted heat ED rate, so the all-age log rate rises by about 0.003 to 0.008 per point of living alone. The change in the temperature coefficient is minus that number times the partial slope of living alone on surface temperature. That partial slope has not been queried; with a between-district SD of living alone of 6 to 8 points, an SD of temperature of 2.0 F and a partial correlation of at most 0.4 in size it is at most 1.6 points per F, giving a change of at most 1.3% per F in size, and 5% only if the odds ratio applied to residents of every age. The sign is taken as negative because one-person households among older adults are expected to be more common in the central districts, which are the hot-surface districts.

claims.plan: Unit: community districts with the original covariates (55 expected). Outcome, exposure, poverty and percent Black are read unchanged from data/derived/heat/bridge_cd.csv. New covariates. Population density: EHDP indicator 2325 measure 992 (total population, ACS 2015-19, CD) divided by the district's land area from EHDP CD.geojson as computed in analyses/heat/bridge.py, in logs. Built-up area: building footprint share of land, the sum over tax lots of bldgarea/numfloors (lots with numfloors > 0 and bldgarea > 0) from PLUTO 64uk-42ks grouped by cd, divided by land area, in percent. Road area: the share of land outside tax lots, 100*(1 - sum of lotarea over lots that are not submerged (lottype not 9) / land area); streets and sidewalks are the land that is in no tax lot. Values are used as computed; districts with a share below 0 or above 60 are listed. Primary model: OLS of surface temperature on z(log tree density), poverty, percent Black, log population density, built-up share and road share, HC3 standard errors; the original model is refitted on the same rows; the change and its paired bootstrap interval (seed 20261113) are computed by analyses/round2_heat_confounders/reanalysis.py, written before this registration and not yet run. VIF is computed for every regressor of the graph-set model with an intercept. Secondary, reported and not deciding: each covariate alone; log built floor area per km2 in place of footprint share; EHDP traffic density (indicator 2112 measure 643, 2019, CD, log) in place of road share; vegetative cover (EHDP 2143) as the exposure; and the same primary model at NTA2010 (n about 190; original +0.44, 95% CI +0.15 to +0.73), with PLUTO grouped by borocode and ct2010 and assigned to NTAs through the 2010 tract-to-NTA equivalency table (8ius-dhrr) and population from indicator 2325 at NTA2010. Descriptive: the share of the tract-level variance of footprint share and floor-area ratio that lies between NTAs, to say what the neighbourhood fixed effects of heat-trees-canopy-within-nta remove. Timing: trees are from 2015, the Landsat scene from 17 July 2018, population from 2015-19 and PLUTO from version 26v2 (2026); buildings completed after 2018 are counted, which is a limit.
claims.power: The original slope has HC3 SE 0.272 (n = 55). The SE of the change is about sqrt(SE_graph^2 - SE_original^2). If the graph covariates explain half of the variance of tree density (VIF 2) and none of the residual variance of temperature, SE_graph is 0.39 and the SE of the change 0.27, so the smallest change detectable with 80% power at the 5% level is about 0.76 F per SD; with VIF 1.5 it is 0.54. The lower part of the predicted band (changes of -0.3 to -0.5) would therefore probably end as unsettled at district level. At NTA2010 the original SE is 0.148 and the same calculation gives a detectable change of 0.41 (VIF 2), which is why the NTA model is registered as a secondary. The test can fail in three ways: the change can be small, it can be positive (adding borough terms to the original raised the slope to +0.61), or the covariates can be too collinear.
alternatives: Mechanical coupling: street trees per km2 of land is street trees per km2 of street multiplied by the road share, so adjusting for road share changes the exposure into trees per unit of street. A fall in the slope then reflects a better exposure measure more than removed confounding. The road-only secondary model shows how much of the change this accounts for.

Over-adjustment: built-up share and vegetative cover are nearly complements, and built-up surface is part of what a tree-poor district is. The footprint share may absorb the effect of having few trees.
Any three district covariates move a slope across 55 units. The poverty and percent Black adjustment moved it by 0.01.
PLUTO is eight years later than the Landsat scene.

The claim is a bridge with an endpoint test and was registered more than six hours after rule 8, so its support condition could not be a test of direction only. The endpoint lies 3.81 standard errors from the composed prediction (1.0073) and 4.19 from no effect, D = 3.0, below the 4 that rule 8 requires, and the registration itself reported an expected D of 0.23. outcome.notes:
Two lines of run.py (170 and 224) were changed after registration: each reads the hour of a shooting as the text before the first colon in place of the first two characters. The earlier wording of this note (one line; unpadded times in 'the file'; no model had run) was inaccurate and was corrected after the referee. The incident file 5ucz-vwe8 has no unpadded time, and the two versions of line 170 give the same hour for all 24,429 incidents. The 390 unpadded times (of 29,744) are in the archived victim file 833y-fsy8, which only heat-school-out uses, so the registered script stopped at line 224. That line comes after the air-conditioning models in main(), so in the failed run those models had been fitted in memory; the script prints and writes only at its end, so no result was displayed or saved before the change. The change alters no number of the three claims' deciding models, none of which uses the hour. Neither changed line is used for heat calls. 15754 calls in May to September on 1920 days with at least one call. Registered secondary results. Bottom against top third -0.018 (-0.085 to 0.049). Within the low-income half -0.121 (-0.229 to -0.012); within the high-income half 0.057 (-0.038 to 0.153). Days with TMAX of 27 C or more -0.009 (-0.077 to 0.058). Without the six Manhattan districts below 59th Street -0.078 (-0.143 to -0.013): the slope is flatter in the low-AC half. District slopes on air-conditioning share per 10 points: 0.014 (-0.058 to 0.086) alone, 0.024 (-0.070 to 0.117) with income, 58 districts. The registered negative binomial fit of the high-AC half's own slope returned a degenerate interval (2.335 to 2.335) and is not used; an exploratory Poisson refit gives 6.835 (6.343 to 7.366) for the low-AC half and 7.011 (6.464 to 7.604) for the high-AC half. 97% of HEAT calls fall in May to September.

After the referee (13 Nov 2026): the verdict is kept. The referee rebuilt the series with separate code; the daily counts agree on all 3,183 days and the refit gives -0.032 (-0.088 to 0.024) on 1,920 days with at least one call. The refutation condition, an upper limit below 0.112 with a lower limit at or below 0, is met. Every full-sample variant the referee ran has a lower limit below 0 and an upper limit below 0.112: for example HAC errors with 7 lags -0.032 (-0.083 to 0.019), year-by-month terms -0.025 (-0.084 to 0.035), LaGuardia -0.020 (-0.070 to 0.030), JFK -0.012 (-0.065 to 0.041), days of 30 C or more -0.017 (-0.111 to 0.078), the night minimum in place of the maximum -0.063 (-0.129 to 0.002).
What the refutation excludes. The yardstick 0.112 assumes that every call comes from a home, that the odds ratio for death (0.23) applies to ambulance calls, and that the hot-day contrast is spread evenly over 10 C. With a share h of calls from homes the same formula gives 0.114 at h = 1 (the registration's 0.112 used unrounded shares), 0.064 at one half, 0.035 at one quarter and 0.021 at 15% (referee). The upper limit 0.024 equals the yardstick at h = 0.17 (re-checked by solving the formula). The result therefore excludes protection of households by air conditioning only if more than about 17% of HEAT calls come from homes. The data do not give that share, and 62% of calls fall between 12:00 and 17:59, which is consistent with many of them coming from outdoors. The comparison with the case-control studies is not like for like, and the outcome does not test them.
Records left out. Of 17,688 HEAT calls, 583 have no community district and 281 carry a code that is not one of the 59 districts (parks and airports), 864 in all. The share without a usable district is 5.8% on days below 30 C and 4.4% on days of 30 C or more, so the loss is not concentrated on hot days. The registered period is May to September 'to the last year in the file'; the calendar in common.py ends on 31 August 2026, so the 23 calls of September 2026 are left out. Neither changes the result.
The negative binomial failure. The dispersion estimate for the high-AC half diverges (to a value near 10^224 in the referee's fit), and count_fit in run.py accepts any finite dispersion above 0.0001, so the diverged value was passed to the model and the slope came back as 2.335 with an interval of no width. The low-AC half fits normally (dispersion 0.277, 6.675, 6.223 to 7.160). The deciding model is the binomial one and does not use count_fit. run.py is left as registered (rule 9); later scripts should bound the dispersion from above.
Rivals (referee). Income: within the low-income half -0.121 (-0.229 to -0.012) on 1,065 calls in six high-AC districts, within the high-income half 0.057 (-0.038 to 0.153), pooled -0.020 (-0.091 to 0.052); the strata differ in sign and the low-income result is one of several secondary results. Manhattan has 37% of HEAT calls and eight of its twelve districts are in the high-AC half; without Manhattan the difference is -0.075 (-0.148 to -0.003), and without Brooklyn 0.010 (-0.054 to 0.074). Period: 0.006 (-0.062 to 0.075) for 2006 to 2019 and -0.112 (-0.207 to -0.017) for 2020 to 2026, so the negative estimate comes from the recent years, when calls rose (1,483 in 2026 against 385 in 2020). Not addressed by any variant: residents of poorer districts may go to an emergency department on foot or not call, and dispatch coding of HEAT may differ between areas.
The day. 3% of HEAT calls fall between 00:00 and 05:59 (472 of the 15,754 in the model), so the definition of the day matters little here. Calendar date first (re-checked): primary -0.032 (-0.088 to 0.024) on calendar dates and -0.027 (-0.083 to 0.028) on the 06:00 day; bottom against top third -0.018 (-0.085 to 0.049) on calendar dates and -0.008 (-0.076 to 0.059) on the 06:00 day; low-income half -0.121 (-0.229 to -0.012) on calendar dates and -0.112 (-0.219 to -0.005) on the 06:00 day; high-income half 0.057 (-0.038 to 0.153) on calendar dates and 0.051 (-0.046 to 0.147) on the 06:00 day; days of 27 C or more -0.009 (-0.077 to 0.058) on calendar dates and -0.003 (-0.069 to 0.062) on the 06:00 day; without Manhattan below 59th Street -0.078 (-0.143 to -0.013) on calendar dates and -0.079 (-0.143 to -0.014) on the 06:00 day; Poisson rate ratios per 5 C, low half 6.835 (6.343 to 7.366) on calendar dates and 6.908 (6.420 to 7.433) on the 06:00 day and high half 7.011 (6.464 to 7.604) on calendar dates and 7.054 (6.507 to 7.648) on the 06:00 day. The refutation condition is met under both definitions. Exploratory, run after the outcomes, and deciding nothing under rule 4 (analyses/critique/round6_six_am_solutions.py; data/derived/round6_heat/six_am_solutions.json).
Stance. The stance is set to null. The value -0.505 read on the strip as city data disagreeing with the case-control studies, which this outcome does not test.

claims.statement: In US cities with many very hot days (Phoenix, Tucson, Dallas, Austin), police-recorded aggravated assaults are less frequent on days with a maximum temperature of 38 C or more than on days at 32 to 35 C in the same city, year, month and weekday position: violence turns down at extreme heat and does not keep rising in a straight line.

graph_evidence.summary: Xu et al. 2020 (nine US cities) report a linear temperature-homicide association, significant in Chicago and New York; Rahman et al. 2023 (California) report a monotonic association, +4.9% homicide per 5 C of same-day maximum. Both abstracts were read in PubMed on 13 Nov 2026. The graph stores three of the four values wrongly (percent stored as odds ratios), as docs/heat.md records; the shape words are from the abstracts.

Lyons et al. 2022 (100 US cities, shootings 2015 to 2020): risk rises almost monotonically with daily maximum temperature, with a local peak at the 84th percentile of each city's temperature range (relative risk 1.17, 1.12 to 1.21, against the median). Abstract read 13 Nov 2026. This is the only graph finding that describes a peak, and it places it at a percentile of the local climate, not at a fixed temperature.

claims.graph_evidence_note: Taken from the concept-level search cached in data/derived/graph/transfer_chicago/temp_violence_studies.json (13 temperature-violence relationships, 23 studies, most on suicide and injury). The graph's findings on temperature and violence therefore predict a monotonic rise (the refuting result here), with one hint of a percentile-based peak. A wider search of study variable names (analyses/heat_extremes/graph_shape.py) was still running when this was registered; its results are reported in docs/heat_extremes.md and did not inform the prediction.

prediction.magnitude: Downturn hypothesis: pooled rate ratio for days at or above 38 C against days at 32 to 35 C between 0.88 and 0.98. Linear-rise alternative: the slope below 35 C carried to the mean temperature of the days at or above 38 C, which is 6 to 9 C above the mean of the reference days; at the published slopes of 5 to 15% per 5 C this is a rate ratio of 1.06 to 1.25.
prediction.support_if: The 95% upper limit of the DerSimonian-Laird random-effects pooled rate ratio over Phoenix, Tucson, Dallas and Austin is below 1.00.
prediction.refute_if: The 95% lower limit of the same pooled rate ratio is above 1.00 (assaults are still more frequent at 38 C and above than at 32 to 35 C; no downturn).
prediction.otherwise: Unsettled: the pooled interval includes 1.00, which is what a plateau gives. The report then says whether the interval excludes the linear prediction computed in test.py (linear_alternative), and gives each city's estimate.

claims.plan:
Data, built by analyses/heat_extremes/build.py before this registration. Daily counts of police-recorded aggravated assaults by date of occurrence from each city's own portal: Phoenix (phoenixopendata.com crime CSV, UCR category AGGRAVATED ASSAULT, distinct incident numbers, Nov 2015 to Nov 2025), Tucson (Tucson Police reported-crimes feature layers 2018 to 2026, UCR summary ASSAULT, AGGRAVATED, distinct incident numbers), Dallas (dallasopendata.com qv6i-rri7, nibrs_crime beginning AGG ASSAULT, distinct incident numbers, 2017 on), Austin (data.austintexas.gov fdj4-gpfu, category Aggravated Assault, 2003 on), and for the descriptive curves Los Angeles (data.lacity.org 63jg-8b9z and 2nrs-mtv8, codes 230, 231, 235, 236, 2010 to 2023), Philadelphia (phl.carto.com incidents_part1_part2, the two Aggravated Assault codes, by dispatch date, 2006 on), Chicago (ijzp-q8t2, FBI codes 04A and 04B, 2006 on) and New York (qgea-i56i, felony assault ky_cd 106, 2006 to 2025). Series end 31 Aug 2026 unless stated. Temperature: GHCN-Daily TMAX at Phoenix Sky Harbor USW00023183, Tucson USW00023160, Dallas Love Field USW00013960, Austin Camp Mabry USW00013958, Los Angeles downtown USW00093134, Philadelphia USW00013739, Chicago Midway USW00014819, Central Park USW00094728.
Qualifying cities. A city enters the pooled test with at least 100 days at or above 38.0 C and 100 days at 32.0 to 34.9 C. From temperatures alone (power.py) these are Phoenix, Tucson, Dallas and Austin. US stations record whole degrees F, so the hot bin is 101 F and above and the reference bin is 90 to 94 F.
Model (analyses/heat_extremes/model.py and test.py, committed with this registration). Per city, a negative binomial GLM of the daily count on indicators for bins of TMAX (below 8, 8-14, 14-20, 20-23, 23-26, 26-29, 29-32, 32-35 as reference, 35-38, 38 and above) with C(dow) + C(month) + C(year) + hol + dom1 + wet, HC0 standard errors; alpha estimated once per city by maximum likelihood with a linear temperature term. The city estimate is the coefficient of the 38-and-above bin. The four log rate ratios are pooled by DerSimonian-Laird random effects; the pooled 95% interval decides the verdict. No resampling and no seed are involved.
Registered sensitivity, reported and not deciding: year-by-month strata in place of month and year; May to September only; without 2020 and 2021; the steps 35-38, 38-41 and 41-and-above each against 32-35; the fixed-effect pool; the linear prediction from the slope below 35 C.
Planned description, not deciding (analyses/heat_extremes/describe.py): the curve by 3 C bin for all eight cities and pooled; the curve by percentile of each city's own TMAX distribution; a comparison of stacked models with one curve common to all cities in degrees C against one common in percentiles (the adaptation question); piecewise-linear slopes below and above 35 C. Exploratory and labelled so: New York shootings by position in runs of days at or above 32 C.
alternatives: Plateau: the rate stops rising above about 35 C and neither falls nor rises (verdict unsettled).
Linear rise: the rate at 38 C and above exceeds the rate at 32 to 35 C by the amount the slope below 35 C predicts (verdict contested).
Seasonal confounding: days at 38 C and above fall in June to August and reference days in spring and autumn; month and year terms, and the year-by-month sensitivity, address this.
Recording: on very hot days fewer assaults may be reported or recorded on the day; the counts are by date of occurrence, which limits this, and it cannot be excluded.
Adaptation: the turning point may lie at a percentile of the local climate and not at a fixed temperature, in which case Phoenix and Austin would differ at 38 C.

can_it_fail.source: data/derived/heat_extremes/power.json, from analyses/heat_extremes/power.py (seed 20261113, 60 simulated series per scenario on the real calendars and temperatures).
can_it_fail.reading: With the larger dispersion tried (alpha 0.15) the pooled standard error is 0.022 on the log scale. The squared standardised distance between a downturn of 0.95 and a linear rise of 1.06 is 24, between 0.95 and 1.00 it is 5.3, and between 1.06 and 1.00 it is 6.8; all exceed the rule 8 threshold of 4. In simulation a true ratio of 1.00 gives 'unsettled' in 97% of series, a true 0.95 gives 'confirmed' in 40 to 68%, and a true 1.06 gives 'contested' in 63 to 83%. The test can therefore return any of the three verdicts.

outcome.notes:
Registered result. Pooled rate ratio 1.035 (1.008 to 1.063); Phoenix 1.038 (0.994 to 1.084), Tucson 1.062 (0.999 to 1.130), Dallas 0.977 (0.906 to 1.052), Austin 1.040 (0.994 to 1.087); I2 = 0.02. The point estimate at 38 C and above is 3.5% above 32 to 35 C, so there is no downturn at 38 C; the rate is level or slightly higher (reworded after the referee). It is also lower than the straight-line prediction from each city's slope below 35 C, 1.075 (1.064 to 1.086) (z = 2.6), so the rise slows. Planned description, not deciding: the piecewise-linear slope above 35 C is 1.003 (0.985 to 1.022) per 5 C against 1.060 (1.046 to 1.073) per 5 C from 20 to 35 C; the steps against 32 to 35 C are 1.010 for 35 to 38 C, 1.041 for 38 to 41 C and 1.007 for 41 C and above. The verdict label 'contested' means that the downturn hypothesis is refuted at 38 C. It comes from the literal condition, a lower limit above 1.00; the registration assigned a plateau to unsettled, and the curve above about 35 C is close to a plateau (reworded after the referee).

After the referee (13 Nov 2026): the verdict is kept and reworded. The referee rebuilt the four daily series from the raw files with separate code; the counts agree on every day and the refit gives 1.035 (1.008 to 1.063), Q = 3.07. The registered refutation condition, a lower limit above 1.00, is met, and rule 1 gives contested. The two conditions were met with very different margins, and the notes now say so.
The downturn. The support condition fails by a wide margin: z = 4.1 against the upper end of the predicted band (0.98), and no variant below has a lower limit under 0.98. The registered downturn at 38 C is excluded.
The rise. The refutation condition is met by 0.008 (z = 2.56 against 1.00, p = 0.010; no single city excludes 1.00). It is not met, that is the lower limit is at or below 1.00, with a Hartung-Knapp interval, the usual correction for a pool of four estimates (0.992 to 1.081); with the daily minimum in the model, 1.019 (0.984 to 1.056); with rain amount and the previous day's maximum, 1.022 (0.987 to 1.059); with second weather stations in Phoenix, Dallas and Austin, 1.017 (0.987 to 1.049); with the day from 06:00 to 05:59, 1.030 (0.993 to 1.069) in the referee's fit and 1.030 (0.994 to 1.068) with the registered code; without 2020 and 2021, 1.027 (0.997 to 1.057); with hot days in June to August only, 1.029 (0.997 to 1.061); with June to September and year-by-month terms, 1.034 (0.980 to 1.092); without 2018 (lower limit 0.998); and without Phoenix (0.989), Tucson (0.997) or Austin (0.989). The point estimate stays between 1.017 and 1.044 (referee). The earlier sentence that the condition was met 'by less than the sampling error (rule 10)' is withdrawn: rule 10 concerns conditions on a point estimate, and this one is on an interval bound.
Wording. The result is: no downturn at 38 C; the rate is level or slightly higher. It is not 'assaults are more frequent at 38 C and above'. The registration assigned a plateau to the verdict unsettled and a linear rise to contested. The label contested comes from the literal condition, a lower limit above 1.00, which a small rise well short of the linear prediction (1.075; the published band starts at 1.06, z = -1.8) meets. The earlier sentence that the data 'fit a plateau better than either registered alternative' described the alternative that the registration tied to unsettled.
Offence definitions. The four series are not the same offence. The Dallas file withholds family violence: 23,299 incidents are coded 'AGG ASSAULT - NFV' and 35 family violence. In Austin 47% of incidents carry the family-violence flag or a family or strangulation offence type (37% in 2003 to 2008, about 50% afterwards), and the category includes deadly conduct (7.5%). Phoenix and Tucson use a UCR summary category with no family-violence field. The difference does not explain the Dallas estimate: in Austin the ratio is 1.039 (0.976 to 1.106) for family violence and 1.038 (0.976 to 1.104) for the rest, and with Austin's non-family incidents the pool is 1.034 (1.005 to 1.064).
Phoenix records. From 3 September 2025 the Phoenix file carries no time of day, September 2025 has 417 incidents against about 570 a year earlier, and the count of all offence rows rises by 40% in October 2025, which looks like a change of records system. The file runs to 31 December 2025 and build.py ends the series on 30 November 2025; neither the registration nor the script gives the reason. Ending Phoenix on 31 August 2025 gives 1.037 for the city and the same pool.
Stations. Camp Mabry records 710 days at 38 C or more and Austin-Bergstrom 443; Sky Harbor 1,112 and Phoenix Deer Valley 854 on the same dates. A fixed threshold at a warm station is partly a comparison at a lower temperature across the city.
Night and hour (referee, exploratory). In Phoenix incidents of the night that follows a hot day rise by 1.129 (1.019 to 1.251) and afternoon and evening incidents do not (1.011, 0.956 to 1.069), so the excess at 38 C and above may belong to the night. Incidents from 12:00 to 23:59 give 0.894 (0.811 to 0.984) in Dallas, in the direction of the daylight downturn that Rotton and Cohn reported for that city; it is one of twelve cells and not significant after correction.
Degrees against percentiles. The statement that one curve in degrees fits better than one in percentiles is withdrawn as evidence on adaptation. The registrant's degree bins hold 2,700 to 6,400 days each and two percentile bins hold about 11,500 days each, so the comparison was unequal: 496 AIC units with those bins, 43 with ten equal-count bins on each scale, about 450 with splines of equal degrees of freedom. A scale of degrees from each city's own mean, which is a relative scale, fits as well as absolute degrees or better (3,053 against 2,822 units with ten bins; 3,227 against 3,217 with twenty). Among the hottest quarter of each city's days degrees are better by 4 to 17 units, and in the four hot cities alone percentiles are better by 5. The comparison shows that the curve is close to linear in degrees and that ranks distort it. It does not show that cities share one absolute curve.
New York heat waves (exploratory). The ratio for days two and later of a run at 32 C or more, 0.836 (0.739 to 0.946) for shootings, does not replicate with the same code in the two other cities with shooting series: Chicago 0.983 (0.913 to 1.057), Philadelphia 1.036 (0.912 to 1.177), the two together 0.996 (0.935 to 1.061). claims.plan: Primary mediator: daily count of FDNY EMS dispatches (76xm-jjuj) with initial_call_type 'DRUG' (drug and alcohol abuse) or 'DRUGFC', by date of incident_datetime, 2006-01-01 to 2026-08-31. Secondary mediators, reported but not deciding: (a) psychiatric dispatches, initial_call_type EDP, EDPC or EDPM, the graph's 'mental disorder' candidate; (b) 311 complaints of complaint_type 'Drinking' (public drinking), 2010-01-01 to 2026-08-31, from 76ig-c548 and erm2-nwe9. The call type DRUG does not separate alcohol from other drugs. Daily series for New York City. Shootings (5ucz-vwe8, distinct incident_key per occur_date), Central Park TMAX and PRCP (GHCN-Daily USW00094728) and the calendar terms are built exactly as in analyses/heat/shootings.py. Base model B0: negative binomial GLM of daily shooting incidents on TMAX/5, day of week, calendar month, year, holiday and rain >= 1 mm (alpha by ML, HC0 errors), refitted on the days for which the mediator exists. First link L1: the same model with the mediator's daily count as the outcome, giving the mediator's IRR per 5 C; and the same with a natural cubic spline of TMAX (4 df) to read the mediator's RR at 21, 27 and 33 C against 15 C. Mediator model B1: B0 plus log(1 + mediator count) on the same day. Attenuation A = 1 - b1/b0, where b0 and b1 are the coefficients of TMAX/5 in B0 and B1. Interval for A: 500 bootstrap resamples of calendar weeks (all seven days of a week kept together), alpha held at its full-sample value, 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles. This is mediation by proxy and not identification: the proxy measures the mediator with error, which pulls A toward zero; an unmeasured cause of both the mediator and shootings that is correlated with temperature pushes A upward; and conditioning on a mediator can open a path through such a cause. Pre-specified sensitivity, the same for every mediator: (s1) year-by-month fixed effects in place of month and year; (s2) 2020 and 2021 excluded; (s3) warm season May to September only; (s4) mediator on the previous day in place of the same day. If A under s1 falls on the other side of a decision threshold from the primary A, the verdict is unsettled. Already seen by the project before this registration: the daily shootings and Central Park temperature series and their relation (heat-shootings: IRR 1.146 per 5 C, 1.130 to 1.163; spline RR against the median TMAX 1.37 at 27 C, 1.46 at 30 C, 1.54 at 33 C); daily FDNY EMS dispatches of type SHOT, T-SHOT and STAB (bridge-shot-ems-link, bridge-heat-shootings-ems); the 2023 totals of EMS dispatches by initial call type (DRUG 88,621; EDP 98,371); 311 noise complaints of 2022-2024 summed by latitude and longitude, not by day (nbhd-noise311-exposure); daily 311 street-flooding complaints (further-tidal-flooding-311); and, for this registration, the number of rows and sensors per year and travel mode in ct66-47at (no count values). No daily series of 311 Noise - Street/Sidewalk, 311 Drinking, EMS DRUG or EDP dispatches, or bicycle counts has been queried or seen.
alternatives: EMS dispatches measure intoxication severe enough for an ambulance, not drinking among people who shoot or are shot; a small A may reflect a poor proxy and does not show that alcohol plays no part.
Dispatch volume depends on people being in public to be seen and reported, so DRUG calls may partly measure street activity.
Coding of call types changed over twenty years; year terms absorb level shifts but not within-year changes.

EMS drug and alcohol dispatches (mean 220 per day) rise 1.045 (1.041 to 1.048) per 5 C and keep rising at the hot end (1.030 (1.020 to 1.039) from 27 to 33 C). Adding them lowers the shootings IRR from 1.146 (1.130 to 1.163) to 1.124 (1.107 to 1.142). Sensitivity: year-by-month terms 0.165 (0.124 to 0.217); without 2020-2021 0.154; May-September 0.111; proxy lagged one day 0.028. The share falls to 0.028 when the proxy is taken from the previous day, so the association is between dispatches and shootings on the same day. Secondary proxies: psychiatric dispatches rise 1.021 (1.019 to 1.024) per 5 C and give A = -0.026 (-0.052 to -0.002), with a negative coefficient in the shootings model; 311 public drinking complaints rise 1.210 (1.191 to 1.229) per 5 C and give A = 0.031 (-0.009 to 0.073). The call type DRUG does not separate alcohol from other drugs, and dispatches may partly measure people in public view.

After the referee (13 Nov 2026): the referee found no error, and the share stays between 0.09 and 0.19 in every variant (0.154 in 2010 to 2019, 0.107 in 2022 to 2026, 0.017 for next-day dispatches). With street-noise complaints already in the model, drug dispatches still remove 0.166 (0.086 to 0.277) of the remaining slope, so the named alternative that dispatches measure people in public view does not account for the result as far as noise complaints measure street presence. The claim of no step is not supported (A is 5.9 standard errors from zero) and a step of a quarter of the slope is excluded (4.6 standard errors below 0.25); the registered rule has no verdict for a small non-zero share other than unsettled. Not addressed: same-day events such as parades, street parties and paydays, which produce both intoxication calls and shootings without heat acting through intoxication. The first-link hit is a match with a range the registrant built by assuming a reference temperature about 20 C cooler, which the abstract of Nori-Sarma et al. does not give.

claims.statement: People outdoors is a step between heat and shootings in New York City: daily 311 Noise - Street/Sidewalk complaints, a proxy for street activity, rise with the day's maximum temperature, and adding them to the daily model removes at least a quarter of the temperature slope of shootings.

graph_evidence.summary: Graph sign for the first link is negative. Kim et al. 2022 (Korea Community Health Survey 2018): odds of walking practice 0.95 (0.94 to 0.97) per 1 C of the preceding week's daily maximum in rural areas and 0.98 (0.97 to 1.00) in urban areas; the graph holds the rural value only. The second association returned (walking after fan precooling, rectal temperature) is a laboratory finding on body temperature and is noise here.

The relationship aggregates report 13 findings; the API returns one. Mora-Rodriguez et al. 2016 (573 adults, Spain, Greece, Germany): self-reported physical activity falls with ambient temperature, r = -0.277.

Ten laboratory findings on exercise time, intensity and heart rate in hot versus temperate chambers, signs mixed (6 plus, 3 minus); grounded to the concept 'hot'. They concern capacity under heat stress, not whether people are outdoors. Not read in abstract; not relied on.

Six of seven findings are negative and run from crime to walking (fear of crime, crime safety, violent crime reduce walking). The graph holds no finding that more people walking or outdoors raises violence; the second arrow of this pathway is absent from the graph.

concepts: violence side: violence, crime, aggression, anger, irritability, hostility, intimate partner violence
graph_evidence.summary: Eight of nine negative: neighbourhood crime lowers physical activity, and active adolescents report less fighting. Again the reverse direction or an individual trait, not a daily exposure effect.

Found only through variable names. Potgieter et al. 2022, Khayelitsha, South Africa, 2006-2016: days at or above 25 C raise the cumulative relative risk of violent crime by up to 32% (the graph stores RR 1.32 without an interval; the abstract gives none). A direct heat-violence finding that the concept search for temperature and violence did not return.

claims.plan: Primary mediator: daily count of 311 service requests with complaint_type 'Noise - Street/Sidewalk' by created_date, from 76ig-c548 (2010-2019) and erm2-nwe9 (2020 to present), 2010-01-01 to 2026-08-31. Secondary mediator, reported but not deciding: daily bicycle counts from ct66-47at (travelmode bike), summed over the sensors that report on at least 90% of the analysed days of a calendar year, year by year, 2014 to 2026; if the aggregation query does not complete, this is reported as not done. The shape comparison (spline RR at 27 and 33 C) is reported for both and is descriptive. Daily series for New York City. Shootings (5ucz-vwe8, distinct incident_key per occur_date), Central Park TMAX and PRCP (GHCN-Daily USW00094728) and the calendar terms are built exactly as in analyses/heat/shootings.py. Base model B0: negative binomial GLM of daily shooting incidents on TMAX/5, day of week, calendar month, year, holiday and rain >= 1 mm (alpha by ML, HC0 errors), refitted on the days for which the mediator exists. First link L1: the same model with the mediator's daily count as the outcome, giving the mediator's IRR per 5 C; and the same with a natural cubic spline of TMAX (4 df) to read the mediator's RR at 21, 27 and 33 C against 15 C. Mediator model B1: B0 plus log(1 + mediator count) on the same day. Attenuation A = 1 - b1/b0, where b0 and b1 are the coefficients of TMAX/5 in B0 and B1. Interval for A: 500 bootstrap resamples of calendar weeks (all seven days of a week kept together), alpha held at its full-sample value, 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles. This is mediation by proxy and not identification: the proxy measures the mediator with error, which pulls A toward zero; an unmeasured cause of both the mediator and shootings that is correlated with temperature pushes A upward; and conditioning on a mediator can open a path through such a cause. Pre-specified sensitivity, the same for every mediator: (s1) year-by-month fixed effects in place of month and year; (s2) 2020 and 2021 excluded; (s3) warm season May to September only; (s4) mediator on the previous day in place of the same day. If A under s1 falls on the other side of a decision threshold from the primary A, the verdict is unsettled. Already seen by the project before this registration: the daily shootings and Central Park temperature series and their relation (heat-shootings: IRR 1.146 per 5 C, 1.130 to 1.163; spline RR against the median TMAX 1.37 at 27 C, 1.46 at 30 C, 1.54 at 33 C); daily FDNY EMS dispatches of type SHOT, T-SHOT and STAB (bridge-shot-ems-link, bridge-heat-shootings-ems); the 2023 totals of EMS dispatches by initial call type (DRUG 88,621; EDP 98,371); 311 noise complaints of 2022-2024 summed by latitude and longitude, not by day (nbhd-noise311-exposure); daily 311 street-flooding complaints (further-tidal-flooding-311); and, for this registration, the number of rows and sensors per year and travel mode in ct66-47at (no count values). No daily series of 311 Noise - Street/Sidewalk, 311 Drinking, EMS DRUG or EDP dispatches, or bicycle counts has been queried or seen.
alternatives: Noise complaints rise in heat because windows are open and complainants are at home, not because more people are on the street; the proxy then overstates the first link.
Complaints and shootings share causes other than temperature within a month (block parties, holidays, the summer of 2020); sensitivity s1 and s2 address part of this.
Physiology (irritability, sleep loss) acts on the same days; a positive A does not exclude it, and a small A may reflect a poor proxy.
Bicycle counts on bridges and commuter routes measure travel, not people lingering outdoors at night when most shootings occur.

outcome.notes:
Verdict by the registered rule: the proxy rises with temperature, its coefficient in the shootings model is positive (0.229, 0.181 to 0.277 per unit of log complaints), A = 0.440 (0.327 to 0.564) on 6087 days, and the year-by-month sensitivity stays above 0.25. Shootings IRR per 5 C falls from 1.151 (1.132 to 1.170) to 1.082 (1.060 to 1.104). Sensitivity: year-by-month terms 0.322 (0.214 to 0.438); without 2020-2021 0.335; May-September 0.203; proxy lagged one day 0.254. The secondary proxy disagrees: bicycle counts (IRR 1.197 (1.182 to 1.213) per 5 C, 4508 days from 2014) give A = 0.039 (-0.048 to 0.132). 311 public drinking complaints, registered under heat-mech-intox, also rise with heat (IRR 1.210 (1.191 to 1.229)) and give A = 0.031 (-0.009 to 0.073). So a series that rises with heat does not by that fact remove the slope; the noise complaints share day-to-day variation with shootings that the other two series lack. This is mediation by proxy. Exploratory, run after the outcome: with a spline of temperature, adding the noise proxy lowers the rise in shootings from 15 to 21 C from 1.303 (1.253 to 1.355) to 1.153 (1.100 to 1.208) and from 21 to 27 C from 1.251 (1.213 to 1.289) to 1.167 (1.130 to 1.206), and leaves the rise from 27 to 33 C unchanged (1.126 (1.069 to 1.185) and 1.138 (1.081 to 1.197)). Bicycle panel sensors per year: {'2014': 8, '2015': 9, '2016': 9, '2017': 12, '2018': 11, '2019': 13, '2020': 14, '2021': 14, '2022': 14, '2023': 19, '2024': 25, '2025': 25, '2026': 17}.

After the referee (13 Nov 2026): the share removed by street-noise complaints is not stable over time. It is 0.24 (0.14 to 0.37) in 2010 to 2019, just under the 0.25 threshold, and 0.84 (0.51 to 1.36) in 2022 to 2026 (referee; re-run). The pooled 0.44 averages two regimes of 311 use, and the registered sensitivity without 2020 and 2021 (0.335) does not show this. On the 2010 to 2019 data alone the claim would have been unsettled. A negative control was run: next-day complaints, which today's street activity cannot cause, remove 0.10 (0.05 to 0.16) of the slope, and complaints seven days later or earlier remove 0.007 and 0.004. A small part of the same-day share therefore comes from variation that complaints and shootings share over a few days. After 2020 complaints are four to ten times their 2010 to 2014 level; either the proxy became a better measure of street gatherings, or complaints now respond to the same gatherings, disorder and police presence that go with shootings, which is a common cause and not a step from heat. The data cannot separate the two. Of three proxies that rise with heat, only this one removes the slope. The graph_effect entry records Kim 2022's rural odds ratio (0.95); the urban value, 0.98 (0.97 to 1.00), is the relevant one for New York, and the study concerns habitual walking over a week in Korea, so no comparison of size can be made.

After the referee of heat-night-minimum (13 Nov 2026): the shootings series of this claim is counted by calendar date, so it includes shootings between 00:00 and 05:59 that precede the day's maximum (35% of incidents). The referee of heat-night-minimum raised this. With shootings assigned to the night-of day (06:00 to 05:59) and the registered procedure otherwise unchanged (500 week resamples, seed 1), the share removed by street-noise complaints is 0.53 (0.41 to 0.66) against 0.44 (0.33 to 0.56) as registered, and 0.41 (0.30 to 0.54) with year-by-month terms (registered 0.32). The shootings slope is 1.143 (1.123 to 1.162) per 5 C and 1.065 (1.042 to 1.088) with the proxy. Complaints created between 00:00 and 05:59 are 28% of the total; with complaints moved to the night-of day as well the share is 0.55 (0.44 to 0.69), and 0.46 (0.36 to 0.60) with year-by-month terms. Every registered condition is met under each assignment, so the calendar-day count did not produce the confirmation; the share is larger on night-of counts. The instability over time that the first referee found was not re-examined on night-of counts. The hot-end comparison is weaker than reported. The rise in shootings from 27 to 33 C, scored above as 1.122 (1.072 to 1.173), is 1.090 (1.041 to 1.141) on night-of counts with the same 4-df spline and 1.051 (0.988 to 1.118) with the piecewise-linear basis of round 2, whose interval includes 1. Complaints and bicycle counts still stop rising at 27 C; the excess in shootings that they do not explain is a quarter to a half smaller on the log scale than stated, and part of the stated excess is shootings after midnight on the hot date. Exploratory, run after the outcomes, and deciding nothing under rule 4 (analyses/critique/round5_night_of_check.py; data/derived/round5/heat_night/night_of_check.json).
