claims.statement: On days with a maximum of 27 C or more, shootings in New York rise with the preceding night's minimum temperature at a fixed daily maximum, and the rise in shootings from 27 to 33 C falls in the hours from 18:00 to 05:59 more than in the hours from 06:00 to 17:59; the same holds in Chicago.

graph_evidence.summary: Two findings, both on indoor temperature. Valham 2012 (randomised crossover, 40 untreated sleep apnoea patients, Sweden): sleep efficiency 6 points lower at 24 C room temperature than at 16 C (71 against 77%, P = 0.012); the abstract adds 30 minutes less total sleep, which the graph does not hold. The other finding is on cold rooms (17 C or less, difficulty initiating sleep, OR 1.79). Neither uses outdoor night temperature.

concepts: bedroom temperature during sleep (variable, grounded to sleep quality)
graph_evidence.summary: Lappharat 2018 (63 sleep apnoea patients, Bangkok): adjusted odds of poor sleep quality 1.46 (1.01 to 2.10) with higher measured bedroom temperature.
The relationship records report 8 findings in 5 studies; the association endpoint returns none of them, as found on 12 November.

Zuurbier 2021 (113 homes of elderly people, two Dutch cities, warm episode): the graph stores r = 0.34; the abstract gives R2 = 0.34 for bedrooms, so the correlation is about 0.58. No slope in degrees per degree is given.

concepts: night or minimum outdoor temperature (variable names)
graph_evidence.summary: Variable-name searches for night temperature, nighttime temperature, nocturnal temperature, minimum temperature, hot nights, tropical night and bedroom temperature and sleep temperature returned about 200 variables (the minimum temperature search is capped at 100). The 23 that name outdoor night heat or bedroom temperature link to preterm birth, mortality, heat hospitalisation, anthrax, eczema, cholesterol, body mass and crop yield. None links to sleep duration, aggression, violence or injury. None of the first 100 sleep duration variables names temperature.

Street 2016 (1,878 Boston high school students): adjusted odds of moderate physical aggression against peers 0.90 (0.81 to 1.00) per hour of sleep. Van Veen 2022 (meta-analysis, 76,761 participants): correlation -0.16 (-0.19 to -0.12) in observational studies; standardised difference after experimental sleep restriction -0.37 (-0.80 to 0.05). One further finding (reactive aggression, aOR 3.13) is on short against adequate sleep.

Every signed finding says worse sleep goes with more aggression (for example preschool children sleeping under 9.44 hours, aggression OR 1.81, 1.36 to 2.41, Scharf 2013). Eight of the 18 run the other way in time: violence exposure as a cause of poor sleep.

claims.graph_evidence_note: Collected on 13 November 2026 by analyses/round5/heat_night/graph.py and variable-name searches, API only (the Dataverse copy is not on this machine), 124 uncached requests; data/derived/round5/heat_night/graph.json. Valham 2012, Lappharat 2018, Street 2016, Van Veen 2022, Zuurbier 2021 and Scharf 2013 were read in PubMed on 13 November 2026. The graph's values match the abstracts except Zuurbier's, where an R2 is stored as r.

composed_prediction.reading: The graph-sized sleep path predicts a rate ratio of about 1.012 (1.000 to 1.031) per 5 C of night minimum. The expected standard error of the endpoint is 0.037 in New York and 0.021 in Chicago, so D is 0.127 and 0.372, far below 4. The test cannot detect an effect of the composed size and is not registered as an endpoint test of the chain (rule 8). It is registered as a test of whether the night minimum carries a large part of the hot-day excess.

prediction.magnitude: (a) New York: rate ratio between 0.98 and 1.08 per 5 C of the preceding night's minimum at fixed maximum, on days with TMAX of 27 C or more; best guess 1.03. Chicago: 0.98 to 1.06. (b) The ratio 33 against 27 C is 1.08 to 1.20 for night shootings and 0.98 to 1.12 for day shootings in New York, and 1.03 to 1.12 and 0.97 to 1.08 in Chicago; the ratio of the night ratio to the day ratio is above 1 in both cities, with an interval that probably includes 1.

prediction.refute_if: (a) in New York: the 95% upper limit is below 1.075 and the lower limit is at or below 1.00. 1.075 is the rate ratio per 5 C of minimum that would carry half of the New York hot-day excess (1.122 from 27 to 33 C), given that TMIN rises 0.66 C per C of TMAX on hot days: exp(0.5 x ln 1.122 x 5 / (6 x 0.66)).
prediction.secondary_registered: (b) For each city, the ratio 33 against 27 C for day shootings and for night shootings, and the ratio of the two from the binomial model. Part (b) is 'met' when the 95% lower limit of the night-over-day ratio of ratios is above 1.00, 'reversed' when its upper limit is below 1.00, otherwise 'not separated'. (c) Chicago is scored on (a) by the same rule with its own threshold 1.035 (half of its excess of 1.058; TMIN rises 0.686 C per C of TMAX). The replication is 'replicated' when Chicago's (a) falls on the same side as New York's (both support, or both refute), 'not replicated' when they fall on opposite sides, otherwise 'inconclusive'. Parts (b) and (c) are reported and do not decide the verdict. The inverse-variance mean of the two cities' log rate ratios is reported.

claims.plan:
Script: analyses/round5/heat_night/run.py at commit 19037d5, run unchanged; model code analyses/round2/hot_end/model.py (SPLINE = 'lin', knots 15, 21, 27 C). No resampling and no random numbers: all intervals are Wald intervals from HC0 standard errors (PRECEDENCE rule 9).
Data. New York: NYPD shooting incidents 5ucz-vwe8, one row per incident_key with occur_date and occur_time, 2006-01-01 to 2026-08-31; Central Park GHCN-Daily (USW00094728) TMAX, TMIN, PRCP through concord/noaa.py. Chicago: Violence Reduction victims gumc-mgzr, distinct case_number with gunshot injury, time from the date field, 2010-01-01 to 2026-08-31, through concord/socrata.py with DOMAIN set to data.cityofchicago.org; Midway (USW00014819).
Day. A shooting day d runs from 06:00 on date d to 05:59 on d+1 (last shooting day 2026-08-30). Day shootings fall from 06:00 to 17:59, night shootings from 18:00 to 05:59. TMAX is that of date d. The preceding night's minimum is TMIN of date d, which normally falls near dawn before the shooting day begins; the following night's minimum is TMIN of d+1. Calendar terms are those of date d: C(dow) + C(month) + C(year) + hol + wet, as in heat-shootings.
(a) Shooting days with TMAX >= 27 C: negative binomial GLM, log link, of the count on TMAX/5 + TMIN/5 + calendar terms. On these days the registered piecewise-linear spline has a single free slope, so TMAX enters linearly. Dispersion by maximum likelihood from the model without TMIN.
(b) All shooting days: the piecewise-linear TMAX spline and calendar terms, no TMIN, fitted to day and to night shootings; ratio 33 against 27 C for each; the ratio of the ratios from a binomial GLM of night shootings out of the shooting day's shootings on the same terms.
Pre-specified secondary results, reported and not deciding: (a) for day and for night shootings; calendar-day counts; the following night's minimum alone and together with the preceding one (a sleep path predicts the preceding night, heat carried into the evening predicts the following night and night shootings); previous-day TMAX added; TMAX >= 30 C; June to August; the ratio 33 against 27 C by six-hour block; the all-day spline model with TMIN added, to show how much of the 33 against 27 C ratio remains; the hourly distribution of shootings by TMAX band (21-27, 27-30, 30 C and over) as a table.
Figure: the night-minimum rate ratios and the day and night hot-day ratios for the two cities.

can_it_fail.source: data/derived/round5/heat_night/prereg_design.json (analyses/round5/heat_night/design.py; weather and calendar only, Fisher information at the published hot-day mean count)
can_it_fail.reading: The smallest rate ratio per 5 C of minimum detectable with 80% power is 1.108 in New York and 1.062 in Chicago. If the night minimum has no effect, the refutation rule is met with probability 0.508 in New York and the support rule with 0.025. If the minimum carries half the excess, support is met with probability 0.508. An unsettled verdict is therefore likely (about one half) under either truth; the test can fail in both directions and cannot be passed by a null result.

claims.already_seen: TMAX-only models of shootings are seen in both cities (linear, 4-df spline, piecewise-linear; New York 33 against 27 C 1.122, 1.048 to 1.202; Chicago 1.058, 1.014 to 1.105). Two earlier scripts fitted TMIN in place of TMAX, alone, on all days: heat-shootings (1.164 per 5 C of TMIN, 1.143 to 1.185) and transfer-chicago-heat-shootings (1.133, 1.119 to 1.147); I read both values. The referee of heat-mech-outdoors added TMIN, previous-day TMAX and rain amount together to an all-day linear model and reported only that the TMAX slope fell from 0.141 to 0.095 per 5 C (critique/heat-mech-outdoors.md); no TMIN coefficient was reported. That drop suggests TMIN or yesterday's TMAX carries about a third of the all-day linear slope, which is known before this test and is why the prediction is positive. No model with TMIN and TMAX together on hot days, and no model, table or query of shootings by hour of day, exists in the repository, the Socrata cache or the documents (searched for TMIN, occur_time, hour). I fitted none before registering. design.py read weather and calendar columns and the published tables of mean count by TMAX bin. run.py was tested before registration on simulated Poisson counts with the real Central Park weather; no shooting record was read.
alternatives: TMIN at fixed TMAX measures humidity and cloud (humid days have warm nights), so a positive coefficient may be humid heat during the day and not the night.
TMIN of date d correlates with TMAX of d-1; heat carried over from the previous day would appear as a night effect. The previous-day TMAX variant addresses it.
The GHCN minimum is the minimum of the calendar day and sometimes falls late in the evening after a front, not at dawn; this adds error to the preceding-night measure.
One station per city: Central Park is cooler at night than dense residential blocks, and Midway differs from the lakefront.
A warmer night keeps people outdoors later, so a night effect on night shootings is also a routine-activity effect and does not by itself show a sleep path.
Reported times of shootings are approximate, and the six-hour shift assigns early-morning shootings to the evening before, which is right for most and wrong for some.

graph_effect.label: Composed from graph findings: room temperature to sleep (Valham 2012) and sleep to aggression (Street 2016), with an assumed outdoor-to-bedroom slope

graph_evidence.summary: Two findings, both on indoor temperature. Valham 2012 (randomised crossover, 40 untreated sleep apnoea patients, Sweden): sleep efficiency 6 points lower at 24 C room temperature than at 16 C (71 against 77%, P = 0.012); the abstract adds 30 minutes less total sleep, which the graph does not hold. The other finding is on cold rooms (17 C or less, difficulty initiating sleep, OR 1.79). Neither uses outdoor night temperature.

concepts: bedroom temperature during sleep (variable, grounded to sleep quality)
graph_evidence.summary: Lappharat 2018 (63 sleep apnoea patients, Bangkok): adjusted odds of poor sleep quality 1.46 (1.01 to 2.10) with higher measured bedroom temperature.
The relationship records report 8 findings in 5 studies; the association endpoint returns none of them, as found on 12 November.

Zuurbier 2021 (113 homes of elderly people, two Dutch cities, warm episode): the graph stores r = 0.34; the abstract gives R2 = 0.34 for bedrooms, so the correlation is about 0.58. No slope in degrees per degree is given.

concepts: night or minimum outdoor temperature (variable names)
graph_evidence.summary: Variable-name searches for night temperature, nighttime temperature, nocturnal temperature, minimum temperature, hot nights, tropical night and bedroom temperature and sleep temperature returned about 200 variables (the minimum temperature search is capped at 100). The 23 that name outdoor night heat or bedroom temperature link to preterm birth, mortality, heat hospitalisation, anthrax, eczema, cholesterol, body mass and crop yield. None links to sleep duration, aggression, violence or injury. None of the first 100 sleep duration variables names temperature.

Street 2016 (1,878 Boston high school students): adjusted odds of moderate physical aggression against peers 0.90 (0.81 to 1.00) per hour of sleep. Van Veen 2022 (meta-analysis, 76,761 participants): correlation -0.16 (-0.19 to -0.12) in observational studies; standardised difference after experimental sleep restriction -0.37 (-0.80 to 0.05). One further finding (reactive aggression, aOR 3.13) is on short against adequate sleep.

Every signed finding says worse sleep goes with more aggression (for example preschool children sleeping under 9.44 hours, aggression OR 1.81, 1.36 to 2.41, Scharf 2013). Eight of the 18 run the other way in time: violence exposure as a cause of poor sleep.

outcome.notes:
Registered secondary results. The following night's minimum (TMIN of d+1), not the preceding one, carries a rate ratio above 1 on hot days: New York 1.112 (1.049 to 1.179), Chicago 1.064 (1.023 to 1.106); with both minima in the model the preceding night is 1.000 (0.929 to 1.076) and 0.992 (0.948 to 1.038) and the following night 1.112 (1.047 to 1.181) and 1.066 (1.023 to 1.110). For night shootings the following-night ratio is 1.171 (1.094 to 1.253) and 1.081 (1.032 to 1.133); for day shootings 0.927 (0.820 to 1.048) and 1.034 (0.968 to 1.104). By six-hour block, the interval of the ratio 33 against 27 C excludes 1 only from 00:00 to 05:59: New York 1.128 (1.021 to 1.246), Chicago 1.129 (1.040 to 1.226); from 18:00 to 23:59 it is 1.001 (0.917 to 1.094) and 1.010 (0.948 to 1.075). In the all-day spline model with both minima, the 33 against 27 C ratio is 1.011 (0.946 to 1.081) in New York and 1.014 (0.967 to 1.063) in Chicago. On shooting days (06:00 to 05:59) the 33 against 27 C ratio for all shootings is 1.051 (0.988 to 1.118) in New York and 1.035 (0.991 to 1.082) in Chicago, smaller than on calendar days. Exploratory, after the results (analyses/round5/heat_night/exploratory.py): on calendar-day counts the same data give 1.102 (1.038 to 1.171) and 1.059 (1.014 to 1.105), so in New York about half of the published hot-day excess comes from shootings before 06:00 on the hot date, which precede that day's maximum. The pooled two-city estimate for the preceding night is 1.016 (0.979 to 1.054). The composed graph prediction, 1.012 (1.000 to 1.031), lies inside both cities' intervals, and so does 1.00; the test does not discriminate (D 0.13 and 0.37).

After the referee (13 Nov 2026): the verdict is kept. The referee rebuilt both daily series with separate code and reproduced every reported number, and none of twelve further specifications of part (a) changes the verdict: the New York estimate lies between 0.997 (LaGuardia) and 1.060 (previous day's maximum and minimum added), every interval includes 1.00 and every New York upper limit is above 1.075, so 1.033 is not a measured effect. The corrections follow.
Units. The ratios for 00:00 to 05:59, 1.128 (1.021 to 1.246) in New York and 1.129 (1.040 to 1.226) in Chicago, are for 33 against 27 C of the daily maximum, which is 6 C. Per 5 C they are 1.106 (1.017 to 1.201) and 1.107 (1.033 to 1.185) (re-checked), about 1.11 in each city, and not 1.13.
Selection after the data. The six-hour blocks were registered as a table, with no prediction about which block would carry the excess, so singling out 00:00 to 05:59 is a choice made after the data and is exploratory under rule 4. Corrected for four blocks the p value is 0.07 in New York (0.018 uncorrected) and 0.016 in Chicago (0.004 uncorrected). The inverse-variance mean of the two cities is 1.129 (1.059 to 1.203), z = 3.7, p about 0.0008 after the correction. The contrast with the evening block, from a binomial model of the 00:00 to 05:59 share of night shootings, is 1.177 (1.037 to 1.334) in New York and 1.132 (1.023 to 1.252) in Chicago (referee). The boundary at midnight is not sharp: 02:00 to 05:59 gives 1.201 and 1.133, 00:00 to 02:59 gives 1.087 and 1.121, and 21:00 to 23:59 gives 1.006 and 0.998.
The following night. This variant was in the registered plan with a stated expectation and is a registered secondary result. It is not robust to one control in New York: with the next day's maximum and a wet-day term for the next date in the model the ratio is 1.073 (0.989 to 1.164) in New York and 1.063 (1.006 to 1.122) in Chicago (referee). The next day's maximum and the following night's minimum correlate at 0.76 on hot days, so the daily record cannot separate a warm night from a hot spell that continues. Two placebo checks pass: the minimum two nights later adds nothing once the following night is in the model (0.984, 0.923 to 1.048; 0.991, 0.953 to 1.031), and day shootings, which precede the following night, do not follow it (0.924, 0.813 to 1.049; 1.039, 0.970 to 1.113). At other stations the following-night ratio is 1.112 (LaGuardia), 1.083 (JFK) and 1.041 (1.000 to 1.084, O'Hare).
One observation. The after-midnight excess, the following-night ratio and the difference between calendar-day and shooting-day counts are the same observation stated three ways: shootings in the small hours follow the temperature of the night in which they occur. They are not three pieces of support. Shootings from 00:00 to 05:59 of a date rise by 1.261 (1.140 to 1.396) in New York and 1.222 (1.125 to 1.328) in Chicago from 27 to 33 C of that date's maximum, which comes later in the day (referee).
Rivals not tested. Humidity was named in the registration and no variant addresses it; dew point is in the hourly airport files and not in GHCN-Daily, so the following-night result may be humid heat. A warm night also keeps people outdoors after midnight, and these data cannot separate that from a sleep path. On 36% of New York hot days and 38% of Chicago hot days the next date's minimum is more than 1 C lower, so the calendar minimum of date d was probably set in the evening; on those days the 'preceding' minimum partly measures the evening of the shooting day, which would raise its coefficient. Without those days part (a) is 1.063 (0.968 to 1.168) and 1.031 (0.975 to 1.090), still unsettled.
Threshold. The refutation threshold of 1.075 was derived from the calendar-day excess of 1.122. On the shooting days this claim uses, the excess is 1.051 (0.988 to 1.118) in New York and 1.035 (0.991 to 1.082) in Chicago, half of which is about 1.032 and 1.021 per 5 C of minimum. Both upper limits (1.109 and 1.054) are above those values as well. The threshold stays as registered.
Code. run.py builds the following night's minimum and the previous day's maximum by shifting rows of the weather file and not calendar days. The Central Park file has no gap. The Midway file lacks 28 February 2012 and 16 August 2017 (re-checked), so on the four adjacent days the shifted value comes from two days away. With a calendar shift Chicago has 1,479 hot days and 13,503 shootings in place of 1,481 and 13,519, and the estimate is 1.009 (0.966 to 1.054) against 1.009 (0.967 to 1.054). The script is left as committed: it was fixed with the registration (rule 9), and the correction changes the registered count of days and one third decimal while changing no result.
Order of events. The registration and script are on the remote branch prereg/heat-night-minimum (commit 44edbc9, 01:24:38); the first query with a time of day was fetched at 01:24:57. Git records the commit time and not the push time, so the repository shows that the registration was committed 19 seconds before the fetch and cannot show that it was pushed before it.
Stance. The stance is set to null. The value 0.416 was the z of the New York estimate against no effect, and on the strip it read as agreement with the research. The registration computed D = 0.13 and 0.37 and said the test is not an endpoint test of the chain; the realised z values are 0.88 against no effect, 0.53 against the composed 1.012 and -1.12 against the threshold, so the estimate does not favour any of the three.
outcome.stance_note: Null after the referee: the test cannot tell the graph-sized effect (1.012) from no effect (D = 0.13 and 0.37 as registered), and a stance computed against no effect showed an unsettled estimate as agreement with the research.
outcome.verdict_note: Unsettled: the preceding night's minimum is compatible with no effect, with the graph-sized 1.012 and with half of the hot-day excess. The rise between 00:00 and 05:59 (about 1.11 per 5 C of maximum in each city) was singled out after the data; it, the following-night ratio and the calendar-day difference are one observation.

claims.plan: Script: analyses/heat_solutions/run.py (sha256 ff13670222b73baa) with analyses/heat_solutions/common.py (sha256 c271c2fae50f98b5), committed with this registration and run unchanged. No resampling and no random numbers; all intervals are Wald intervals from HC0 standard errors (rule 9). The script was exercised before registration on simulated records only (--simulate, seed 1). School calendar: first and last day of classes for each year (common.FIRST_DAY, LAST_DAY; 2006-07 to 2018-19 agree with the daily attendance files, later years from Department of Education calendars). The June 2020, September 2020 and June 2021 transitions are left out (remote teaching). Days: Monday to Friday, not public holidays, within 42 calendar days of a transition, 2006 to August 2026. A day is out of school if it is after the last day or before the first day. Closures inside the term (religious holidays, Juneteenth after 2022) are counted as school days unless they are federal holidays, which are dropped. Outcome: shooting incidents per day (5ucz-vwe8). Model: negative binomial GLM, log link, on out + TMAX/5 + a linear trend in days from the transition for each kind of transition + C(dow) + wet + a term for each transition (kind by year); dispersion by maximum likelihood.

can_it_fail.reading: Expected standard error 0.045 on 2260 weekdays; D for a ratio of 1.10 is 4.491 (rule 8 needs 4). With no effect the refutation rule is met with probability 0.563. The count of victims under 18 can detect only a ratio of 1.428 or more (D for 1.25 is 3.081), so the age results are reported and decide nothing.

claims.already_seen: The citywide daily series of shootings and its temperature models; the hourly distribution by temperature band. I have not tabulated shootings by date relative to the school calendar, and no script in the repository uses a school calendar with shootings. The victim age field has not been queried by this project.
alternatives: Season: late June and July differ from May and early June in daylight and outdoor life beyond what temperature captures; the linear trends absorb only smooth change.

Events tied to the calendar and not to school: the weekend of 4 July and the West Indian Day parade on Labor Day fall just after and just before the transitions; public holidays are dropped but the days around them are not.
Summer programmes: the Summer Youth Employment Program starts in early July, about a week after the last day, and would offset a school effect inside the window.
Most victims and shooters are over 18; an effect on school-age youth is diluted about tenfold in the total, which is why the age split is reported.

outcome.verdict_note: Unsettled: the rate ratio is 1.105 (0.997 to 1.224), with the lower limit 0.003 below the threshold 1.00 and the upper limit above 1.10. outcome.notes:
Two lines of run.py (170 and 224) were changed after registration: each reads the hour of a shooting as the text before the first colon in place of the first two characters. The earlier wording of this note (one line; unpadded times in 'the file'; no model had run) was inaccurate and was corrected after the referee. The incident file 5ucz-vwe8 has no unpadded time, and the two versions of line 170 give the same hour for all 24,429 incidents. The 390 unpadded times (of 29,744) are in the archived victim file 833y-fsy8, which only heat-school-out uses, so the registered script stopped at line 224. That line comes after the air-conditioning models in main(), so in the failed run those models had been fitted in memory; the script prints and writes only at its end, so no result was displayed or saved before the change. The change alters no number of the three claims' deciding models, none of which uses the hour. Registered secondary results. Window of 21 days 1.217 (1.057 to 1.402). Quadratic trends 1.106 (0.998 to 1.224). End of term only 1.067 (0.920 to 1.238); start of term only 1.131 (0.983 to 1.301). Victims under 18 1.195 (0.897 to 1.593) (944 victims, to 2024); 18 to 24 1.112 (0.939 to 1.317); 25 or older 1.129 (0.971 to 1.312). Odds that a victim is under 18 on days out of school 1.094 (0.817 to 1.466). The heat-shootings model on all days: 1.146 (1.130 to 1.163) per 5 C without a term for the summer recess and 1.144 (1.127 to 1.161) with it; the term itself is 1.139 (1.047 to 1.238) and removes 1.5% of the log slope. The arithmetic done before registration gave the same answer: The coefficient of TMAX/5 in a regression of the summer-recess indicator on the terms of heat-shootings is 0.011. A school effect of ln g on shootings biases the log slope by ln g x 0.011: 0.8% of the slope if g = 1.10 and 1.8% if g = 1.25. For the school calendar to produce a tenth of the 14.6%, shootings would have to be 3.353 times as frequent when school is out. Exploratory, after the results, by hour block with temperature held fixed: 00:00 to 05:59 1.404 (1.144 to 1.723); 06:00 to 14:59 0.829 (0.648 to 1.062); 15:00 to 19:59 0.903 (0.741 to 1.100); 20:00 to 23:59 1.140 (0.970 to 1.339).

After the referee (13 Nov 2026): the verdict is kept. The referee rebuilt the window with separate code: the same 2,260 weekdays, 1,125 days out and 7,199 shootings, with identical counts on every row, and 1.105 (0.997 to 1.224). Neither registered condition is met, so the verdict is unsettled. The referee found four problems, all accepted.
1. The morning after a public holiday. Shootings before 06:00 are counted on the calendar date. Public holidays are dropped from the window, and the weekday after one is kept and carries the holiday night's shootings after midnight. The twelve weekdays dated 5 July have a mean of 6.08 shootings before 06:00 against 0.89 on other days. These are the night of 4 July, counted as days out of school about a week after the last day of classes. The window has 74 weekdays that follow a public holiday, 29 of them out of school. Without those weekdays the ratio is 1.060 (0.957 to 1.173); with a term for them 1.078 (0.976 to 1.190); with only their shootings before 06:00 removed 1.022 (0.924 to 1.130); on days from 06:00 to 05:59 1.044 (0.951 to 1.146) (referee; re-checked with the registered functions). The whole registered excess is in shootings before 06:00: from 06:00 to 23:59 on the calendar date the ratio is 0.999 (0.890 to 1.120). On the log scale 42% of the excess goes without the mornings after holidays and 57% on the 06:00 day. Events tied to the calendar were a rival named in the registration, and the first outcome did not address it.
2. The window. The ratio is 1.169 (0.992 to 1.379) at a half-width of 14 days, 1.217 (1.057 to 1.402) at 21, 1.167 (1.030 to 1.322) at 28, 1.126 (1.006 to 1.260) at 35, 1.105 at the registered 42, 1.079 (0.981 to 1.186) at 49, 1.071 (0.981 to 1.170) at 56, 1.052 (0.968 to 1.144) at 63 and 1.024 (0.945 to 1.109) at 70. A lasting effect of the recess would not shrink as the window grows. Without the days within 7 days of a transition the ratio is 1.055 (0.910 to 1.224), and within 10 days 0.961 (0.820 to 1.125). The excess is a peak of about two weeks around the turn of June and July and is not a change of level that lasts through the recess. 'A 10% rise' is therefore replaced as the summary by the range across windows, 1.02 to 1.22.
3. School-side days that are not school days. In the windows covered by the attendance file (September 2006 to June 2019), 66 school-side weekdays outside the last 12 days of term have no attendance record (Anniversary Day, Clerical Day, Eid, Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur), about 8% of school-side days. Dropping them gives 1.139 (1.004 to 1.291) against 1.153 (1.019 to 1.305) for the same years as registered; counting them as out gives 1.083 (0.977 to 1.202). High schools hold Regents examinations and no regular classes from about the middle of June, so for students of high-school age classes end one to two weeks before the registered last day. Both facts bias the estimate towards 1, and the date of the transition is uncertain by more than a week for the age group the claim is about. Moving every transition one day earlier gives 1.143 (1.032 to 1.266) and one day later 1.083 (0.977 to 1.201).
4. Dates counted twice. The end window runs to about 7 August and the start window begins about 28 July, so 184 dates are stacked in both as days out of school, and HC0 errors treat the copies as independent. With errors clustered by date the interval is 0.995 to 1.227; with each date kept once the ratio is 1.114 (1.002 to 1.238).
The margin. The lower limit is 0.003 below 1.00, which is smaller than the effect of the window, the error estimator, the remote-schooling years or a one-day change in the dates: model-based errors give 1.105 (1.003 to 1.217), keeping the 2020 and 2021 transitions 1.102 (1.001 to 1.213), 2006 to 2019 alone 1.155 (1.025 to 1.300), 2022 to 2026 alone 0.953 (0.765 to 1.187), and leaving out one year a lower limit between 0.973 and 1.019. The same data would have read confirmed under some of these. Without the mornings after holidays every one is unsettled again (1.060, 0.964 to 1.166 with 2020 and 2021; 1.115, 0.991 to 1.254 for 2006 to 2019). The refutation rule is met under no variant; the smallest upper limit is 1.109. The realised standard error is 0.052 against the 0.045 expected at registration. The reference to rule 10 in the earlier verdict note is dropped: that rule concerns conditions on a point estimate, and this condition is on an interval bound.
The exploratory hour blocks. The ratio 1.404 (1.144 to 1.723) for 00:00 to 05:59 is the largest of four blocks chosen after the data (p = 0.005 corrected for four), and its boundary differs from the registered table of victims by hour, which used 00:00 to 07:59. Without the mornings after holidays it is 1.182 (0.970 to 1.440), and counted with the preceding day it is 1.126 (0.959 to 1.321). A placebo transition 28 days inside the term gives 0.681 (0.499 to 0.927) for this block, so the linear trends do not describe how shootings after midnight grow through May and June and the nominal interval is too narrow. The figure 1.40 should not be quoted as a recess effect; 1.18 with an interval that includes 1 is what the data support. The block also rises on weekend dates in the same windows, 1.100 (0.926 to 1.306), which answers the second research_needed question: the data do not show that the excess is specific to weekdays.
Victims under 18 (exploratory, after the data). The registered table has 16 cells and no intervals: 51 victims under 18 between 00:00 and 07:59 on school days and 108 on days out, and the other age groups move the same way (18 to 24: 375 to 615; 25 or older: 632 to 837). In the referee's count models the ratio for victims shot before 06:00 is 3.56 (1.52 to 8.33) for under 18, 1.57 (1.13 to 2.18) for 18 to 24 and 1.35 (1.04 to 1.76) for 25 or older, and without the mornings after holidays 2.19 (0.88 to 5.41), 1.31 (0.94 to 1.83) and 1.14 (0.88 to 1.48). Without those mornings the share of under-18 victims shot before 06:00 is 8.5% on school days and 21.1% on days out, and the interaction of out with under 18 is 2.04 (1.25 to 3.33) on 118 victims. Victims under 18 do shift towards the hours after midnight more than adults do. The result was found after the data among at least 16 cells and 4 blocks, has no control for season beyond temperature and year, and needs its own registration.
Season (referee). On Saturdays and Sundays in the same windows the ratio is 1.011 (0.895 to 1.142). Placebo transitions 22 to 35 days inside the term or the recess give 0.912 to 1.085 with 21-day windows. For 1 to 14 September, where the same day of the month is in and out of school in different years, the ratio is 1.253 (0.867 to 1.810) on 171 weekdays. These are compatible with a school effect and with none.
Every quoted estimate on the 06:00 day (re-checked), calendar date first: 21-day window 1.217 (1.057 to 1.402) on calendar dates and 1.134 (0.997 to 1.290) on the 06:00 day; victims under 18 1.195 (0.897 to 1.593) on calendar dates and 1.189 (0.905 to 1.563) on the 06:00 day; 18 to 24 1.112 (0.939 to 1.317) on calendar dates and 1.009 (0.863 to 1.179) on the 06:00 day; 25 or older 1.129 (0.971 to 1.312) on calendar dates and 1.061 (0.922 to 1.220) on the 06:00 day; the heat-shootings slope without the recess term 1.146 (1.130 to 1.163) on calendar dates and 1.135 (1.118 to 1.152) on the 06:00 day and with it 1.144 (1.127 to 1.161) on calendar dates and 1.133 (1.116 to 1.150) on the 06:00 day; the recess term 1.139 (1.047 to 1.238) on calendar dates and 1.121 (1.036 to 1.214) on the 06:00 day, which removes 1.5% and 1.4% of the log slope. Victims under 18 per 100 weekdays between 00:00 and 07:59 are 4.9 on school days and 10.6 on days out on calendar dates, and 8.0 and 16.2 when those shot before 06:00 are counted with the preceding day. No registered condition changes side on the 06:00 day: the verdict is unsettled under both. Exploratory, run after the outcomes, and deciding nothing under rule 4 (analyses/critique/round6_six_am_solutions.py; data/derived/round6_heat/six_am_solutions.json).
Stance. The stance is set to null. The value 0.741 (z = 1.9) placed the claim well towards agreement on the strip. The graph holds no finding on school terms and shootings, graph_effect is null, and the one cited paper (Jacob and Lefgren 2003, cited from memory) reports more juvenile violent crime on days when school is in session, the opposite direction.
Not accepted as a rule. The referee suggests a rule for all shootings claims that would count shootings before 06:00 on the previous date or drop the day after each excluded holiday. The criticism is accepted and the re-estimates are recorded here and in the other heat outcomes. No verdict rule is added, as in Round 5: under rule 4 a count chosen after the data cannot decide a verdict already given. New registrations on shootings by date should state the day.

literature.citation: Ziter CD, Pedersen EJ, Kucharik CJ, Turner MG. Scale-dependent interactions between tree canopy cover and impervious surfaces reduce daytime urban heat during summer. PNAS 2019;116:7575-7580.
literature.finding: Bicycle transects in Madison, Wisconsin, summer 2016. Daytime air temperature fell nonlinearly with canopy cover, most above 40% canopy. Going from none to full canopy corresponded to a mean daytime decrease of 0.7 C for canopy within a 10 m radius, 1.3 C within 30 m and more than 1.5 C within 60 or 90 m. At 90 m, raising canopy from 40% to 80% gave about 1 C. At night the decrease from none to full canopy was 0.3 to 0.5 C. (Numbers read from the results text on PubMed Central, PMC6462107, on 12 Nov 2026.)

claims.plan: Sensors and temperature: Hyperlocal Temperature Monitoring (NYC Open Data qdq3-9eqn, data.cityofnewyork.us), summers 2018 and 2019. Sensor-day mean of airtemp over hours 12 to 18, by SoQL (group by sensor_id, day), keeping sensor-days with at least 5 of the 7 hours, converted to C; this is the earlier claim's query and is read from the cache. Sensor position, NTA and mount type from the same dataset; a sensor listed at two positions keeps the one with the most readings. Exposure: USDA NAIP, 2022 New York State flight only (0.6 m, four bands), from the Microsoft Planetary Computer STAC collection 'naip'; New Jersey tiles of 10 July 2022 that overlap western Manhattan and the Bronx are not used. The catalogue shows tiles dated 19 July 2022 west of about longitude -73.875 and 15 September 2022 east of it, so the September tiles cover Queens and also the eastern Bronx and eastern Brooklyn; where the two overlap the 19 July tile is used. For each sensor, NDVI = (NIR - red)/(NIR + red) on a 0.6 m grid; the vegetation share is the share of imaged pixels with NDVI above 0.2 within 50 m (primary) and 100 m of the sensor; the mean NDVI in the same discs; and the vegetation share of the ring 200 to 300 m away (placebo). Each sensor's flight date is the date of the tile at its position. Sensors with imagery for less than 95% of the 50 m disc are dropped. Model: OLS of sensor-day afternoon temperature on the 50 m vegetation share (scaled to 10 percentage points) and a light-pole indicator, with fixed effects for NTA by flight date by day, so that no comparison crosses neighbourhoods, days or flight dates; cells with one sensor are dropped; standard errors clustered by sensor. The unit of identification is the sensor (about 420 in 23 NTAs). Pre-specified sensitivity checks, none of which decides the verdict except as written in support_if: S1 share within 100 m; S2 mean NDVI within 50 m and 100 m (per 0.1) in place of the thresholded share; S3 sensors under 19 July tiles only, and under 15 September tiles only; S4 dropping sensors whose 100 m disc mixes two dates or lacks 5% or more of its pixels; S5 street-tree mounts and light-pole mounts separately (the referee of the earlier claim noted that a tree-mounted sensor sits under canopy by construction); S6 days when the Central Park maximum (GHCN-Daily USW00094728) was 30 C or more; S7 adding the 2015 street-tree count within 50 m from the earlier claim. Secondary outcome: mean temperature over hours 0 to 5 (at least 5 of 6 hours), same model. Placebo: the ring 200 to 300 m share in place of the 50 m share, and jointly with it. Ziter's largest scale was 90 m, so a ring coefficient as large as the local one would point to block-type or neighbourhood gradients, not to the vegetation near the sensor. Descriptive only: coefficients for bins of the 50 m share (10-20, 20-30, 30-40, 40% and over, against under 10%), the correlation of the share with the street-tree count, and the share by mount type. Code: analyses/heat/canopy_naip.py, written before registration and run on two Staten Island points only.
limits_stated_in_advance: The imagery is from summer 2022 and the temperatures from summers 2018 and 2019. Trees planted, grown or removed in the three to four years between add error to the exposure, which biases the slope toward zero. The 2019 NAIP flight is not used because its near-infrared band is shifted and the fixed threshold classes roofs as vegetation (concordance-kit aerial-naip notes).
NAIP is 8-bit digital numbers, not reflectance. The 0.2 threshold is a convention, not calibrated; it is applied within one flight year, and the two dates are never compared with each other.
NDVI counts lawns and shrubs as well as tree canopy, and shadowed canopy can fall below the threshold. Ziter measured canopy.
Sensors were sited in high heat-vulnerability neighbourhoods on trees and light poles, not at random; the result applies to those 23 NTAs.
alternatives: Mount type: a sensor in a street tree is shaded by that tree and has vegetation within 50 m by construction (light-pole indicator; S5)
Block type: greener blocks are residential side streets with less traffic, lower buildings and less waste heat (ring placebo; within-NTA comparison)
Exposure error from the 2018-2019 to 2022 gap and from NDVI in shadow (attenuation; cannot be separated, stated as a limit)
Flight-date radiometry: the same threshold marks different things on 19 July and 15 September (flight date in the fixed effect; S3)
Sea-breeze or elevation gradients inside an NTA that happen to align with vegetation (not separated)
claims.prior_note: Probability of 'confirmed'. The street-tree count gave a weak negative slope with an interval including zero on the same sensors, the exposure range probably lies mostly below Ziter's 40% threshold, and the imagery is three years late. Probability of 'contested' 0.03; the rest unsettled.

Placebo: ring share alone -0.35 (-0.45 to -0.25); jointly, ring -0.24 (-0.34 to -0.15) and 50 m share -0.17 (-0.22 to -0.13). Descriptive bins against under 10%: 10-20% -0.08 (-0.26 to 0.10), 20-30% -0.22 (-0.43 to -0.00), 30-40% -0.36 (-0.60 to -0.12), 40% and over -0.82 (-1.10 to -0.54) C. Unregistered check of georeferencing: within 5 m of the sensor the vegetation share is 0.59 at street-tree mounts and 0.11 at light-pole mounts. Limits stated in the registration apply: imagery three to four years after the temperatures, uncalibrated NDVI, grass counted with canopy, sensors sited in 23 high-vulnerability NTAs. The afternoon temperatures had been used by the earlier claim before this registration; the vegetation values had not been seen.

After the referee (13 Nov 2026): what is confirmed is the association and not the causal edge. The vegetation share 200 to 300 m away stays as large as the local share in every model, as the settle field already says. The referee reproduced the estimate and it survives clustering by NTA (-0.261 to -0.141), other NDVI thresholds and leaving out one NTA. A model with all rings together gives -0.165 (-0.214 to -0.115) for 0 to 25 m, nothing from 25 to 200 m and -0.212 (-0.332 to -0.093) for 200 to 300 m; the ring widths were chosen after the data. An alternative not addressed is shade on the sensor housing as distinct from cooler air: all of the local association lies within 25 m, which fits shading of the instrument at least as well as cooling. The slope differs by year (-0.14 in 2018, -0.24 in 2019) with largely different sensors. The published temperature file is a balanced panel (every sensor-day has 7 of 7 afternoon hours), so it was gap-filled or cleaned before publication and the registered 5-of-7 filter removed nothing. On like-for-like radius the city slope is larger than Ziter's. The graph row for PMID 35060045 stores r = -1.0, which is not a published number; it was used for direction only.
outcome.verdict_note: The association is confirmed. Vegetation 200 to 300 m away predicts temperature as strongly as vegetation within 50 m, so the local causal reading is not supported.

outcome.settle: The association is too large to be the effect of commuting on body weight. Individual-level data (CHS microdata with commute mode, or a cohort) and a change design, such as obesity before and after new bike lanes or Citi Bike stations arrive in a neighbourhood, would settle the causal question.

I predicted a strong unadjusted association (1.3-3 per 10 ppb) carried by poverty, which would shrink by more than half on adjustment. The unadjusted estimate is 1.32 (0.65-2.65), imprecise, and adjustment moved it only to 1.22 (0.81-1.85), because NO2 and poverty are almost uncorrelated across UHF neighbourhoods (r = 0.05). claims.plan: Unit: 2020 census tracts with at least 500 residents. Complaints: 311 Service Requests 2020-present (erm2-nwe9), created 2022-01-01 to 2024-12-31, complaint_type 'Noise - Residential' (primary), also 'Noise - Street/Sidewalk' + 'Noise - Vehicle', 'Noise - Commercial', and all types beginning 'Noise'; aggregated with SoQL group by latitude, longitude and complaint_type, then joined to tracts locally. Nightlife: active on-premises liquor licences per tract (NY State Liquor Authority data, data.ny.gov). Neighbourhood change: change in median gross rent (B25064, inflation not adjusted, in log) and in non-Hispanic white share (B03002) from ACS 2008-2012 (2010 tracts, area-weighted to 2020 tracts with the Census relationship file) to ACS 2018-2022. Controls: log population density, poverty share, borough fixed effects. Bootstrap tracts (1,000 draws) for the coefficient difference. SONYC sensor data used only if a public levels file is found; otherwise noted as unavailable. Figure: tract maps of complaint rate and modelled noise; coefficient plot with the research dose-response (per 10 dB) noted beside it.
alternatives: Residential complaints concern neighbour noise, which the transport noise map does not model; a weak link to modelled noise is then expected even if complaints measure exposure to their own source.
Rent change and nightlife are collinear (new bars follow rising rents); the rent coefficient may carry real noise from new venues.
Population density drives both complaints and actual neighbour noise.
The noise map is coarse (classes, no values under 45 dB) and models traffic volume, not observed levels.
Reporting propensity differs by language, trust in government and tenure, independent of change.

outcome.prediction_scored: partial. Two of three parts hit: residential complaint rates were weakly related to modelled transport noise (Spearman rho 0.22; predicted below 0.25), and street and vehicle complaints were positively related to it (rho 0.30; predicted 0.15-0.45). The registered contrast missed: rent change had no association with residential complaints (0.004 per SD), so the contrast was -0.03 (95% CI -0.09 to 0.02) against a predicted +0.05 to +0.30.
outcome.settle: Neither the registered contrast nor its opposite is supported, and the deeper question, whether complaints measure exposure, cannot be answered with a transport noise model because residential complaints are mostly about neighbours. It would be settled by measured sound levels at a sample of addresses or blocks stratified by complaint rate and by demographic change: SONYC sensor Leq series (if released at block level), a DEP or DOHMH monitoring campaign, or smartphone dosimetry. With measured levels, complaints per resident can be modelled as level times reporting propensity, and propensity estimated from repeated reports of the same incident (the method of the 2025 Annals of Applied Statistics paper on 311 reporting bias).

outcome.notes:
n = 2171 2020 tracts with at least 500 residents and complete ACS change measures. 311 totals 2022-2024 in tracts: residential 1,052,123, street/sidewalk 459,165, vehicle 162,585, commercial 196,679, DEP 'Noise' 154,110, helicopter 114,024. In the joint model for residential complaints the largest coefficients were poverty share (0.21 per SD) and change in the non-Hispanic white share (0.13); modelled noise was 0.04 (-0.00 to 0.08). A secondary contrast that the registered statement names but the support rule does not use, change in non-Hispanic white share minus modelled noise, was 0.10 (95% CI 0.04 to 0.15). This agrees with Legewie and Schaeffer (2016) that complaints follow ethnoracial change, but it is reported as secondary, not as the test. For street and vehicle complaints, modelled noise (0.13) and liquor licences (0.26) both mattered, and the rent-minus-noise contrast was negative (-0.10, -0.15 to -0.04): street complaints partly track the sources the noise model contains. Commercial complaints followed liquor licences (rho 0.58). Using the energy-mean Leq in place of the class mean gave a modelled-noise coefficient of -0.02. The noise map was read from rendered tiles of the US DOT service by legend colour at zoom 12 (about 29 m pixels; deeper levels are not cached); areas below 45 dB are unpainted and were set to 40 dB. SONYC data were not used: no public block-level sound-level file was located in this session. The ACS change measures come from the Census Bureau summary files because the Census API now requires a key; 2008-2012 values on 2010 tracts were moved to 2020 tracts by land-area weights from the Census relationship file. Rents are nominal.

After critique round 1b: Settling this needs street noise (outdoor sensors) separated from neighbour noise (indoor measurement or survey). Housing form and repeat callers are not addressed.

outcome.prediction_scored: partial. The direction and the unadjusted magnitude were right (Spearman rho 0.84; predicted 0.5-0.8). I expected adjustment to remove most of the association and leave an unsettled verdict. It did not: the coefficient fell by 31%, from 0.68 to 0.47 (95% CI 0.06 to 0.87), above the predicted 0.00-0.20, and the registered support condition holds.
outcome.settle: The NYC estimate is ecological across 42 neighbourhoods, and the rodent measure is almost collinear with housing problems (rho 0.90) and strongly related to poverty (rho 0.70). It cannot show that rodent allergen causes the excess ED visits. What would settle the bridge: (1) household-level data in NYC linking measured mouse allergen or reported rodents to child asthma ED use, for example the NYC KIDS survey microdata or a cohort such as the Columbia Center for Children's Environmental Health; (2) the same neighbourhood model with race and ethnicity, smoking, PM2.5 and primary-care access added; (3) a within-neighbourhood test, such as change in asthma ED rates after integrated pest management in NYCHA developments.

outcome.notes:
Primary model per registration: n = 42 UHF neighbourhoods, 2017 data (latest year common to the NYCHVS rodent and housing measures and the SPARCS asthma ED rates on the EHDP portal). Adding the cockroach share left the rodent coefficient at 0.53; the adult ED outcome gave 0.41 (0.03 to 0.78). The CHS 2012 measure of adults reporting mice or rats inside gave 0.23 (-0.05 to 0.50). The city's operational rodent data behaved differently. The share of DOHMH initial inspections failed for rat activity, 2022-2024, was barely related to the survey measure (rho 0.19) and not to child asthma ED rates in 2023 (adjusted -0.08, -0.21 to 0.05). 311 rodent complaints per 1,000 residents correlated with the survey measure at rho 0.38 and with asthma at rho 0.34, but not after adjustment (0.06, -0.11 to 0.23). Inspections and complaints mostly record rats outdoors and around buildings; the research concerns indoor mouse allergen among sensitised children. The survey measure joins mice and rats. The bridge is therefore graph (household mouse allergen to asthma morbidity) plus city survey data (neighbourhood rodents to child asthma ED rates), and it does not pass through the city's operational rodent datasets. Rodent inspections were aggregated by ZIP code; each ZIP's mean inspection coordinate was assigned to a UHF42 polygon (UHF neighbourhoods are unions of ZIP codes). Alternatives not handled: race and ethnicity, smoking, outdoor air pollution, primary-care access.

After critique round 1b: This result is fragile. The housing-problems control (EHDP measure 1248, fallback 86) itself includes rodents and cockroaches, which is why it correlates with the exposure at 0.90, so the adjusted coefficient is not rodents net of housing. Adding the non-Hispanic white share gives 0.35 (-0.09 to 0.78); dropping Sunset Park gives -0.06 to 0.90. A re-analysis needs a housing control without pests and adjustment for race and ethnicity. It should not support a bridge until then.

outcome.notes:
Unit: 2208 2020 census tracts with at least 500 residents and lot area in MapPLUTO 26v2. Vacant land (land use 11) is 7.8% of NYC tax-lot area. 6913 of 7043 shooting incidents 2019-2024 fell in the analysed tracts. Shooting rates rose from 0.96 per 10,000 residents per year in the lowest vacant-share quintile to 1.67 in the highest. The association held without Staten Island (IRR 1.17) and after adding the non-Hispanic white share (IRR 1.13). It was not linear in the share: per SD of the untransformed share the IRR was 0.99 (0.94-1.05), because the top quintile runs from 2.8% to 94% and the tracts with the most vacant land are industrial or waterfront tracts with few residents. Exploratory, not registered: private vacant land IRR 1.13 per SD (1.03-1.22); City-owned vacant land 0.96 (0.91-1.01). Data note: in Shootings (2006-Present), 5ucz-vwe8, the latitude column holds longitudes and the longitude column holds latitudes (checked 12 November 2026); the script detects and swaps them. Distinct incidents per year in 5ucz-vwe8 match the archived 833y-fsy8 table within one incident. The registration's literature note corrects the brief: the Branas et al. 2018 greening trial was published in PNAS, not JAMA Network Open. The PNAS trial is not present as a variable in the graph; the graph holds the cross-sectional Philadelphia study, the abandoned-housing trial (South et al. 2023) and the Rochester demolition study.

After critique round 1b: The association is between neighbourhoods. With NTA fixed effects the IRR is 0.98 (0.94 to 1.01); with NTA-clustered errors the interval is 1.10 to 1.25. It is therefore consistent with neighbourhood-level confounding. The NYC and Philadelphia figures use different outcomes, exposures, units and scales, so they are similar in size but not equal. The exposure is PLUTO 2026 and the shootings are 2019-2024.

outcome.notes:
The DCP headline count is reproduced to within 7 units from the public portal copy, using the rule that the Housing Database data dictionary implies: new-building jobs whose first certificate of occupancy fell in 2025 (compltyear), counted by proposed Class A units (classaprop, which equals classanet for new buildings). The release used is 26Q2.1, later than the 25Q4 release the snapshot used. The completion counts barely moved between releases: R1 for 2024 is 33,859, the same as DCP's 25Q4 figure. The 25Q4 archive was found after the first draft of the registration and before commit; it was not downloaded, because a file download needs Jeff's approval. Exploratory, not a test: of the 38,689 units completed in 2025, 23,669 (61%) were in jobs first permitted in 2022, the year of the 421-a deadline rush, and 6,875 in jobs permitted in 2023. Units completed in new buildings rose from 33,859 in 2024 to 38,689 in 2025, while units in new-building permits issued in 2025 were 18,539 (P1). The high 2025 completion count is therefore the 2022 permit surge reaching certificates of occupancy, not a rise in new starts. The aggregate table dbdt-5s7j gives 43,654 net units for 2025 across all job types (alterations and demolitions included, counted incrementally), so the aggregate tables do not equal the new-building figure and should not be quoted as it. R2 shows that units_co, the field a reader might choose for 'units completed', overstates the snapshot by 4.9%, because certificates can include Class B and hotel units.

After the referee (13 Nov 2026): the match (38,689 against 38,682) is on release 26Q2.1, later than the 25Q4 release the snapshot used. Of the 2025 completions, 209 jobs with 19,800 units were updated after 15 January 2026 and DCP edited classaprop by hand on 19 jobs, so the agreement is a match after revision and not proof that DCP used exactly this rule. The referee recomputed R1 at row level and under three further variants and obtained 38,689 each time. The permit figure is not reproduced (18,539 against 17,673), and the referee found no simple rule that gives 17,673 in this release; permits dated December 2025 hold 4,138 units, so late recording is a plausible source. A row-level copy of the new-building rows was in the project cache before registration; the registration says only its headers were read, which cannot be verified. The interval in city_effect is the size of one earlier revision and not a sampling interval, so the stance computed from it had no statistical meaning and is now null, as for repro-dot-2025-deaths. Follow-up of 13 November 2026 on the snapshot's own release. Jeff approved the download of nychdb_25q4_csv.zip from DCP's archive on nyc.gov (9,278,590 bytes, SHA-256 76f16a63...8cada2, fetched 13 November 2026 07:36 EST; every row carries version 25Q4). The registered follow-up, R1 on this file, gives 38,691 units in 1,014 jobs, 9 units (+0.023%) above the stated 38,682 and inside the exact band of 2%. The registration says that this result is secondary and does not change the verdict, which stays confirmed. The stated figure is not matched to the unit even on its own release. The following numbers on 25Q4 were not registered for this file and are exploratory. The boroughs are Brooklyn 18,048 (stated 18,048), Bronx 5,683 (5,683), Manhattan 4,874 (4,874 by subtraction), Queens 9,608 (9,600) and Staten Island 478 (477), so the 9 units are 8 in Queens and 1 in Staten Island; the cause is not known. R2 is 40,569 and R3 equals R1. R1 for 2024 is 33,861 against DCP's 33,859. The permit count P1 is 17,669 against the stated 17,673 (-4 units), and no 2025 new-building permit job is withdrawn in 25Q4, so P2 equals P1. The permit figure is therefore reproduced on the snapshot's release, and the 4.9% excess found on 26Q2.1 is revision between releases. A job-level comparison of the two releases shows that the revision is mostly edited unit counts and not late-recorded permits: 22 jobs present in both releases changed ClassAProp for a net +1,082 units, 6 jobs entered the 2025 permit set (+145 units, of which 2 jobs with 10 units were absent from 25Q4), and 5 jobs left it (-357 units). For completions the same 1,014 jobs are in both releases and one job changed by -2 units. The registered secondary permit condition was written for the portal copy and remains not met there.

The permit figure was not reproduced on 26Q2.1 (18,539) and is reproduced on 25Q4 (17,669 against 17,673; exploratory).

claims.plan:
All queries through concord/socrata.py (SoQL aggregation), recording rowsUpdatedAt for each dataset. Readings of the unstated parts of the method:
DEATHS. D1 (primary): persons table f55k-p6yu, count of rows with person_injury = 'Killed', crash_date in the calendar year (2025, and 2024 for the comparison). D2: crash table h9gi-nx95, sum(number_of_persons_killed) by crash_date in the calendar year. D3: deaths dated by date of death rather than crash date; the open tables carry no date of death, so D3 cannot be computed; its effect is bounded by reporting D1 for crashes on 1 to 31 December of the prior year (deaths of those victims may fall in the next year) and noted as not computable.
PEDESTRIANS. P1 (primary): persons table, person_type = 'Pedestrian' and person_injury = 'Killed'. P2: crash table sum(number_of_pedestrians_killed).
BOROUGH. B1 (primary): borough field of the crash record (h9gi-nx95), with deaths taken as sum(number_of_persons_killed) grouped by borough, crashes with a blank borough reported as unassigned. B2: borough from coordinates: killed-person crashes (crash table rows with number_of_persons_killed > 0) placed by point-in-polygon in the DCP Borough Boundaries dataset gthc-hcne; points outside all polygons go to the nearest polygon if within 500 m, otherwise they keep the record's borough field; rows with no coordinates keep the borough field. B1 and B2 are compared for 2025 and 2024, since the project found a change in geocoding in 2025 (critique/bridge-crz-injury-crashes.md).
INJURIES. I1 (primary): crash table sum(number_of_persons_injured), crash_date from 1 January to 15 December inclusive, for 2025 and for 2024 (same window both years). I2: persons table count of person_injury = 'Injured', same window. I3: 2025 Jan 1 to Dec 15 against 2024 full calendar year (if the release compared a partial 2025 with a full 2024). I4: window ending 14 December inclusive (if 'as of December 15' means data through the previous day). The vintage of the data (DOT read it about 15 December 2025; the open tables now hold rows added later) cannot be reconstructed from Socrata and is noted.
Report each number under each reading against the stated number, the signed gap in counts and percent, a figure in figures/reproduction/, and an outcome scored with concord.claims.outcome. No other measures decide the verdict; anything added after the data are seen is labelled exploratory.
alternatives: DOT's reconciled file adds deaths that occur after the crash report (NYPD records the injury at the scene; the person later dies) and so exceeds the NYPD counts.
DOT's definition excludes deaths that NYPD tables include (deaths on highways under state jurisdiction, medical events, suicides, crashes on private property), so the NYPD counts exceed DOT's.
Late additions and revisions to the open tables since January 2026 move the counts away from what DOT read.
Borough attribution differs by method (crash record field vs coordinates); the 2025 change in geocoding moves crashes between blank and named boroughs.
Date field: DOT may date a death by the date of death, moving late-December crashes across the year boundary.

outcome.notes:
All counts were computed from the NYPD Motor Vehicle Collisions tables as published on 12 November 2026 (crashes h9gi-nx95 rows updated 2026-11-12T14:31:25Z; persons f55k-p6yu rows updated 2026-11-12T17:31:19Z), with code in analyses/reproduction/dot_2025_deaths.py and results in data/derived/reproduction/dot_2025_deaths.json.

Deaths. The persons table (rows with person_injury = Killed) and the crash table (sum of number_of_persons_killed) give the same totals: 229 in 2025 and 268 in 2024, by crash date. DOT states 205 and 253. The open data exceed DOT by 24 deaths (11.7 percent) in 2025 and 15 deaths (5.9 percent) in 2024, both outside the registered 5 percent tolerance. The gap is in the opposite direction from deaths added after the crash report, so it cannot be explained by DOT's later additions. The date-of-death reading (D3) cannot be computed, but it cannot close the gap: the NYPD tables record 17 deaths for crashes in December 2024 and 19 for crashes in December 2025, so moving late-December deaths across the year boundary changes the 2025 count by at most a few deaths in either direction. The most likely explanation is that DOT's reconciled file excludes deaths that NYPD records in the collision tables (DOT's count is restricted to traffic deaths under its definition, and DOT revises its own counts, as the MMR shows for Fiscal 2025). The person type breakdown in the NYPD table also changed: occupant deaths fell from 111 to 66 and 'Other Motorized' deaths rose from 11 to 34, while DOT reports a 40 percent fall in occupant deaths and a 32 percent fall in motorcyclist deaths.

Pedestrians. Both readings give 124 in 2024 (DOT 122, within tolerance) and 119 in 2025 (DOT 111, +8, outside the tolerance of 5.55).

Boroughs. Under the primary reading (borough field of the crash record) 2025 is close for the Bronx (33 against 33), Manhattan (41 against 39) and Queens (59 against 57), but Brooklyn is 70 against 63 and Staten Island 7 against 13, and 19 deaths have no borough. In 2024 the borough field is blank for 103 of 268 deaths, so every borough except Staten Island is far below DOT's figure. Placing crashes by coordinates (B2) leaves 33 deaths unassigned in 2024 and 4 in 2025, and brings 2024 Brooklyn (67 against 69) and Manhattan (43 against 44) within tolerance, but puts 2025 Brooklyn, Queens and Manhattan further above DOT because the citywide total is 24 above. The 2024 result shows the geocoding change found in critique/bridge-crz-injury-crashes.md: blank boroughs were common in 2024 and rare in 2025, so a borough comparison across the two years from the record's borough field is not valid. DOT's year-on-year borough changes (for example Queens 74 to 57) cannot be checked with the borough field and only partly with coordinates (64 to 64).

Injuries. Every reading with a 1 January to 15 December window reproduces DOT within 0.5 percent: 47,744 against 47,557 in 2025 and 51,775 against 51,540 in 2024 (crash table and persons table agree). The window ending 14 December comes closer (47,589 and 51,671, within 0.3 percent). The full-year 2024 reading (54,030) does not match, so DOT compared the same partial window in both years. The small excess over DOT is consistent with rows added after mid-December 2025. Serious injuries (2,947 and 3,031) were not reproduced because the open tables have no field matching DOT's severity definition.

Verdict. By the registered rule, contested: the 2025 death count is outside tolerance under every computable reading. The injury numbers reproduce, so the release mixes a reproducible injury count with a death count that comes from a file the public cannot see, and which is lower than the open record by about one death in nine.

After the referee (13 Nov 2026): contested here means that the open NYPD collision tables do not reproduce DOT's reconciled count. It does not mean that DOT's count is wrong; DOT's file is not published and the claim cannot test it. The referee re-queried both tables and obtained the same 229 and 268. Removing fatal crashes whose contributing factor is a medical event removes 12 deaths in 2025 and 8 in 2024 (217 and 260), so the one exclusion visible in the open data accounts for at most half of the 2025 gap, and 2025 stays outside the tolerance. Deaths that NYPD later reclassifies (suicides, homicides by vehicle, private property) are corrected in DOT's file and not in the open table. November 2025 has 7 recorded deaths against 13 to 29 in the other months and 23 in November 2024; if November is incomplete in the open table the gap is larger than 24. DOT's fall from 2024 to 2025 is 19.0% and the open tables give 14.6%. The referee recalled, without checking, that the open tables were also about 24 deaths above DOT in 2019 to 2021; if so the gap is the usual one and the 5% tolerance would be missed in most years. That is not verified here.
outcome.verdict_note: The open NYPD tables do not reproduce DOT's reconciled count of deaths (229 against 205). This is not a finding that DOT's count is wrong. The injury counts reproduce within 0.5%.

outcome.notes:
The trip-record reproduction uses the 38 MTA CBD taxi zones for both pickup and drop-off, weekday pickups from 8AM to 6PM, federal holidays excluded, and total miles over total hours. It gives 6.94, 6.95 and 6.62 mph for FY24, FY25 and FY26 against the MMR's 6.9, 6.9 and 6.5. The parquet files match the NYC Open Data copies of 2024 and 2025 (rwwi-khbc, irx2-vgm4) exactly in trip count for most months of 2024 and within 0.31% for every month; the 2025 Open Data copy holds slightly fewer trips from April 2025 on, which suggests a later revision of one of the two copies. The MTA series 6p29-6xqn (all hours, taxi and FHV) ends in August 2025 and runs about 1.7 mph higher (8.57 and 8.66 mph in FY24 and FY25), so it is not the MMR's source. Reconciliation with mob-crz-traffic. The MMR number has no comparison area and uses fiscal years. FY25 holds six untolled months (July to December 2024, 6.66 mph under R1) and six tolled months (January to June 2025, 7.24 mph), so the toll's effect is averaged with the slow pre-toll autumn and FY25 equals FY24. FY26 holds the second half of 2025 (6.66 mph) and January to June 2026 (6.57 mph). In January to June 2026 taxi speeds fell everywhere in the city: by 9.2% in the CBD, 5.9% in Manhattan north of 60th Street and 6.5% in the rest of the city against January to June 2025, and the fall appears for both taxi vendors (exploratory check). The fall in the MMR number from 6.9 to 6.5 mph is therefore a citywide fall, not a fall in the CBD relative to elsewhere. Relative to the rest of the city the CBD gained: the ratio of CBD to rest-of-city speed rose 5.1% from calendar 2024 to calendar 2025, close to the +5.7% of mob-crz-traffic, and in January to June 2026 it was still 2.9% above January to June 2024. Relative to Manhattan north of 60th Street, the gain was 2.6% in January to June 2025 and had disappeared by the second half of 2025 (-0.5% against the second half of 2024) and January to June 2026 (-1.0% against January to June 2024). The two published results are both reproduced by the same trip records; they answer different questions, and the choice of comparison area changes the size and persistence of the effect. These comparison-area figures are descriptive outputs named in the registration's plan, not tests.

After the referee (13 Nov 2026): the referee rebuilt R1 from the 36 trip files and obtained 6.949 and 6.617 mph, identical to the outcome. Fiscal 2026 reproduces to 0.12 mph, which rounds to 6.6 and not to the published 6.5. The method is not identified: five of the nine registered readings pass, and the 0.2 mph tolerance is half of the 0.4 mph change the indicator reports. Ten of eleven further trip filters stay within tolerance (fiscal 2026 from 6.44 to 6.70); standard-rate trips or positive fares give 6.44 and 6.87, which round to 6.4 and 6.9. A jackknife over days gives a standard error of 0.05 mph, so R1 is 2.3 standard errors from the stated fiscal 2026 value and is accepted because of the registered tolerance. The share of vendor 1, whose trips are 0.1 to 0.3 mph slower, fell from 25% to 19% of trips, and a change in the trip records is not ruled out as part of the fiscal 2026 fall; weather in February 2026 was not examined. The registration has no statement of which data the registrant had seen; the MTA speed series fetched earlier that day runs 1.7 mph higher and could not have been used to tune R1.

stance.note: The interval is the range over the five readings that reproduced both years, so it is conditioned on success and is narrower than the spread of the nine registered readings (fiscal 2026: 6.43 to 9.13 mph).

outcome.verdict_note: Level and direction reproduce within the registered 0.2 mph. Fiscal 2026 is 6.62 against the published 6.5, and several trip filters pass, so DOT's method is not identified.

critique.answer: accepted; verdict kept

claims.plan: Script analyses/restaurants/complaints_test.py at commit 0c147b3 (no resampling, no seed). Cohort: first Cycle Inspection / Initial Inspection with a score per CAMIS, 2023-01-01 to 2025-06-30, citywide live 43nn-pn8j, restricted to CAMIS whose 10-digit BBL holds exactly one CAMIS in the live data from 2022 on. Exposure: score >= 14 against 0-13. Outcome: count of erm2-nwe9 complaints, type Food Poisoning, location type Restaurant/Bar/Deli/Bakery, at the BBL, created on days 1-365 after the inspection. Model: Poisson GLM, HC1 robust SE, covariates borough, cuisine group (top 20), chain (dba with >= 10 CAMIS), inspection quarter. Placebo: same model with Noise - Commercial complaints at the BBL. Secondary, deciding nothing: C-range (>= 28) against A; per 10 points; NTA fixed effects; Manhattan only; complaints in the 365 days before the inspection.
alternatives: Volume: busy restaurants have more diners, so more complaints, and more chances for violations; the noise placebo and cuisine and chain controls address part of this.
Reporting propensity: neighbourhoods and clienteles that complain more to 311 also draw stricter inspections or are in areas inspected differently.
Persistent quality: a restaurant's hygiene is stable, so the association reflects the restaurant, not the inspection; the pre-window secondary shows this and does not make the result causal.
Survivorship: the live data keep only restaurants open now; restaurants that closed after a bad score and many complaints are missing, biasing the IRR towards 1.
Linkage: single-CAMIS BBLs are smaller buildings and differ from food halls and towers.

claims.plan: Exposure comes from the dose map only (data/derived/transit/dose_map_long.csv, built from MTA hourly entries before any outcome was queried). For a group of station complexes, E = ln(MF/TWT in Nov 2025-Oct 2026) - ln(MF/TWT in 2019), where MF is mean Monday and Friday entries and TWT mean Tuesday-to-Thursday entries, for 06:00-19:59 unless the AM peak (06:00-09:59) is named. E is negative where Mondays and Fridays thinned. Files: data/derived/round2/retimed_consequences/exposure_taxi_zone.csv, exposure_community_district.csv, exposure_groups.json; code analyses/round2/retimed_consequences/exposure.py. Estimator (analyses/round2/retimed_consequences/lib.py, written before registration): for each unit and period, r = ln(mean Monday and Friday count / mean Tuesday-to-Thursday count) over retained weeks, and Y = r(recent) - r(baseline). Retained weeks have no federal holiday and no day from 24 December to 1 January, as in the dose map; the weeks of Monday 26 January and Monday 23 February 2026 are also dropped, because subway entries on those Mondays were 38% and 20% of the week's midweek level (docs/transit.md), which was known from entries before any outcome was seen. Intervals are the 2.5 and 97.5 percentiles of 2,000 bootstrap draws that resample weeks within each period and, for a slope across units, the units as well. Outcome: NYPD complaints with ky_cd 107 (burglary), prem_typ_desc in RESIDENCE - APT. HOUSE, RESIDENCE-HOUSE or RESIDENCE - PUBLIC HOUSING, cmplnt_fr_dt on a Monday to Friday of a retained week and cmplnt_fr_tm from 08:00:00 to 17:59:59, from qgea-i56i (to 2025) and 5uac-w243 (2026). The day and time are the start of the period in which the burglary could have happened, as reported by the victim. Baseline: 2015 to 2019. Recent: January 2023 to September 2026; the CBD Monday and Friday deficit in entries was 14.1% in 2023, 13.0% in 2024, 12.7% in 2025 and 13.8% in the latest 12 months, so the exposure has been in place since 2023. Primary: all complaints citywide, pooled. Sending areas, defined now from the dose map and listed in exposure_groups.json: community districts outside the CBD with a reliable station complex, split at the median AM-peak E (-0.0753) into 24 higher-sending and 24 lower-sending districts; complaints are assigned to districts by latitude and longitude (NYC Open Data 5crt-au7u). Sensitivity, not deciding: complaints whose end date equals the start date; baseline 2017-2019 only; Monday and Friday separately; attempted burglaries excluded. Placebo: 2015-2017 against 2018-2019. Power: a design query that pooled Monday to Friday, and so showed nothing about the outcome, counted 17,299 such complaints in 2015-2019 and 8,500 from 2023 to September 2026 (design_burglary_weekday_totals.json). With 40% of them on Mondays and Fridays the Poisson standard error of Y is 0.027; with 15% added for clustering it is 0.031. The central prediction Y = -0.075 is 2.4 standard errors from zero (D = 5.9); the lower end, -0.05, is 1.6 (D = 2.6), so the test can confirm only a fall of about 6% or more, and an estimate above +0.011 would refute. The district contrast has a standard error near 0.06 against a predicted -0.07 (D = 1.3); it cannot separate the hypothesis from no effect and is reported as secondary for that reason. Verdict by concord.claims.PRECEDENCE rules 1 to 4: support_if met gives confirmed, refute_if met gives contested, otherwise unsettled; no_test if the registered data cannot be read. Secondary and placebo results decide nothing.
claims.already_seen: Earlier claims queried NYPD complaints for seven felony offences by month, hour and premises (further-subway-crime claims) and for shootings by day; none tabulated burglary by weekday. For this registration I queried counts of the outcome pooled over Monday to Friday by year, 2014 to 2026, which show the yearly level and not the weekday split.
alternatives: Burglars' own schedules, and those of police, changed between the periods for reasons other than occupancy.
Victims who are at home notice and report a burglary on the day; victims who are away report the day they left. A change in who is at home changes the recorded day as well as the true day.
The mix of residential burglary changed (package and lobby theft recorded as burglary in apartment houses), with its own weekday pattern.
Burglary fell by half between 2015 and 2019, so the baseline pools years with different offender populations (the 2017-2019 baseline checks this).
Subway entries understate work at home among car commuters and overstate it where service was cut.

33,259 complaints on weekdays, of which 13,965 fall in the 209 retained baseline weeks and 6,660 in the 152 retained recent weeks; 3 had no usable coordinates. Friday is the peak day in both periods (index 1.20 and 1.25 of midweek). Monday changed by -2.1% and Friday by +3.9% relative to midweek. Secondary, registered as not deciding: in the 24 districts that send more commuters the ratio changed by -4.6% (-13.3 to +5.7), in the 24 that send fewer by +9.9% (+1.1 to +19.8); the difference is -13.2% (-23.9 to -1.2). The sign is the one registered, but the difference comes from a rise in the lower-sending districts and not from a fall in the higher-sending ones, and the registration gave this contrast a D of 1.3. The same difference in the placebo (2015-17 against 2018-19) is -1.8% (-17.5 to +16.4); with a 2017-19 baseline it is -16.7% (-28.8 to -1.8); for complaints ending the day they began -12.1% (-24.9 to +3.1); for completed burglaries -12.0% (-23.5 to +1.2). Citywide sensitivity: placebo +0.9% (-6.2 to +8.6); baseline 2017-19 +2.5% (-4.8 to +11.0); same-day end -2.8% (-9.6 to +4.7); completed only +0.7% (-5.4 to +7.4). In the six business-district community districts the ratio changed by -16.4% (-33.9 to +7.7) on 1,499 complaints. The yearly ratio of Monday-and-Friday to midweek burglaries ranges from 1.05 to 1.20 with no trend (by_year in burglary_results.json). The recorded day is the start of the period in which the burglary could have happened, as reported by the victim.

After the referee (13 Nov 2026): the verdict is changed from contested to unsettled. The second refutation condition (lower bound of the 95% interval above 0.95) was met by 0.003 with the one seed that was run, and the registration fixed 2,000 draws but no seed. The referee found the lower bound between 0.947 and 0.956 over 40 other seeds, above 0.95 in 62% of them, 0.9509 with 50,000 draws and 0.9499 in the registrant's own check with 20,000 draws. The registered procedure therefore does not place the bound on either side of the threshold, the condition is neither met nor unmet, and rule 2 applies (rule 9, added after this result, states this). Seven of eight further specifications run by the referee have a lower bound below 0.95 (recent period 2023-2025 0.999 (0.936 to 1.061); public housing excluded 0.985 (0.925 to 1.049); start and end within one day 0.988 (0.920 to 1.055)). Two things the outcome did not examine. Public housing rose from 5.2% to 10.9% of complaints and its ratio is 1.24 (1.00 to 1.52), which raises the citywide ratio. The recorded day is the start of the victim's absence, and complaints with a window of two days or more have a ratio of 1.11 (0.96 to 1.29) against 0.99 (0.92 to 1.06) for those within one day, which is what more Friday departures for long weekends would produce. What stands: no fall is seen, and a fall of more than about 5% to 7% is unlikely. The district contrast (-13.2%) has a permutation p of 0.08 over the 48 districts, so its bootstrap interval is too narrow. The graph finding PMID 35491751 concerns alcohol outlets and has no bearing on occupancy.
