prediction.support_if: The 95% interval of C lies below zero (elasticity interval above zero).
prediction.refute_if: The 95% interval of C lies above zero, or its lower bound is above -0.013 (elasticity below 0.2 throughout the interval).

claims.plan: Exposure comes from the dose map only (data/derived/transit/dose_map_long.csv, built from MTA hourly entries before any outcome was queried). For a group of station complexes, E = ln(MF/TWT in Nov 2025-Oct 2026) - ln(MF/TWT in 2019), where MF is mean Monday and Friday entries and TWT mean Tuesday-to-Thursday entries, for 06:00-19:59 unless the AM peak (06:00-09:59) is named. E is negative where Mondays and Fridays thinned. Files: data/derived/round2/retimed_consequences/exposure_taxi_zone.csv, exposure_community_district.csv, exposure_groups.json; code analyses/round2/retimed_consequences/exposure.py. Estimator (analyses/round2/retimed_consequences/lib.py, written before registration): for each unit and period, r = ln(mean Monday and Friday count / mean Tuesday-to-Thursday count) over retained weeks, and Y = r(recent) - r(baseline). Retained weeks have no federal holiday and no day from 24 December to 1 January, as in the dose map; the weeks of Monday 26 January and Monday 23 February 2026 are also dropped, because subway entries on those Mondays were 38% and 20% of the week's midweek level (docs/transit.md), which was known from entries before any outcome was seen. Intervals are the 2.5 and 97.5 percentiles of 2,000 bootstrap draws that resample weeks within each period and, for a slope across units, the units as well. Outcome: EMS incidents (76xm-jjuj) with incident hour 06 to 19, by communitydistrict and date. Baseline: 2018 and 2019. Recent: 1 October 2024 to 30 September 2026, the last two years in the dataset. Units: the community districts (codes ending 01 to 18) that hold a reliable station complex, 54 in all; the CBD group is the six districts whose complexes are all inside the MTA business district (101 to 106), and the rest are the other 48. The reported effect is the elasticity C / -0.0639 with its interval; whether the interval includes 1 is reported as the test of proportionality. Secondary, not deciding: the slope of Y on E across the 54 districts; Monday and Friday separately; hours 06-09 and 10-15; high-severity incidents (initial severity 1 to 3) only; baseline 2019 and recent 12 months only. Placebo: 2016-2017 against 2018-2019. Power, from years outside the test: the same estimator applied to 2017 against 2018 gave C = -0.013 (-0.038 to 0.012), standard error 0.0129, and a slope standard error of 0.27 (design_ems_placebo_2017_2018.json); weekday incidents in the band averaged 375 a day in the CBD districts and 2,305 in the rest. With two years on each side the standard error of C should be about 0.009, or 0.14 as an elasticity. The central prediction, elasticity 0.4 (C = -0.026), is 2.8 standard errors from zero (D = 8); elasticity 0.2 is 1.4. A true elasticity of zero would meet refute_if about a quarter of the time and support_if 2.5% of the time. The slope across districts can detect only an elasticity near 0.8 and is secondary for that reason. Verdict by concord.claims.PRECEDENCE rules 1 to 4: support_if met gives confirmed, refute_if met gives contested, otherwise unsettled; no_test if the registered data cannot be read. Secondary and placebo results decide nothing.
claims.already_seen: Earlier claims queried EMS incidents by day for shootings and stabbings, drug and psychiatric calls, and asthma, citywide; none tabulated incidents by community district or by weekday against midweek. For this registration I queried all daytime incidents by district and date for 2017 and 2018 only, to estimate sampling error; 2018 is therefore in both the design check and the baseline, and I have seen the 2017-to-2018 change in its weekday ratio (C = -0.013), not its level against any later year.
alternatives: Residents of the CBD districts, about 600,000 people, stay in the district when they work at home, which offsets the loss of commuters.
Calls in Midtown come largely from visitors, shelters, hospitals and transit hubs, whose week did not change.
EMS call triage and telemedicine changed after 2020 and may have changed call volume differently by district.

The contrast is against the rest of the city, where people working at home add daytime presence on Mondays and Fridays; a negative C mixes a fall in the CBD with a rise elsewhere (the two pooled Y values are reported separately).
The district recorded is where the incident was, and incidents without a district code are dropped.

outcome.settle: A count of people present by district and day (mobile-device or turnstile exits) to replace entries as the denominator, and the incident location type, to separate calls from workplaces from calls from homes, streets and stations. The call type, which the dataset already holds, would separate office-hours illness and injury from calls tied to events, hotels and shelters in Midtown, where the fall is concentrated.

research_needed.question: How does emergency call volume scale with the daytime population of a business district, by call type?

outcome.notes:
Incidents between 06:00 and 19:59, 84 retained weeks in 2018-19 and 79 from October 2024 to September 2026; 377 and 354 a weekday in the six business-district districts, 2301 and 2454 in the other 48. The Monday-and-Friday ratio changed by -4.0% (-5.7 to -2.1) in the business district and by -1.2% (-2.2 to -0.1) in the rest. The rest of the city did not gain incidents on those days, so the contrast is a fall in the business district and not a rise elsewhere. Friday changed more than Monday in the business district (-5.3% against -2.5%). Placebo (2016-17 against 2018-19): -0.002 (-0.020 to 0.016). With 2019 and the last 12 months only: -0.022 (-0.047 to 0.003). By hours: 06-09 -0.023 (-0.060 to 0.015), 10-15 -0.030 (-0.055 to -0.004), 16-19 -0.031 (-0.064 to 0.003). High-severity incidents (initial severity 1 to 3): -0.037 (-0.064 to -0.009). The slope across the 54 districts is 0.30 (-0.17 to 0.75), which the registration said could not be estimated well. The standard error of the contrast, 0.0087, matches the 0.009 expected from the design check. Entries are fare-paid boardings and miss people who walk, drive or arrive by commuter rail, so the elasticity is per unit of subway thinning and not per person.

After the referee (13 Nov 2026): the result depends on Midtown. Without community district 105 the contrast is -0.016 (-0.036 to +0.004), and against the six other Manhattan districts it is -0.021 (-0.043 to +0.002); both intervals include zero. District 105 alone gives -0.071 and 104 gives -0.039, while 103 and 106 give 0.000 and +0.011 although 106 has nearly the largest thinning of entries. A dose-response within the business district is therefore not shown, and something particular to Midtown on Mondays and Fridays (events, hotels, shelter intake sites, a change in unit coverage) is not separated from office attendance. In favour of the claim, a night placebo (20:00 to 05:59) gives +0.009 (-0.014 to +0.032), every pairing of a baseline year with a recent year gives a negative contrast, and five other seeds give the same upper bound. The interval of the elasticity treats its denominator (-0.0639) as known and is somewhat too narrow; the verdict rests on the contrast. Incidents without a district code rose from about 1.0% to 2.4% of daytime incidents from January 2026, spread evenly over weekdays. Part of the contrast is a midweek rise (Wednesday index 0.998 to 1.013), which the statement 'fell on Mondays and Fridays' does not say. The estimator and exposure files were committed with the outcome, so their state at registration rests on file times.
outcome.verdict_note: Confirmed under the registered pooled contrast. The fall is concentrated in Midtown (district 105); without it the interval includes zero.

critique.answer: accepted; verdict kept, dependence on district 105 recorded

claims.statement: Between February-March 2019 and February-March 2026, daytime taxi and high-volume for-hire pickups on Mondays and Fridays fell relative to Tuesday-to-Thursday pickups in the taxi zones whose subway entries thinned most on Mondays and Fridays, in proportion to between 0.3 and 1.0 of the thinning of entries.

graph_evidence.summary: System Public Graph, variable searches (data/derived/graph/retimed_week/gap_checks.json and data/derived/round2/retimed_consequences/graph_gap_check.json, graph_leads.json): no finding has this outcome with commuting, working at home, day of week or daytime population as the exposure. 82 variables match taxi, ride-hailing, ridesharing or uber. The nearest are rideshare trips per taxi zone-hour as an exposure for injury crashes (odds ratio 1.046, PMID 32253258) and an elasticity of 0.004 between ride-hailing use and transit ridership with no PubMed id. Neither is a finding on demand by day of week.

prediction.refute_if: The 95% interval of b lies below zero, or its upper bound is below 0.3 (any effect is smaller than registered).

E is negative where Mondays and Fridays thinned. Files: data/derived/round2/retimed_consequences/exposure_taxi_zone.csv, exposure_community_district.csv, exposure_groups.json; code analyses/round2/retimed_consequences/exposure.py. Estimator (analyses/round2/retimed_consequences/lib.py, written before registration): for each unit and period, r = ln(mean Monday and Friday count / mean Tuesday-to-Thursday count) over retained weeks, and Y = r(recent) - r(baseline). Retained weeks have no federal holiday and no day from 24 December to 1 January, as in the dose map; the weeks of Monday 26 January and Monday 23 February 2026 are also dropped, because subway entries on those Mondays were 38% and 20% of the week's midweek level (docs/transit.md), which was known from entries before any outcome was seen. Intervals are the 2.5 and 97.5 percentiles of 2,000 bootstrap draws that resample weeks within each period and, for a slope across units, the units as well. Outcome: pickups with pickup hour 06 to 19 by pickup zone and date, yellow taxi plus high-volume for-hire (Uber, Lyft), from TLC trip records. This is a sample of months, not full years: February and March 2019 (7 retained weeks; high-volume for-hire records begin in February 2019; local parquet copies) against February and March 2026 (6 retained weeks; yellow from local parquet, high-volume for-hire by remote column scan of the TLC parquet files, which are not saved). Green taxis and other for-hire bases are left out. Units: the taxi zones that contain at least one reliable station complex (150) and have at least 200 pickups per weekday in the band in both periods. b is the unweighted OLS slope of Y on E. Sensitivity, reported and not deciding: slope weighted by 2019 pickups; yellow and for-hire separately; zones outside the CBD only; hours 06-09 against E for the AM peak. Placebo: yellow taxi February-March 2018 against 2019. Power, from data outside the test: random half-splits of the 10 retained weeks of January-March 2018 (yellow plus all for-hire, 147 zones) give a null standard deviation of 0.166 for b and 0.016 for the contrast; scaled to 7 and 6 weeks the expected standard errors are about 0.15 and 0.014 (design_taxi_placebo_2018.json). The smallest slope detectable with 80% power is about 0.41. At b = 0.5 the predicted contrast is -0.038, 2.7 standard errors from zero (D = 7.6, above the kit's threshold of 4). A true slope of zero would meet refute_if about half the time. The split-half error leaves out differences between zones that built up over seven years, so the real interval may be wider. Secondary and placebo results decide nothing.
claims.already_seen: The project holds TLC pickups by zone and day for January-March 2018 and 2019 (transit-fhv-price-subway, used for totals near subway complexes, not by weekday), June-October 2023 and June-September 2024 (transit-gtrain-substitution, G-train zones), and zone totals for commute-fhv-subway-distance. None was tabulated by weekday against midweek. For this registration I read yellow and for-hire pickups for January-March 2018 only, to estimate sampling error. I have not tabulated 2019 or 2026 pickups by weekday.
alternatives: Yellow taxis lost share to for-hire vehicles unevenly across zones, and the two services have different weekday patterns (separate estimates by service address this).
Tourists and residents, who did not change their week, make most daytime trips in Manhattan, so pickups need not follow office attendance.
Weather differed between the sampled weeks of 2019 and 2026; a storm on a Monday or Friday moves the citywide ratio, though less the difference between zones.
The congestion charge from January 2025 lowered trips in the CBD on all weekdays; it biases the result only if its effect differs between Monday or Friday and midweek.
MTA service changes on Mondays and Fridays alter entries without altering presence, which would weaken the slope.

outcome.notes:
Yellow taxi and high-volume for-hire pickups, 06:00-19:59, 147 zones, weeks ['2019-02-04', '2019-02-11', '2019-02-25', '2019-03-04', '2019-03-11', '2019-03-18', '2019-03-25'] and ['2026-02-02', '2026-02-09', '2026-03-02', '2026-03-09', '2026-03-16', '2026-03-23'] (the weeks of Presidents' Day and of the 23 February 2026 storm are dropped). Mean weekday pickups in these zones were 525,709 in 2019 and 455,842 in 2026. Weighted by 2019 pickups the slope is 0.67. Yellow only (44 zones): slope 0.86 (0.47 to 1.30), contrast -8.7% (-12.1 to -5.3). For-hire only: slope 0.46 (0.04 to 0.78), contrast -0.5% (-3.0 to +2.2). Zones outside the business district (120): slope -0.33 (-0.84 to 0.10), contrast +3.0% (+1.0 to +5.4), the opposite sign. Placebo, yellow 2018 against 2019: slope -0.30 (-0.63 to 0.01). Exploratory, not registered: pooled over the 27 business-district zones the Monday-and-Friday ratio changed by -4.5% (-8.5 to -0.8); outside it, the half of zones whose stations thinned more changed by +2.4% (+1.1 to +3.9) relative to the other half. The positive slope therefore comes from the difference between the business district and everywhere else; within residential zones the relation runs the other way. The registered thirds mix the two, which is why the contrast is near zero. The standard error of the slope (0.17) is close to the 0.15 expected from the 2018 design check. Green taxis and other for-hire bases are not counted. The 2026 for-hire months were read by a remote column scan of the TLC parquet files; nothing was saved except the zone-day counts.

After the referee (13 Nov 2026): the two registered measures disagree and the outcome did not say by how much. A slope of 0.5 implies a contrast of -0.038 between thirds, and the observed contrast (-0.011) is 2.1 standard errors from that prediction and 0.9 from no effect, so on the contrast the data favour no effect. The rank correlation between the two changes across the 147 zones is 0.11 (p = 0.17); the least-squares slope depends on a few zones with large thinning. With a business-district indicator the slope is 0.26 (SE 0.15). A weekend placebo fails: the change in the weekend-to-midweek ratio of pickups has a slope of -0.79 (SE 0.19) on the same exposure, so Mondays and Fridays are not the only days that moved and the registered ratio does not isolate office days. The bootstrap resamples seven and six weeks and its interval is too narrow; the 2018 against 2019 placebo gave a slope of -0.30. Leaving out one week at a time changes neither condition. An alternative that fits the pattern was not tested: trips moved to the home end on days worked at home. The February 2019 congestion surcharge falls in the baseline months. The registration's summary of PMID 32253258 omits that the odds ratio is per 100 additional trips.

critique.answer: accepted; verdict kept

Treatment data: red-light camera intersections and the first month with tickets, from Parking Violations Issued FY2024-FY2027 (8zf9-spf8, m5vz-tzqv, 9mwx-gamw, pvqr-7yc4; violation code 7, sampled on the 1st and 15th of each month; analyses/street_safety/rlc_sites.py), geocoded to OpenStreetMap intersections and the LPI gazetteer (geocode_sites.py). Treated: intersections first ticketed January-August 2026 with no ticket in earlier sampled months. Post window: months a+1 to a+9 (a = first month), ending October 2026; pre window: the same calendar months in 2024 and 2025. Controls: 3 LPI intersections (xc4v-ntf4, LPI before 2024) per treated site, same borough, at least 300 m from any camera, matched on the pre-window count of all crashes. Crashes (h9gi-nx95, with vehicles bm4k-52h4) within 50 m. Estimator: ratio of ratios (treated post/pre over control post/pre); 95% percentile interval from a cluster bootstrap over matched sets. Traffic diverted from camera intersections to nearby streets; controls are at least 300 m from every camera, which limits but does not exclude spillover.
A warning or test period before the first ticket, or tickets dated after the violation, shifting the true activation month.
Changes in police crash reporting or geocoding in 2026 that differ between camera and control intersections.

outcome.notes: Design: 283 intersections first ticketed January-August 2026, 3 matched LPI intersections each (pool 4590), 323683 geolocated crashes January 2023-October 2026. All outcomes, ratio of ratios (95% interval): rear-end proxy 1.327 (1.061-1.650); persons injured or killed 1.038 (0.907-1.192); pedestrians injured or killed 1.289 (1.029-1.637); 'Traffic Control Disregarded' crashes 1.111 (0.722-1.734); all crashes 1.181 (1.081-1.289). Registered placebo (same sites and windows one year earlier, before any camera): rear-end 1.250 (1.052-1.488); injured 1.263 (1.100-1.445); pedestrians 1.357 (1.031-1.749); red-running 0.866 (0.582-1.280); all crashes 1.296 (1.183-1.418). The placebo shows the design producing ratios of 1.25-1.36 where no camera existed. The likely reason is that controls were matched on their pre-window crash counts, so controls with unusually high counts were chosen and then fell (regression to the mean in the controls), while the camera sites, chosen by DOT on other grounds, did not fall in the same way. The design therefore carries a bias of roughly +25% in every outcome, and the registered estimates must be read against the placebo. Excluding the 3 sites near a 2024-26 street improvement project changes little: rear-end 1.301 (1.057-1.616), injured 1.027 (0.904-1.166). EXPLORATORY, not a test (rule 4): the ratio of the 2026 estimate to the placebo estimate, with a joint bootstrap, is rear-end 1.062 (0.797-1.395), persons injured 0.821 (0.672-0.993), pedestrians 0.95 (0.661-1.348), all crashes 0.911 (0.805-1.039). Read this way, the cameras show no clear rise in rear-end crashes and a fall of about 18% in persons injured, but the adjustment was chosen after the data were seen.
outcome.notes_referee: Referee reproduced 1.038 (0.907 to 1.192). Unsettled stands. The matching bias works against this prediction: unmatched comparisons (chosen after the data, exploratory) give 0.84 (0.75 to 0.93) and 0.81 (0.70 to 0.92). A successor must be registered on data not yet read, such as the 2027 windows with later-activated sites as controls.

claims.plan: Data, built by analyses/simulate/build_data.py (fixed and committed with this registration): MTA Congestion Relief Zone vehicle entries (data.ny.gov t6yz-b64h) summed over classes by date and hour; yellow-taxi trips that start and end in the 38 zone taxi zones under the R1 filter of repro-mmr-cbd-speed, speed = miles / hours; EMS incidents (76xm-jjuj) in community districts 101-106 with a valid response time and initial severity 1 to 3, mean travel time of the first unit. Unit: date by band of hours (night 21:00-04:59, am 05:00-09:59, mid 10:00-15:59, pm 16:00-20:59), non-holiday weekdays, 24 December to 1 January dropped. Estimator, analyses/simulate/fit_links.py (fixed): calibration fit by OLS of log speed on log entries with band x month and band x weekday effects, one pooled coefficient, standard errors clustered by ISO week; and log travel time on log speed with the same effects. Test (function holdout_test): on the held-out days, OLS of log speed on z = fitted elasticity x log entries with band x month and band x weekday effects of the held-out period; S1 is the coefficient of z, interval = estimate +/- 1.96 clustered se. S2 is the same for log travel time on fitted elasticity x log speed. No resampling is used, so there is no seed. Secondary, reported and not deciding: (a) S2 scored by the same two conditions as S1; (b) S1 with the band-specific elasticities; (c) level errors by band (function level_test), against the same band and weekday in 6 January to 30 June 2025: speed predicted from the change in entries; travel time predicted from the predicted speed (the chain); travel time predicted from the observed change in speed (the ambulance link alone). A level prediction counts as a hit if its mean absolute error over the four bands is at most 4% and smaller than the error of predicting no change. Can the test fail (rule 8)? A rehearsal inside the calibration year (fit January-June 2025, test July-December 2025; fits_calib.json) gave a standard error of 0.142 for the held-out speed elasticity and 0.091 for the ambulance elasticity. On the slope scale these are 0.35 and 0.16, so if the fitted elasticities are right the expected D against no relation is 8.3 for S1 and 39.4 for S2, both above 4. A world with no relation would meet support_if about 2.5% of the time. The rehearsal itself gave S1 = 2.5 (1.1 to 3.9): the first-half elasticity was -0.20 and the second-half one about -0.51, so the elasticity is not stable within 2025 and an interval that excludes 1 is a live possibility; that outcome is unsettled, not confirmed. What I have already seen of the held-out period: the half-year mean zone speeds for weekdays 08:00-17:59 in the outcome of repro-mmr-cbd-speed, 7.24 mph in January-June 2025 and 6.57 mph in January-June 2026, a fall of 9%. I have not seen 2026 vehicle entries, 2026 speeds by day or hour, or any EMS travel time for 2026. Because of the 9% fall, the speed level test (c) is not blind: with the fitted elasticity it would take about 25% more entries to produce that fall, which I do not expect, so I expect the model to over-predict the 2026 speed level by 5% to 9% in the am and mid bands and to do little better than predicting no change. The ambulance level test is blind: with the fitted elasticity a 9% fall in speed predicts about 5% longer travel times in the am and mid bands in 2026 than in the same months of 2025. Verdict by PRECEDENCE rule 1 on the primary conditions; otherwise unsettled. The slopes are associations between days: a day with more entries also has more pedestrians and deliveries, so a confirmed slope does not show what a toll-induced change in entries would do to speed.
rivals: Days with more vehicle entries are days with more people and deliveries in the zone, which slow traffic on their own; the slope then overstates the effect of entries.
Congestion inside the zone holds vehicles at the crossings and lowers counted entries, which biases the slope toward zero.
Changes in the taxi fleet's routes or trip mix between years move measured taxi speed without a change in traffic.
EMS travel time depends on unit availability and call volume, which vary with the same days.

outcome.notes:
Exploratory, after the outcome was read, and not part of the verdict. The standard error of S1 (0.05) is a seventh of the one expected at registration (0.35). The held-out period contains two storm days, 26 January and 23 February 2026, when vehicle entries were 40% and 13% of a normal weekday. On those days entries collapsed and taxi speed rose little, and they fix the estimate. Without the four weekdays whose entries were under 80% of the median, the held-out elasticity is +0.08 (se 0.54), which neither supports nor refutes the fitted value; pooled over 2025 and 2026 without those days it is -0.23 (se 0.23). The two storm Mondays were known from subway entries (transit-weekday-pattern) and the registration should have excluded them; it did not, so the verdict stands as registered. The level result does not depend on the storm days: from January-June 2025 to January-June 2026 vehicle entries per weekday fell from 507,000 to 480,000 and zone taxi speed fell in every band. Yellow-taxi trips inside the zone also fell, from 51,000 to 45,000 a weekday, so the speed series comes from a changing set of trips. On 2025 weekdays, Mondays and Fridays have 2.8% fewer daytime vehicle entries than Tuesday to Thursday, 10.1% higher taxi speed and 6.8% shorter ambulance travel times: the weekday pattern of speed follows people present in the zone (subway entries are 13.8% lower on those days) and not vehicle entries.

After the referee (13 Nov 2026): the verdict stays contested under rule 1. The registered refutation condition is met, it remains met when the error of the fitted elasticity is carried into the ratio (standard error 0.088, interval 0.11 to 0.46), and no rule allows a day to be excluded after the data. The verdict means that the fitted link did not predict the held-out days as registered. It does not measure the elasticity on ordinary days. After the registered fixed effects, 23 February carries 74% and 26 January 10% of the variation in log entries of the held-out period. On 23 February entries were 78% to 95% below normal by band and taxi speed was 18% to 71% above normal; a constant elasticity of -0.41 predicts a rise of about 150% for a 90% fall in entries, so those days show that the log-linear form fails at large changes. Without 23 February alone the upper bound of S1 is 0.51 and the refutation condition is not met. On the remaining days the held-out elasticity runs from +0.10 (se 0.43) without the two storm days to -0.47 (se 0.36) without the eight days under 0.90 of median entries, -0.93 (se 0.16) without the 22 days under 0.95 and -1.14 (se 0.16) on dry days. Day-level data cannot identify the relation in either year. In 2025 the residual standard deviation of log entries is 0.032, 65% of band-days lie within 2% of their expected entries and 93% within 5%, and the day after Thanksgiving alone carries 31% of the variation. The 2025 coefficient falls from -0.41 to -0.09 (se 0.11) when the number of taxi trips inside the zone is added and returns to -0.37 when mean trip distance is also added; it differs from zero only in the last quarter. Taxi and for-hire entries, which do not respond to the entry toll, have the same coefficient as other entries (-0.22 each). The level miss of the speed link cannot be assigned to the link. From January 2026 taxi speed fell across the city: trips under three miles that neither start nor end in the zone slowed by 10.1%, 13.1%, 5.4%, 4.0%, 4.3% and 2.6% in January to June against a year earlier, and trips inside the zone by 8.5%, 13.2%, 6.0%, 5.9%, 5.4% and 9.4%. In December 2025 both were within about 2% of the year before. Within 1,344 pairs of origin and destination zones speed fell 8.9%, with recorded miles per trip down 1.1% and minutes up 8.6%. Both vendors show the fall. Bus speeds do not: in the zone they fell 3.9% over the half-year, mostly in January to March, and outside it 0.6%. Weather explains a small part (the 2026 effect on log speed is -0.066, se 0.009, with weather controls). The cause was not found. Until it is, the taxi speed series should not be compared across the two years. The ambulance link does not depend on the low days: S2 is 1.22 (0.76 to 1.69) without the two storm days and 1.12 (0.60 to 1.64) without the eight days under 0.90, and its D against no relation is 32. Its size falls from about -0.6 to about -0.4 within weeks (-0.39, se 0.09) or on dry days (-0.38, se 0.12), so part of the registered slope is weather that slows taxis and ambulances together. The holiday list holds federal holidays only, and the night band joins the end of one night with the start of the next; neither changes a number that decides the verdict. The stance was +0.994, computed against no relation, which placed a contested claim at the agreeing end. It is now measured against the registered threshold. No successor was registered. On ordinary days the standard error of S1 is 1.32 on 119 days; a discrimination of 4 between S1 = 1 and S1 = 0 needs a standard error of 0.5, which is about 827 ordinary weekdays, more than three years, so a day-level test with the data to autumn 2026 could not fail (rule 8).

stance.note: Measured against the registered refutation threshold, S1 = 0.5 (half the fitted elasticity), with the error of the fitted elasticity carried (se 0.088). The earlier value, +0.994, was measured against no relation and placed a contested claim at the agreeing end. The value rests on two storm days; without them S1 is -0.23 (se 1.05) and the stance is not determined.

claims.statement: In New York City, within the same month and year, days in the cool half of the year (October to March) that are colder have more FDNY EMS dispatches for asthma, and the slope is more positive (or less negative) in the warm half of the year (April to September).

graph_evidence.summary: The graph's 22 positive and 8 negative findings do not disagree about temperature level once the variable names and abstracts are read. I recoded each finding by what was measured. 17 findings are short-term effects of temperature level; 16 of them (7 studies: Taipei, Hong Kong twice, Hefei, Lanzhou, a US emergency department, the Bronx) say colder days or falling temperatures bring more asthma visits or admissions, and they are stored with a positive sign because the variable is named 'low temperature' or 'cold (5th percentile)'; one (Guangzhou-type subtropical city, respiratory morbidity) says heat. 9 findings are about temperature change or variability, not level, and disagree by season: in Shanghai a day-to-day rise raises childhood asthma visits in the warm season (RR 1.98) and a drop lowers them (RR 0.31), with no effect in the cool season; Hefei and a dry-climate city find variability effects mainly in the cool season; a US case-crossover study finds a negligible inverse effect. 3 are cross-sectional comparisons of climates (prevalence is higher in warmer places in China, Costa Rica and Italy), a different question. One is an interaction with air quality. Eight of the 30 rows are four results from PMID 35817164 stored twice.

prediction.magnitude: Cool half-year: incidence rate ratio of asthma dispatches per 5 C higher mean temperature over lags 0 to 3 days between 0.95 and 0.99. Warm half-year: rate ratio between 1.00 and 1.05. Difference of log rate ratios (warm minus cool) positive.

prediction.moderator_prediction: Secondary, scored separately and not deciding the verdict: the warm-minus-cool difference of log rate ratios is positive with a 95% interval excluding 0. Reasoning from the moderators: the cold effect in the literature is a cool-season, low-percentile effect, and the only seasonal analysis of rises (Shanghai) finds them harmful in the warm season only.

City side: Central Park daily temperature (NOAA GHCN-Daily) has been used with shootings, heat-illness ED visits and EMS dispatches of type SHOT, STAB, DRUG, DRUGFC, EDP, EDPC, EDPM. outcome.notes:
Deviation from the registration: the asthma call types first appear on 2006-09-28, so the series starts 2006-10-01, not 2006-01-01. 326,660 dispatches on 7,275 days. Warm half-year rate ratio 1.012 (0.993 to 1.032). Sensitivity analyses (final call type, lag 0, lags 0-7, minimum temperature, excluding March 2020 to June 2021) all give cool-season rate ratios between 1.001 and 1.006 with intervals including 1. Exploratory, by calendar month: June 1.064, July 1.132 (1.079 to 1.187), August 1.080, September 0.899 (0.869 to 0.931), February 0.963 (0.937 to 0.990). The September slope is confounded with the date: asthma rises after schools open while days cool, and month fixed effects do not remove a trend inside a month. The half-year split chosen at registration averages a positive summer slope with this negative September one.

After the referee (13 Nov 2026): the bound in the outcome applies to variation within a calendar month at lags of up to four days, and not generally. The sign of the cool-season slope depends on how time is controlled: with year effects and four annual harmonics it is 0.985 (0.972 to 0.9985), which would have met the support condition, and with year-month effects and lags 0 to 21 it is 1.027 (1.006 to 1.049). Neither was registered and neither changes the verdict. The named alternative that asthma calls are absorbed by difficulty-breathing codes on cold days was tested by the referee and does not hide a cold effect: those codes rise with temperature in the cool half-year (1.0125, 1.0055 to 1.0196). Asthma dispatches fell from about 24,000 a year in 2014 to about 9,000 in 2024, which may reflect a change in call typing; the slope is the same before and after 2013. On the graph side, PMID 35817164 supplies several rows that are strata of one analysis (2.16 is the relative risk on days with high PM2.5 and 1.64 on days with low PM2.5), so '16 of 17 findings' overstates the number of independent results and '7 studies' is the better count.

claims.statement: In New York City, 2020 to 2025, weeks that follow warmer-than-normal weather for the time of year have slower growth of COVID-19 hospital admissions; and the raw correlation between daily temperature and daily case counts within single quarters, the design behind most positive findings in the graph, takes both signs depending on where the quarter falls in an epidemic wave.

graph_evidence.summary: The positive findings are mostly unadjusted Spearman or Pearson correlations between daily temperature and daily or cumulative case counts in one place over the first weeks or months of 2020, when cases and spring temperatures rose together (Jakarta, Oslo, India, Russia, Jordan, Korea, Pakistan). The negative findings mostly model transmission (reproduction number, growth, lagged incidence) with distributed lags, case-crossover designs or controls for government response (Wuhan and Hubei cities, four European countries, 153 countries above the turning point, US temperate regions, Mexico City, a meta-analysis). Four positive rows are not positive in substance: PMID 34189495 is '1 C decrease' and case fatality, PMID 34966171 is the relative risk at the 1st temperature percentile (cold raises transmissibility), PMID 35257688 says in its abstract that higher temperature goes with lower reproduction although the row is +0.875, and PMID 34375443 is body temperature (fever thresholds) grounded to 'temperature'. So the moderator is design and outcome: raw count correlations in a growth phase give either sign; models of transmission give negative.

prediction.magnitude: Change in the weekly log growth rate of hospital admissions per 1 C of temperature anomaly averaged over days 7 to 20 before the week's midpoint: between -0.030 and -0.003. Raw quarterly Spearman correlations of daily mean temperature with daily confirmed cases: at least 25% of quarters significantly positive and at least 25% significantly negative (p < 0.05, ignoring autocorrelation, as the source studies did).

Weeks are Monday to Sunday; H_t is the weekly sum of hospitalized_count; g_t = log(H_t / H_{t-1}); weeks from 2020-03-16 with H_t and H_{t-1} at least 20. Exposure: Central Park daily mean temperature (TMAX+TMIN)/2 minus its day-of-year normal (two-harmonic fit to 2010-2025), averaged over days 7 to 20 before the Thursday of week t. Model: OLS of g_t on the anomaly, g_{t-1}, year fixed effects and two annual harmonic pairs; Newey-West standard errors with 4 lags. Sensitivity, reported but not deciding: anomaly window days 0 to 13 and days 14 to 27; cases instead of admissions; dropping 2020; dropping the Omicron weeks (2021-12-13 to 2022-02-13). Secondary: for each calendar quarter from 2020 Q2 to 2025 Q3, Spearman correlation of daily mean temperature with daily case_count. Disclosure of what the project had seen before this registration. Graph side: all findings of both relationships and their PubMed abstracts were read (data/derived/graph/splits/findings.json, abstracts.json). City side: Central Park daily temperature (NOAA GHCN-Daily) has been used with shootings, heat-illness ED visits and EMS dispatches of type SHOT, STAB, DRUG, DRUGFC, EDP, EDPC, EDPM. For EMS dispatches (76xm-jjuj) the project has seen the count of every initial_call_type for calendar 2023 (ASTHMB 7,130; ASTHFC 2,813) and the date range of the file (2005-01-01 to 2026-09-30). For the COVID-19 daily counts (rc75-m7u3) I queried the column list and the first and last date (2020-02-29, 2025-10-13; 2,054 rows) and nothing else; no other agent has queried it.
alternatives: Behaviour: warm anomalies move people outdoors and cold ones indoors; this is part of the weather effect and is not separated from virus survival.

Power check (rule 8): with a stall rate near 0.4 the standard error of D1 is about 0.021 and of D2 about 0.031, so an effect of 0.10 gives z_null about 4.8 for D1 (D = 23) and 3.2 for D2 (D = 10); D1 discriminates for effects above about 0.06 and D2 for effects above about 0.06. alternatives: Interest-rate and cost shock of 2022-2023 affecting all jobs started in 2022 (D2 separates it partly; the 2023 cohort faces the same rates)
System change: 65% of the 2022 window is DOB NOW and all controls are legacy BIS; DOB NOW CO recording or BBL coding may differ (legacy-only secondary comparison)
Composition: the rush brought larger projects, which take longer than 36 months whether or not they stall

outcome.notes: Registered run: rates of no CO within 1,096 days of the first initial foundation permit, BBL matching: 2017 0.677 (n 541), 2018 0.626 (n 516), 2019 0.449 (n 497), 2020 0.310 (n 290), 2021 0.331 (n 393), 2022 0.379 (n 807), 2023 0.287 (n 366). The control windows 2017 and 2018 (0.68 and 0.63) were far above 2019 (0.45). A check after the result, by job number, showed that the registered BBL matching misses certificates for older jobs: for 2017 legacy jobs, 59% had a CO under the same job number within 36 months, against 32% found by BBL. The permit's lot and the certificate's lot differ for many older jobs, probably because lots were merged, split or converted to condominium billing lots after the permit. EXPLORATORY (analyses/stalled/vesting_exploratory.py, decides nothing): matching by job number or BBL, the 36-month no-CO rates are 2017 0.396, 2018 0.490, 2019 0.406, 2020 0.300, 2021 0.323, 2022 0.375, 2023 0.279. D1 under this matching is -0.055 (-0.096 to -0.014), so the refutation does not depend on the matching defect; legacy jobs only, D1 is -0.014 (-0.079 to 0.047). Against the 2021 window D1 is 0.052 (-0.004 to 0.108). The rush window had 807 foundation starts against about 520 a year in 2017-2019. At 48 months its no-CO rate (0.235) is within the range of 2017-2019 (0.25 to 0.30). By November 2026, 140 of the 807 rush-window jobs have no CO. The rush to pour footings before the deadline therefore added about 300 starts, most of which were completed at the usual rate; it did not produce a measurable excess of stalled foundations citywide. The 2023 window stalls less than 2022, which fits a composition change (jobs that could not vest are smaller or condominium projects) as well as the vesting account.

graph_evidence.summary: System Public Graph variable searches (data/derived/street_space/graph_evidence.json, graph_detail.json). No variable for busway, transit priority, road-space reallocation, traffic evaporation or displaced traffic; 'road closure' and 'street closure' match nothing relevant; 'travel time' matches travel to health care. Nearest findings, abstracts read: Peace Bridge traffic fell 50% after 11 September 2001 with respiratory admissions nearly significant (PMID 14743825; the graph stores the 50% as a mean difference of 50); Busan traffic control in 2002 lowered pollutants 1-25%, childhood asthma RR 0.73 (0.49-1.11) (PMID 17824287); bus stops on a bus-only lane in Lima, pedestrian collision OR 2.36 (1.02-5.42) (PMID 24357516). None bears on travel time or displacement.

Probe-vehicle runs on single streets, not door-to-door trips.

Reasoning: trips that used 14th Street must use one-way side streets (12th, 13th, 15th, 16th, 17th) or turn off at the next avenue; a detour of a block or two on a 1.5-mile trip is 3-7% for the trips affected, perhaps a third to a half of them.

prediction.refute_if: The upper 95% bound of E is below +1.5% (the predicted central detour is excluded).

claims.plan: Data: TLC yellow-taxi trip records (monthly parquet, d37ci6vzurychx.cloudfront.net/trip-data/yellow_tripdata_YYYY-MM.parquet), July 2016 to February 2020, held in ~/opt/nyc-concordance/tlc_yellow_1720/. Scripts: analyses/street_space/common.py (zones, windows), extract.py (aggregation by directed pair, date and hour; filter 0<mi<=50, 60 s to 3 h, 0.5-50 mph), series.py (monthly contrast c_m: treated pairs minus control pairs of pair-demeaned mean log outcome; pairs with at least 20 trips in every month), test.py (the estimator E and its standard error), all committed before this registration. Treated: directed pairs between {Meatpacking/West Village West 158, West Village 249, East Chelsea 68, Greenwich Village North 113} and {East Village 79, Stuy Town 224, Alphabet City 4, Gramercy 107}. Control: the same kind of east-west pairs in Midtown ({48, 50, 100, 230} with {170, 162, 233, 229}) and downtown ({231, 125, 211} with {148, 232, 144, 45}). Sample: weekdays except federal holidays, pickup hour 07 to 18. d_m = c_m - c_(m-12). E = mean d_m over October 2019 to February 2020 minus mean d_m over July to September 2019. se = s*sqrt(1/5+1/3), s = sd of d_m from July 2017 to September 2019; 95% interval E +/- 1.96 se; percent = 100(exp(.)-1). No resampling, so no seed enters the verdict. Verdict by PRECEDENCE rules 1 and 2; conditions are on interval bounds (rule 10). Secondary, not deciding: all-day busway hours (06-21) and overnight (22-05) samples; the plain year-over-year DiD with a day bootstrap (estimate.py, 2,000 draws, seed 20261113); per-pair changes; a monthly event-study figure. The pair set is fixed by the 20-trips-every-month rule over the whole input, so adding the post months may drop a pair and move the placebo values slightly; the outcome reports both. Outcome: log metered trip distance (s_ld).
alternatives: Year-to-year drift of the contrast between the 14th Street corridor and the control corridors (seen in the design run: +3.4% from 2017-18 to 2018-19 in the plain year-over-year DiD), which the summer-netted estimator is meant to remove.

The L train weeknight and weekend slowdown (27 April 2019 to 26 April 2020), present in both July-September 2019 and October 2019-February 2020; the primary sample is weekday daytime when the L ran normally.

claims.plan: Unit: Chicago community area (n = 77). Indicators: the 37 in analyses/round5_chicago_matrix/chicago_indicators.py, each a Chicago Health Atlas topic matched to a New York indicator key, so that the New York concepts, polarities and literature signs apply unchanged. Two topics that report absence (uninsured, physically inactive) are reversed as 100 minus the value. Each topic is read at the community-area layer for the total population, at the latest period (by end year; the longer window on a tie) with a value for at least 70 of the 77 areas; a topic with no such period is dropped (fetch.py). Qualifying rule, as in New York: signed findings from at least 3 studies and at least 80% of signed findings on one side. City sign, as in New York: Spearman correlation across areas, raw, and with poverty partialled out (correlation of the residuals of each indicator's ranks on poverty's ranks); the partialled correlation decides, and the raw correlation decides for pairs that include poverty. matrix.py copies spearman_matrix, partial_matrix and decide from analyses/graph_concordance/matrix.py and was checked before registration to reproduce New York's 72 of 109, 10 of 27 and 29 of 56 from the New York files. Reported for Chicago: agreement overall and by kind of pair (the four kinds of graph_concordance/explore.py and the referee's three role kinds), each with a 95% bootstrap interval over areas; the agreement of an always-positive rule and the margin over it with an interval; the area-shuffle null (each indicator shuffled across areas, poverty fixed) and the sign-shuffle null (literature signs shuffled among qualifying pairs), 2,000 draws each; the Spearman correlation of PM2.5 with poverty with a bootstrap interval. New York is recomputed with the same code on all its qualifying pairs and on the pairs that qualify and are computable in both cities, and the difference in the air-and-traffic share on the same pairs is reported with an interval from independent bootstrap draws. Seed 20261113 (numpy default_rng([seed, 0]) for Chicago, [seed, 1] and [seed, 2] for New York), 2,000 draws. The verdict is computed by verdict() in matrix.py from the conditions above. Under PRECEDENCE rule 9 the run is repeated with 20,000 draws and with five other seeds (--draws, --seed, --tag, --no-null); if the bootstrap condition is met under some and not others, the verdict is unsettled. Scripts fixed at commit 0ba7f1a43b4ef768eee2a0516459991a9d6405b3 on local main and identified by content: {'analyses/round5_chicago_matrix/chicago_indicators.py': {'sha256': '400fd529dad0471065aacd33d66e7a7e9f7b92c710225e7e124a084228069e68', 'git_blob': '25227bd5d3cfb7b2cb158ddc07e8da20113e6452'}, 'analyses/round5_chicago_matrix/fetch.py': {'sha256': 'f6a64c975191269a8a8479ec433c14b94ebaec43f530c0e6a2380c4c4e15034f', 'git_blob': 'bd48953db77251ef99b485193153dc1cd4ae8c90'}, 'analyses/round5_chicago_matrix/matrix.py': {'sha256': '90d9f9d96345bc6368f8149073a5ab2c8fd27390ec7f8c8a8642030ccacf3b76', 'git_blob': '11a54aa41fba79bf7ad7bf98af6ea2ee03c51d5d'}}. The support condition is on pairs of an exposure with an outcome, where the literature's sign says something about a cause, and not on the overall rate, which the always-positive rule nearly reproduces (referee report critique/graph-concordance-matrix.md). Within the fifteen air and traffic pairs every literature sign is positive, so agreement there equals the always-positive rate and the comparison is between cities, not against that rule. Differences from New York that the design does not remove: PM2.5 and ozone are EPA EJSCREEN regional model surfaces, smoother than New York's street-level survey, and ozone may vary very little across the city; traffic is proximity to traffic, not vehicle miles; asthma is survey prevalence, not emergency visits; premature death is years of potential life lost; low birthweight is not restricted to term births; depression is a CDC PLACES model estimate built partly from demographic predictors. Notes per indicator are in chicago_indicators.py. New York indicators with no Chicago match: no2 (no NO2 topic); black_carbon (diesel particulate matter (DPM) exists but is a different quantity and concept); noise (no noise topic); surface_temp (no surface temperature topic); green_cover (green space proximity (EKG) is discontinued and measures distance, not cover); park_access (no park access topic); ac (no air conditioning topic); housing_problems (no maintenance topic); cockroaches (no pest topic); transit_commute (active transportation (ACT) mixes walking, cycling and public transport); walk_commute (same); asthma_child (youth asthma ED visits (CHAOHOB) are not published by community area); psych_hosp (behavioural health hospitalisations (HDBHR) are not published by community area). Disclosure: before registration the registrant read only metadata from the Chicago Health Atlas API (the topic list with names, units and descriptions; the coverage endpoint, which lists periods and population groups for 59 topics; the layer list) and, to learn the response format of the data endpoint, one response for the topic POP (total population, not an indicator in this study), of which about a dozen community-area population counts were displayed. No value of any of the 37 indicators was loaded, and no file under data/cache/chicago_atlas existed. The project's earlier Chicago claims (transfer-chicago-heat-shootings, -hot-end, -weekday-pattern) used citywide daily series, not community-area indicators. The New York side is fully seen. The registrant knows from general reading that Chicago's South and West sides are poorer, have worse health and hold the industrial corridors, that traffic is densest near the expressways and the Loop, and that EJSCREEN PM2.5 varies by about 1 microgram per cubic metre within a city.
alternatives: Measurement: a smooth regional PM2.5 or ozone surface ranks community areas by position in the region (a north-south gradient), so its correlation with outcomes may reflect geography and not exposure.
Ozone: in New York ozone pairs agreed (5 of 6) because ozone is lowest in the dense core; the same chemistry may or may not hold on the EJSCREEN surface.

Partialling poverty removes much of what sorting adds in a city where pollution follows poverty, so agreement after partialling may still fail even if the sorting explanation is right; the raw correlation is reported beside it.
Racial segregation: in Chicago health outcomes follow race more closely than the poverty rate, and a poverty partial leaves that in.
Common valence and dependence: fifteen pairs share three exposures and a handful of outcomes, so the effective number of independent pairs is small; the bootstrap over areas carries this.
Different measures of the outcomes in the two cities (prevalence against emergency visits, years of life lost against death before 65).

After the referee (13 Nov 2026): the verdict is kept under rule 1 and its meaning is narrowed. The referee reproduced the counts, the interval (0.533 to 0.867 under another seed) and the correlations with separate code. Every registered support condition is met: 15 pairs, a share of 80%, a lower bootstrap limit of 0.533 against 0.370, and 12 against New York's 6 on the same pairs. verdict() in matrix.py did not check the last of these; it is met. What is confirmed is the count. The clause of the statement about the residential-sorting explanation is not tested by any registered condition, and the referee's results are evidence against reading the count as support for it.
One exposure. The difference between the cities is PM2.5: 0 of 6 pairs in New York and 5 of 6 in Chicago. Without the PM2.5 pairs Chicago agrees in 7 of 9 and New York in 6 of 9. Six pairs that share one exposure are close to one observation.
A regional gradient. Chicago's PM2.5 ranges from 8.63 to 9.33 micrograms per cubic metre (coefficient of variation 1.8%, against 10.7% in New York). A plane in the centroid coordinates explains 85% of its variance across community areas and 58% of ozone's; Moran's I is 0.83 for each. PM2.5 rises toward the southwest, and health is worse there. With the coordinates partialled out together with poverty, 1 of the 6 PM2.5 pairs agrees and Chicago agrees in 9 of 15 (New York 3 of 15). When PM2.5 is replaced by a plane tilted in each compass direction, 38% of directions give at least 5 of 6 positive pairs and 38% give at most 1 of 6. A contrast of 0.7 micrograms would not produce correlations of 0.35 to 0.55 with obesity, diabetes and early death through any causal path, so agreement with the literature's sign in Chicago says no more about the literature than disagreement did in New York.
Dependence. With the Clifford and Richardson correction the effective number of areas is 12 to 31 for five of the six PM2.5 pairs (54 for asthma) and 16 to 45 for the ozone pairs, and at those sizes none of the fifteen correlations has p below 0.05 (smallest 0.08). The bootstrap resamples areas as independent, so its intervals are too narrow. The mean bootstrap share is 0.70, 3% of resamples fall below 60%, and leaving out one area gives 10 to 12 agreeing pairs.
Chance and regression to the mean. When the three exposures are shuffled together across areas, the count has mean 7.5 and standard deviation 2.3; 12 or more occurs with probability 0.04, and a count as far from 7.5 in either direction with probability 0.08. Fisher's test of 12 of 15 against 6 of 15 gives 0.06 and assumes independent pairs. New York's 6 of 15 was known before registration and is low; on the other 60 pairs Chicago agrees in 43 and New York in 44, so a city with nothing particular about its pollution would be expected near 70% on the fifteen pairs and would also have met the condition. The threshold 0.370 was registered as a constant although New York's 10 of 27 has its own sampling error.
Controls. With foreign-born share, high-school completion or unemployment added to poverty, Chicago agrees in 9 of 15, exactly the 60% threshold; with density added, in 12. Agreement is higher after partialling poverty (12) than before (10), so measured poverty does not carry the result. Racial segregation, which the registration named, is not measured in the indicator set.
The two cities' PM2.5 measures differ in instrument (street-level survey against regional model) and in geography (highest in the dense core against highest in low-density areas), and with two cities the design cannot separate these from sorting.

claims.statement: In Chicago, the daily number of shooting incidents with a gunshot injury rises with the day's maximum temperature at Midway Airport by about the same proportion as in New York (IRR 1.146 per 5 C, 1.130 to 1.163), under the same model, so that the New York result transfers.

graph_evidence.summary: Two case-crossover studies. Rahman et al. 2023 (California 2014-2019): homicide odds +4.9% (1.6 to 8.1) per 5 C Tmax lag 0. Xu et al. 2020 (9 US cities 2007-2017): intentional homicide +9.5% (4.3 to 15.0) per 5 C mean temperature in Chicago and +8.8% (1.5 to 16.6) in New York, lag 0-7. The graph stores Xu's estimates as odds ratios 0.095 and 0.088 and Rahman's as odds ratios 4.9 and 6.2; the abstracts give percent changes, so the graph values are mis-extracted (true ORs about 1.095, 1.088, 1.049, 1.062).

Girma et al. 2023, New York City ED visits 2005-2011 (SPARCS), warm season: intentional injury among 20-25 year olds OR 1.54 (1.28 to 1.85) for daily minimum 77 F vs 48 F, lag 0-5. The only NYC violence-temperature finding in the graph.

The gun violence concept has no relationship with temperature, air temperature, heat wave, hot or extreme heat. Violence (2qLKgaxkm_), crime, aggression and violent crime have none either. The graph's heat-violence evidence is homicide and injury only.
Self-directed violence rises with temperature in 8 studies (e.g. RR 1.35, 1.26 to 1.45, PMID 35394808; per 1 C IRR 1.008, PMID 34034696). Context for the violence claim.

claims.graph_evidence_note: Copied from heat-shootings. The graph holds no temperature-gun violence finding; its Chicago evidence is Xu et al. 2020 (homicide, +9.5% per 5 C mean temperature, 4.3 to 15.0). Descriptive, run after the city test and not part of the verdict. For temperature concepts paired with violence-side concepts (homicide, assault, aggression, violent crime, suicide, injury, gun violence) and for telework or commuting variables, list every study behind the relationships (sysgraph.relationship_studies, sysgraph.study) and tabulate the population field by country and by setting. Predicted before the lookup: fewer than 25% of studies with a readable population name a US city or a US metropolitan area, fewer than 5 studies name Chicago or New York, and the telework and commuting findings are dominated by non-US samples (UK, Netherlands, China, Australia). The graph's population field is free text and sparse, so the share with a readable population is reported with the shares.

plan.outcome_unit: Daily count of distinct case_number among rows of gumc-mgzr with gunshot_injury_i in ('Y','YES'), by date (date_trunc_ymd). A case can have several victims; New York's unit is the distinct incident_key, so the case is the analogous unit. Non-fatal shootings begin in 2010 in this dataset, so the period is 2010-01-01 to 2026-08-31 (the end date used for New York), with days without rows counted as zero.
plan.weather: GHCN-Daily USW00014819 (Chicago Midway), TMAX and PRCP, via concord/noaa.py. Midway is nearer the south and west sides, where most shootings occur, than O'Hare. If Midway TMAX is missing on more than 5% of days in the period, O'Hare (USW00094846) becomes primary and the registration's primary reading is taken to be that file.
plan.model: The same as heat-shootings: negative binomial GLM, log link, dispersion by maximum likelihood, robust HC0 standard errors; n ~ TMAX/5 + C(day of week) + C(month) + C(year) + holiday + (PRCP >= 1 mm). Holidays are the federal holidays plus 1 January, 4 July and 31 December (analyses.heat.common.holidays). IRR per 5 C with a 95% interval.
sensitivity: S1 TMAX averaged over lags 0-1
S2 TMIN instead of TMAX
S3 May-September only
S4 2010-2019 and 2020 onward separately
S5 O'Hare TMAX in place of Midway
S6 the 2012-2016 window of Reeping and Hemenway
S7 homicide victims only (victimization_primary = 'HOMICIDE'), distinct case_number
S8 Crimes (ijzp-q8t2): daily count of primary_type = 'HOMICIDE' plus primary_type = 'BATTERY' with description containing 'AGGRAVATED' and 'HANDGUN' or 'FIREARM'
S9 exploratory, not decisive: temperature interacted with a weekend-or-holiday indicator, for comparison with Reeping and Hemenway
plan.figure: figures/graph/transfer_chicago.png: NYC and Chicago side by side for both results.

alternatives: Different seasonal structure: Chicago's colder winters and larger seasonal range change how much of the temperature signal month terms absorb.
Different reporting: gunshot victimization is recorded by victim in the Chicago dataset; case-level counting merges victims of one event.
Different policing and gang-conflict dynamics, and the 2016 Chicago shooting spike, which year terms absorb only in level.
Temperature measured at an airport 13 km from the Loop, with a lake-breeze gradient that Central Park does not have in the same degree.
Time outdoors as the mechanism; the design cannot separate it from physiology in either city.

outcome.notes:
Same negative binomial model as heat-shootings, fitted to 6,085 days and 41,063 cases in Chicago from 2010 (when the portal's non-fatal shooting series begins) to 31 August 2026. Midway TMAX was missing on 0.03% of days. Within-city seasonality is absorbed by month and year terms, so the estimate describes day-to-day deviations from the month's level.

After the referee (13 Nov 2026): the referee rebuilt the daily series, obtained the same estimate (1.131, 1.120 to 1.143) and found it inside the transfer band under six further specifications; errors that allow for serial correlation widen the interval by about a tenth (1.119 to 1.144). What transfers is the average slope and not the shape of the dose-response. Fitted separately below and above 20 C, Chicago's slope is 1.148 (1.133 to 1.164) below and 1.104 (1.084 to 1.124) above, and New York's from 2010 is 1.137 (1.112 to 1.164) below and 1.174 (1.139 to 1.210) above. Chicago flattens on hot days and New York steepens, and the average slopes agree in part because Chicago has more cold days. The claim transfer-chicago-hot-end addresses the shape. New York refitted from 2010 gives 1.151 (1.132 to 1.170), so the difference in periods does not matter.

claims.statement: In Chicago, as in New York, a daily proxy for people outdoors (Divvy bicycle trips) stops rising with maximum temperature between 27 and 33 C while shootings keep rising, and adding the proxy to the shootings model removes part of the rise in shootings from 15 to 21 C and little of the rise from 27 to 33 C.

graph_evidence.summary: Graph sign for the first link is negative. Kim et al. 2022 (Korea Community Health Survey 2018): odds of walking practice 0.95 (0.94 to 0.97) per 1 C of the preceding week's daily maximum in rural areas and 0.98 (0.97 to 1.00) in urban areas; the graph holds the rural value only. The second association returned (walking after fan precooling, rectal temperature) is a laboratory finding on body temperature and is noise here.

The relationship aggregates report 13 findings; the API returns one. Mora-Rodriguez et al. 2016 (573 adults, Spain, Greece, Germany): self-reported physical activity falls with ambient temperature, r = -0.277.

Its signed findings on heat and being outdoors are negative (Kim 2022, odds of regular walking 0.95 per 1 C rural and 0.98 urban; Mora-Rodriguez 2016, r = -0.28), which is the source of the prediction that outdoor activity flattens on hot days. new_york_values.note: Exploratory in New York (run after the outcome of heat-mech-outdoors). The published New York figures used a natural cubic spline with 4 df and knots at quantiles (q4). Recomputed here with the piecewise-linear basis that this registration uses (lin). All from data/derived/graph/heat_mechanisms/mediators_daily.csv by analyses/round2/hot_end/ny_bike_by_range.py.

prediction.magnitude: (a) Divvy trips change by a factor between 0.90 and 1.03 from 27 to 33 C (New York proxies: 0.92 and 0.93 with the linear basis, 0.97 and 0.98 with the published basis). Shootings rise by a factor between 1.05 and 1.18 over the same range (New York 1.12, 1.05 to 1.20). (b) Adding log(1 + Divvy trips) removes 20 to 55% of the log rise in shootings from 15 to 21 C (New York street noise: 41%, 29 to 57) and less than a quarter of a New York-sized rise from 27 to 33 C (New York: none). The New York bicycle counts removed 2% (-1 to 6) of the 15 to 21 C rise, so part (b) is predicted from the noise proxy and is the part most likely to fail with a bicycle proxy.
prediction.support_if: Both parts hold with the piecewise-linear basis. (a) The 95% upper limit of the Divvy ratio 33 C against 27 C is below 1.06, and the 95% lower limit of the shootings ratio 33 C against 27 C, fitted on the full Chicago window 2010-01-01 to 2026-08-31, is above 1.00. (b) On the Divvy window, the share of the shootings log rise from 15 to 21 C removed by the proxy is at least 0.20 with a bootstrap lower limit above 0.10, and the amount removed from the log rise from 27 to 33 C (log rise without the proxy minus log rise with it) is below 0.028 (a quarter of ln 1.12, the New York hot-day rise) with a bootstrap upper limit below 0.057 (half of it).
prediction.refute_if: Part (a) fails in the opposite direction: the 95% lower limit of the Divvy ratio 33 C against 27 C is above 1.06 (outdoor activity keeps rising), or the 95% upper limit of the full-window shootings ratio 33 C against 27 C is below 1.06 (shootings flatten).
prediction.otherwise: Unsettled. In particular, if (a) is supported and (b) is not, the verdict is unsettled and the report says that the shape transfers and the decomposition does not with this proxy. Each part is reported with its own numbers whatever the verdict.

claims.plan:
Data. Shootings: daily distinct cases with a gunshot injury, Chicago Violence Reduction victims dataset gumc-mgzr, 2010-01-01 to 2026-08-31, and Midway (USW00014819) GHCN-Daily TMAX and precipitation, both as already built by analyses/transfer/chicago_heat.py (data/derived/graph/transfer_chicago/chicago_heat_daily.csv). Proxy: Divvy Trips, Chicago portal dataset fg6s-gzvg, trips per day by start_time and user_type, queried through concord/socrata.py with DOMAIN set to data.cityofchicago.org. The portal copy covers 27 June 2013 to 31 December 2019 (from the catalog metadata). The Divvy window is 2013-07-01 to 2019-12-31. A day in the window with no row in the result counts as 0 trips. The primary proxy is all trips; trips by user type Customer (casual) and Subscriber are secondary and do not decide the verdict.
Model. Negative binomial GLM with log link and HC0 standard errors, calendar terms C(dow) + C(month) + C(year) + hol + wet as in heat-shootings, and temperature as a piecewise-linear spline of TMAX with knots at 15, 21 and 27 C (analyses/round2/hot_end/model.py, SPLINE = 'lin'). Dispersion alpha is estimated by maximum likelihood from the linear-temperature model on the same days. The ratio for 33 against 27 C is exp(6 x slope above 27 C). The share removed over a range is 1 - (log rise with log(1 + trips) in the model) / (log rise without it), on the Divvy window, with a 95% interval from 500 resamples of calendar weeks (seed 1).
Why this basis. A simulation on the Chicago weather and calendar (analyses/round2/hot_end/power.py and the check recorded in docs/round2.md) showed that the 4-df quantile-knot basis of the New York exploratory analysis overstates the 27 to 33 C ratio by 0.04 to 0.07 when the true curve bends sharply at 27 C (true 1.00 estimated as 1.07; true 0.98 estimated as 1.05), because it has no knot near 27 C. The piecewise-linear basis was unbiased in the same simulation (1.00 estimated as 1.00, 0.98 as 0.98). The New York values were recomputed with it before this registration and keep their sign and size.
Pre-specified sensitivity, reported and not deciding: the q4 basis; a natural cubic basis with knots at 9, 15, 21, 27 C; year-by-month terms in place of month and year; May to September only; the shootings ratio on the Divvy window; Customer and Subscriber trips separately; the proxy from the previous day.
Figure: the two cities' curves side by side (shootings and the outdoor proxy against TMAX, relative to 15 C).

can_it_fail.source: data/derived/round2/hot_end/power.json: 120 simulated series per scenario on the Chicago weather and calendar with the registered basis; shootings simulated at 6.7 a day, the proxy with day-to-day noise of sd 0.25 on the log scale. Standard errors of the shares in the simulation are the spread across simulated series, standing in for the bootstrap.
can_it_fail.minimum_detectable: With 80% power at the two-sided 5% level, the smallest detectable shootings rise from 27 to 33 C is 7.5% on the full window (New York: 12%) and 13% on the Divvy window, which is why part (a) takes shootings from the full window. When shootings are simulated flat above 27 C and the proxy rising 12%, part (a) is met in no series. Part (b)'s support rule is met in a large majority of series when 45% of the 15 to 21 C rise passes through the proxy and in none when nothing passes through it (p_b_support in the scenarios).

claims.already_seen: Chicago shootings and Midway temperature were fetched and analysed by transfer-chicago-heat-shootings. That study saw the linear rate ratio (1.131 per 5 C, 1.120 to 1.143) and eight linear variants, and also the unadjusted mean daily count by 3 C bin of TMAX (data/derived/graph/transfer_chicago/heat_by_tmax_bin.csv, drawn in panel A of figures/graph/transfer_chicago.png): 8.30 at 24-27 C, 8.88 at 27-30 C, 9.53 at 30-33 C, 8.91 at 33-36 C (202 days) and 9.58 at 36-39 C (24 days). I read that table before registering. It suggests an unadjusted rise of roughly 7 to 10% from 27 to 33 C and a dip above 33 C, so the shootings half of part (a) is partly known and is not a blind test. No spline or range-specific model of Chicago shootings had been fitted, and I fitted none before registering. No Divvy value has been queried by this project: the Socrata cache holds no fg6s-gzvg file, and no script or document in the repository mentions Divvy. For this registration I read only catalog metadata for fg6s-gzvg and for the 311 dataset v6vf-nfxy (column names, the date range, the user types and the most frequent request types). The power simulation read the weather and calendar columns of chicago_heat_daily.csv and not the shootings column. New York's proxies, curves and decomposition are all seen and are the source of the predicted sizes.
claims.not_used: Chicago's 311 system has no street-noise or other outdoor-gathering request type among its most frequent types (noise complaints go to the police non-emergency line), so no 311 proxy is registered. The Park District publishes beach water and weather sensor readings and no attendance counts. CTA ridership is not an outdoor proxy. Divvy trips after 2019 exist only as zip archives on the operator's site and are not downloaded.
alternatives: Divvy trips fall on hot days because riders switch mode, not because fewer people are outdoors; a bicycle proxy measures travel, not evening street presence.
The system grew from 300 to about 600 stations in the window; growth within a year that coincides with season would distort the curve. Year terms and the year-by-month variant address it.
Shared causes of trips and shootings that move with temperature (festivals, holidays, school terms) would raise the share removed without any causal step.
A proxy measured with error removes less than the pathway carries, so a small share does not show that street activity is unimportant.
Lake breeze: Midway can be several degrees warmer than the lakefront where many casual trips start, which blurs the temperature at which the proxy bends.
claims.prior_note: Part (a) about 0.55; part (b) about 0.25 given that New York's bicycle counts removed 2 to 4% of the slope.

prediction.magnitude: Between +0.05% and +1.3% of zone weekday entries, most likely about +0.2%. Worked before data from published and approximate figures: about 550,000 for-hire and taxi trips a weekday touch the zone (an assumption from TLC totals of about 700,000 FHV trips a day in 2019 and the zone shares of app and taxi trips); the published first stage is -11% and -8% (Li and Vignon 2024), so about 53,000 fewer trips a day; with 1.3 riders a trip, a quarter of them moving to the subway and three quarters of those boarding inside the zone, about 13,000 more zone entries on a base of roughly 3.2 million (assumed 58% of 5.5 million weekday riders), less the matching rise outside, gives about +0.2%. The upper figure uses 1.5 riders, half moving to the subway and all boarding inside the zone. The final composed range p_lo, p_c, p_hi is recomputed from the measured first stage with the constants in `compose`.
prediction.support_if: confirmed if all four hold: (1) the primary estimate b is positive and its 95% interval excludes zero; (2) that interval overlaps the composed range [p_lo, p_hi]; (3) the placebo interval (2018 against 2017) includes zero; (4) b is positive under both control-group sensitivities S1 and S2.
prediction.refute_if: contested if the upper end of the 95% interval of b is below p_lo (which is at least zero), and the placebo interval includes zero. In practice this needs a significant relative fall in zone entries.
prediction.unsettled_if: Any other case, including a positive significant b whose interval lies wholly above p_hi, and any case where the placebo interval excludes zero.
prediction.no_test_if: The ridership cannot be fetched for all six windows; or fewer than 60 complexes inside or 150 outside pass the coverage rule; or the first-stage estimate for FHV and taxi pickups combined is not negative with a 95% interval excluding zero (if trips did not fall, there is no diversion to look for).
prediction.detectability: Rule 8 reasoning applied to a single link. With D = (b/se)^2 - ((b - p_c)/se)^2, an estimate equal to the central composed effect p_c gives D >= 4 only when se <= p_c / 2, about 0.1 percentage points if p_c is 0.2%. The registrant expects se between 0.3 and 0.8 points from station-level variation, before allowing for year-to-year differences in service and weather. The test can therefore detect only an effect near the top of the plausible range, and the expected verdict is unsettled. D and the minimum detectable effect (2.8 x se) are reported with the outcome.

compose.formula: dT = T0 x (1 - exp(f)), where T0 is mean weekday FHV plus taxi trips with pickup or drop-off in the zone in the 2019 pre window and f is the first-stage log estimate. X = occupancy x diversion x dT. p = 100 x (s X / E_in - (1 - s) X / E_out), where s is the share boarding in the zone and E_in, E_out are mean weekday entries inside and outside in the 2019 pre window. p_lo uses the low constants and is floored at 0; p_c the central; p_hi the high.
compose.status_of_constants: Occupancy, diversion share and boarding share are assumptions of the registrant, not verified figures.

plan.areas: Inside: complexes with borough Manhattan lying south of the straight line through the 96 St (1/2/3) and 96 St (Q) stations (LINE_96), more than 300 m from that line. Roosevelt Island is excluded. Outside: complexes in Manhattan north of the line by more than 300 m, and all complexes in the Bronx, Brooklyn and Queens. The 300 m band removes the 96 St stations, which serve both sides.
plan.excluded_days: Saturdays and Sundays (primary); federal holidays; the day after Thanksgiving; Good Friday; days with Central Park snowfall of 76 mm (3 in) or more (GHCN-Daily USW00094728, SNOW)
plan.unit: station complex; a complex is kept if it has positive entries on at least 90% of included days in each of the four windows used by an estimate
plan.model: For complex c and year Y, y = log(mean daily entries in post) - log(mean daily entries in pre). D_c = y(2019) - y(2018). b is the coefficient on `inside` in a weighted least-squares regression of D_c on a constant and `inside`, weights equal to the complex's mean daily entries in the 2018 pre window, standard errors clustered on 1.5 km grid cells. Reported as 100 x (exp(b) - 1) with a 95% interval. This is a triple difference: inside against outside, after against before, 2019 against the same weeks of 2018, which removes any seasonal difference between the areas.
plan.placebo: The same estimator one year earlier: D_c = y(2018) - y(2017), same areas, weights from the 2017 pre window. No price change occurred in February 2018.
plan.first_stage: The same estimator with taxi zones as units and weekday pickups as the outcome, for FHV (all bases, including high-volume) and taxis (yellow and green) combined and separately, 2019 against 2018. Inside zones are Manhattan taxi zones whose centroid lies south of LINE_96, without Roosevelt Island, Randalls Island and the harbour islands. Zones 264 and 265 (unknown, outside the city) are dropped and the share of trips with no pickup zone is reported for each window; if it exceeds 10% of FHV trips in any window, the FHV first stage is reported as unreliable and the gate uses taxis alone.

alternatives: Differential subway service changes between the zone and the rest of the system in early 2019 against early 2018 (Subway Action Plan improvements, weekend and night work, station closures for renovation in 2018 that moved riders to neighbouring stations)
Weather: four nor'easters in March 2018 fall in the comparison year; the snow-day rule removes only the days at or above 76 mm
Employment and tourism growth in the Manhattan core, which raise zone entries without any substitution
The citywide driver minimum-pay rule of 1 February 2019, which raised app fares everywhere; it differences out between areas but adds a citywide push toward transit that this design cannot see
The August 2018 cap on new for-hire vehicle licences
Control contamination: a diverted trip between the zone and an outer borough adds an entry outside as well as inside, which biases the estimate toward zero; the composition allows for it
Riders moving to buses, bicycles, walking or pooled rides, or not travelling, which would give a first stage without a subway effect
Fare evasion and changes in how entries are estimated across years in the MTA series

outcome.prediction_scored: not scored. The registration made the test conditional on a first stage: FHV and taxi pickups inside the area had to fall relative to outside, with an interval excluding zero. More than 10% of FHV trips had no pickup zone in three of the four windows (19.3% and 18.3% in 2018, 10.9% in January 2019), so by the registered rule the gate used taxis alone, and taxi pickups changed by +1.82% (-0.85 to +4.57). The combined series gives -1.06% (-2.35 to +0.26) and FHV alone -1.86% (-3.39 to -0.31). The gate failed, so the verdict is no_test. The registered subway estimate is -0.71% (-2.02 to +0.62), with a placebo of -0.45% (-1.14 to +0.23); had the gate passed, the verdict would have been unsettled.
outcome.settle: Two things. First, a first stage that measures the treatment: the surcharge applies to any trip that touches the area, so a trip from an airport to Midtown is charged although its pickup is outside. Trips touching the area need a comparison that is not charged, for example trips of similar length wholly outside it, from records with complete zones (the high-volume files from February 2019 are complete; the 2018 FHV files are not). Second, a subway measure that can see an effect of a few tenths of a percent: entries by hour and fare type at stations nearest the places where short for-hire trips fell most, or the MTA origin-destination estimates, which begin only in 2021 and so cover the 2025 toll but not the 2019 surcharge.

outcome.notes: Subway, 2019 (registered): 77 complexes inside and 331 outside, 156 grid cells; mean weekday entries in the 2019 pre window 2,478,997 inside and 2,652,729 outside. Sensitivities: control Manhattan north of 96th St -0.92% (-2.57 to +0.76); control Bronx, Brooklyn and Queens -0.67% (-2.15 to +0.83); unweighted +0.17% (-0.80 to +1.15); with the 96 St complexes -0.69% (-2.00 to +0.63); without L complexes -0.90% (-2.29 to +0.52); 16-week post window -0.99% (-2.40 to +0.43); nights 20:00-04:00 +2.17% (-0.42 to +4.83) with a night placebo of -1.11% (-3.40 to +1.23); weekends +1.07% (-16.90 to +22.92); 2019 alone -0.85% (-2.43 to +0.76). The standard error is 0.679 log points x 100, so the smallest effect the test could detect with 80% power is about 1.92%, above the +1.3% registered as the largest plausible effect. The registered composed range could not be computed as planned because the gate series did not fall. Exploratory, not registered: FHV and taxi trips touching the area were 590,902 a weekday before and 569,645 after, against 565,502 and 569,898 in the same weeks of 2018, a change of -4.34% with no comparison area (about 25,651 trips a weekday). With the registered constants this would add 0.174% to zone entries (range 0.026% to 0.776%), which the subway test cannot distinguish from zero. Li and Vignon (2024) report larger falls (11% ride-hail, 8% taxi). Secondary, 2025 zone toll (descriptive): entries at CBD complexes against all others, January-March 2025 against autumn 2024, less the same a year earlier, -1.23% (-2.75 to +0.33); placebo +1.44% (-0.24 to +3.16); against Manhattan north of 60th St -0.24% (-1.85 to +1.40); nights -0.60% (-2.97 to +1.82). Entries are counted where riders board, so a commuter who leaves a car at home adds an entry outside the zone in the morning and one inside in the evening. One week of 2019 ridership (13-19 May, used only by the 16-week sensitivity) timed out as a weekly query and was fetched day by day. Two-week queries cached before the chunk size was changed are not used.
