graph_evidence.note: The System graph API key is not on this machine, so no live lookup was made; a live lookup is pending. The cached evidence in this repository (data/derived/commuting/graph_evidence.json and the registration of commute-fhv-subway-distance, 12 Nov 2026) records that the graph has no concept for ride-hailing, taxis or the subway, that 'public transport' links to health outcomes only, and that a variable search found 7 associations mentioning ride-hail, all from one study. The research side of this claim therefore rests on the transport literature below.

literature.citation: Hall JD, Palsson C, Price J (2018). Is Uber a substitute or complement for public transit? Journal of Urban Economics 108:36-50.
literature.finding: Difference in differences across US metropolitan areas by Uber entry date and penetration. Uber is a complement for the average transit agency, increasing ridership by five percent after two years, with heterogeneity by city and agency size. Checked against the abstract.
literature.data_used: FTA National Transit Database monthly ridership by agency; Uber entry dates; Google Trends as penetration
literature.access_note: Replication code and data at openICPSR project 115490.

literature.citation: Graehler M, Mucci RA, Erhardt GD (2019). Understanding the recent transit ridership decline in major US cities: service cuts or emerging modes? Transportation Research Board 98th Annual Meeting, paper 19-04931.
literature.finding: Panel of major US cities 2002-2018. For each year after ride-hail companies enter a market, heavy rail ridership falls by 1.3% and bus ridership by 1.7%. Checked against the TRID abstract. Conference paper, not journal-reviewed.
literature.data_used: FTA National Transit Database monthly ridership by mode; TNC entry dates

literature.citation: Diao M, Kong H, Zhao J (2021). Impacts of transportation network companies on urban mobility. Nature Sustainability 4:494-500.
literature.finding: US metropolitan areas: ride-hail entry raised road congestion, reduced transit ridership by about 9% (the figure usually quoted is 8.9%; we confirmed only 'approximately 9%' from a press summary of the paper, not from the paper itself), and did not change vehicle ownership significantly.
literature.data_used: Urban Mobility Report congestion measures, National Transit Database ridership, vehicle ownership by metropolitan area, TNC entry dates

literature.citation: Erhardt GD, Mucci RA, Cooper D, Sana B, Chen M, Castiglione J (2022). Do transportation network companies increase or decrease transit ridership? Empirical evidence from San Francisco. Transportation 49:313-342.
literature.finding: San Francisco 2010 to 2015: ride-hail accounts for a net bus ridership decline of about 10% (8.6% to 10.8% across models); no significant effect on light rail. Checked against abstracts and summaries; the DOI was not checked by resolving it.
literature.data_used: Trip data scraped from the APIs of two ride-hail companies; SFMTA automated passenger counts
literature.access_note: The scraped trip data were processed by the San Francisco County Transportation Authority; route-level counts come from the agency.

literature.citation: Babar Y, Burtch G (2020). Examining the heterogeneous impact of ride-hailing services on public transit use. Information Systems Research 31(3):820-834.
literature.finding: Staggered entry across US locations: ride-hail significantly reduced city bus use and increased commuter rail use, varying with city size, crime, weather, fuel price and transit quality. Direction checked against the abstract; the abstract gives no percentages and we quote none.
literature.data_used: FTA National Transit Database; ride-hail entry dates

literature.citation: Borowski E, Soria J, Schofer J, Stathopoulos A (2023). Does ridesourcing respond to unplanned rail disruptions? A natural experiment analysis of mobility resilience and disparity. Cities 140:104439.
literature.finding: Chicago, 28 unplanned rail disruptions, November 2018 to October 2019: ride-hail demand rose during disruptions, more on weekdays, in severe disruptions and in whiter and more affluent areas. This is the closest published design to ours. Direction checked against the abstract; we did not find an effect size to quote.
literature.data_used: City of Chicago Transportation Network Providers trip records; CTA service alerts

literature.citation: Barajas JM, Brown A (2021). Not minding the gap: does ride-hailing serve transit deserts? Journal of Transport Geography 90:102918.
literature.finding: Chicago: more ride-hail trip ends where rail service is prevalent; ride-hail does not concentrate in transit deserts (the complement pattern in the cross-section). Already cited by commute-fhv-subway-distance.
literature.data_used: City of Chicago Transportation Network Providers trip records

treated_zones.rule: A zone-day has closed_here = 1 when at least one station in the zone served only by the G (no other line in the station complex) had no G service on that day. A zone-day of a treated zone has cut_elsewhere = 1 when it is inside the shutdown (29 June to 2 September) and closed_here = 0, since the line was cut at another point. The reference days for treated zones are therefore 1 to 27 June and 4 to 30 September.

plan.control_zones: Brooklyn and Queens taxi zones with no G station, not airports (132, 138), whose centroid is within 5 km of a G station between Court Sq and Fulton St (35 zones by the shapefile). plan.outcome: log of daily pickups, Uber (HV0003) plus Lyft (HV0005).
plan.model: OLS: log(pickups) on closed_here and cut_elsewhere with zone fixed effects and date fixed effects, standard errors clustered by zone. The primary coefficient is closed_here, pooled over the seven treated zones and their phases.
plan.inference: Because there are only seven treated clusters, a placebo-in-space permutation is also required for support: 2,000 draws in which seven control zones chosen at random receive the seven treated schedules, the treated zones are left out, and the model is re-estimated; the p-value is the share of draws with an absolute coefficient at least as large as the estimate.
plan.first_stage: Daily entries (ridership) at the ten G-only station complexes (282, 283, 284, 286, 287, 288, 289, 290, 291, 292 in wujg-7c2s). Passes when, for the stations coded closed, mean daily entries during their closed phase are at least 70% below their mean over 1 to 27 June 2024, pooled over stations. A station that does not show the fall is reported, and the coding is not changed after the data are seen.
plan.placebo: The same model on 2023 pickups (u253-aew4) with every date moved back 364 days so that days of the week align (window 3 June to 2 October 2023; pseudo-phases 1 July to 4 September 2023). A first-stage check on 2023 entries at the same stations confirms that there was no comparable closure.

controls: drop the control zones that touch a treated zone (spillover from riders walking to another line)
implied diversion: extra pickups per day in treated zones divided by entries lost per day at their closed stations

The project had queried c5iv-bn4s (Pickups and Drop-offs by Taxi Zone and Industry) three ways: monthly trip counts by industry and zone from January 2023 onward (34,771 rows, fetched 12 Nov 2026 15:18 for mob-crz-traffic), 2024 annual totals by industry, pickup or drop-off and zone (for commute-fhv-subway-distance), and row counts by month. The monthly file contains app trips by zone for June to September 2023 and 2024, at monthly and not daily resolution. The registrant did not open that cached file or any result derived from it for these zones and months, and has seen no pickup counts for the treated or control zones. The registrant read the outcome of commute-fhv-subway-distance (2024 annual cross-section). The station table 39hk-dx4f and the taxi zone shapefile were read to define treated and control zones. No subway ridership values were seen.
alternatives: Shuttle buses, walking to the L, 7, C, J and M, and bicycles (Citi Bike) absorb the displaced riders, so that a small or null effect does not show that ride-hail and the subway are unrelated
Trips are cancelled or moved (working from home in July and August), which lowers all travel from the zone

Neighbourhood-specific summer trends (new housing in Greenpoint and Long Island City, McCarren Park and waterfront events) that differ from the control zones; the 2023 placebo and the triple difference address this
Spillover: displaced riders are picked up in adjacent control zones, which biases the estimate toward zero; the drop-adjacent sensitivity addresses this
Supply response: more drivers and surge pricing near the closed stations change pickups without a change in rider demand

The shutdown also made the G unreliable in zones coded cut_elsewhere, so the reference period is only June and September, when school and work schedules differ from midsummer; date fixed effects absorb the citywide part only

outcome.prediction_scored: partial: the estimate is +0.043 (+0.001 to +0.084) log points, inside the predicted +0.02 to +0.12, and the 2023 placebo is -0.002 (-0.031 to +0.027), inside its predicted band. Support conditions (a), (b) and (d) are met. Condition (c) is not: the placebo-in-space permutation p-value is 0.19 (required below 0.05). The refutation condition is not met either, because the upper end of the interval (+0.084) is above +0.02. The verdict is unsettled.
outcome.settle: The zone-day counts cannot separate a 4% rise in seven zones from ordinary differences between neighbourhood summers: random sets of seven control zones given the same schedules produce coefficients with a standard deviation of 0.032. Three kinds of information would settle it. Pickup coordinates or pickups within a few hundred metres of each closed station entrance, which TLC holds but publishes only by zone, would raise the share of affected trips in the treated unit. Hourly counts would allow a test confined to the hours when the displaced riders travel. A second event of the same kind gives an out-of-sample test: the G was cut again between Court Sq and Bedford-Nostrand Avs on nights and weekends from 14 July to 18 August 2025, and the registered model can be run on it with the Greenpoint and Clinton Hill effects as the prediction.

outcome.notes:
First stage: entries at the G-only stations coded closed fell 98.9% from their 1 to 27 June mean during their closed phase (1,144,686 entries over the shutdown); every station coded closed fell by at least 97%, and Nassau Av and Bedford-Nostrand Avs, coded as terminals, kept their entries. In 2023, on the same days moved back 364 days, no station shows a closure. Stations on the open part of the line lost 15% to 60% of their entries while the line was cut elsewhere. The reference period is not clean: on Saturday 8 and Sunday 9 June 2024 entries at the ten stations fell by about three quarters, which indicates a weekend closure before the shutdown; the coding was not changed. Sample: 7 treated and 32 control zones, 120 days, 4680 zone-days; Astoria Park, Green-Wood Cemetery and Saint Michaels Cemetery/Woodside were dropped by the volume rule. Registered secondary and sensitivities, in log points: G-dependent zones (Greenpoint, Bedford, Clinton Hill) +0.072 (+0.011 to +0.132), 2023 placebo for them -0.012 (-0.041 to +0.017); phase 1 +0.087 (+0.022 to +0.153), phase 2 +0.039 (-0.005 to +0.083), phase 3 +0.043 (-0.002 to +0.087); triple difference with 2023 +0.045 (+0.006 to +0.083); Poisson on counts +0.016 (-0.022 to +0.054); all Brooklyn and Queens controls +0.036 (-0.000 to +0.072); controls not touching a treated zone +0.035 (-0.005 to +0.076); weekdays +0.051 (+0.004 to +0.099); Uber +0.039 (-0.000 to +0.077); Lyft +0.052 (-0.001 to +0.105). By zone (one treated zone each, so the intervals are not reported): Greenpoint +0.122, Long Island City/Hunters Point +0.054, Clinton Hill +0.062, Bedford +0.022, Fort Greene +0.018, East Williamsburg +0.017, Williamsburg South Side -0.005. The effect is largest where the G is the only line in the zone (Greenpoint) and absent where the L is at the same complex (Williamsburg South Side), which is the pattern substitution predicts, but this ordering was not a registered test. Implied diversion: about 55,377 extra pickups over 246 treated zone-days against 1,144,686 entries lost at the closed stations, or 4.8 pickups per 100 lost entries (0.2 to 9.3 from the clustered interval). Entries lost at a closed station overstate trips lost, since many riders entered at another station. Relation to commute-fhv-subway-distance (contested): that claim found fewer app pickups per resident in zones farther from the subway (elasticity -0.30) in the 2024 cross-section. This claim removes subway service from the same zones for weeks and finds a rise of about 4% that is not established. The two do not conflict: the cross-section compares places that differ in density and car ownership, and the shutdown measures the short-run response of people who already live without a car near a station. At most about one displaced entry in twenty became an app trip, so the subway and app trips are weak substitutes at this margin. Deviations from the task text, all fixed in the registration before any data were queried: the shutdown was in 2024, not 2023, so the trip data are 2024 with 2023 as the placebo year; phase 3 ran to Church Av with the F serving the shared stations. A wording error in the registration: Court Sq is served by the 7, E, F and G in the station table, not the 7, E and M. The trip counts came from the TLC parquet files (the registered fallback), read remotely with DuckDB; nothing was stored outside the repository. The graph evidence rests on cached responses; a live lookup is pending.

After the referee (13 Nov 2026): the stance now uses the permutation standard deviation (0.032, z = 1.32) in place of the zone-clustered interval (z = 2.02), which the outcome itself called too narrow. The estimate is not a 4% rise in pickups overall: weighted by June pickups it is +0.020 (SE 0.020), in line with the registered Poisson (+0.016), so the result leans on the smaller treated zones. In the other direction, a triple difference with 2023 has a permutation p of 0.047 (1,000 draws); that was not a registered condition and decides nothing, but it suggests the registered permutation was the less powerful of two reasonable designs. The registration contradicts itself on zone 256, which is listed as treated for Metropolitan Av although that station shares a complex with the L; without it the estimate is +0.051 and p is 0.15. Several stations lie within metres of a zone border, so some substitute trips were recorded in control zones. The reference period is itself affected: with June as the only reference the estimate is +0.057 (permutation p 0.052), and treated zones were 2.8% above their June level in September after service returned. Support needed a coefficient of at least 0.064, so the lower half of the predicted range could not have been confirmed.

stance.note: From the permutation standard deviation (0.0324), not the zone-clustered interval, which is too narrow with seven treated zones.

claims.statement: In the Manhattan central business district, weekday subway entries in the 12 months to October 2026 are about equal on Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday and at least 8% lower on Monday and Friday, and this Monday/Friday deficit is at least 4 percentage points larger than it was in 2019.

edge.cause: hybrid work (working from home concentrated on Mondays and Fridays since 2020)
edge.effect: day-of-week pattern of subway entries in the Manhattan CBD (Monday and Friday below Tuesday-Thursday)

graph_evidence.note: The System graph API key is not on this machine and the Dataverse deposit is not downloaded here, so no live lookup was made. A live lookup of the concept pairs (telework | public transport use), (telecommuting | commuting) and (day of the week | transit ridership) is pending. The repo's cache (data/cache/sysgraph, 947 responses, 136 distinct searches; data/derived/graph_audit/evidence, 4 pairs) holds no search on telework, remote work, working from home, hybrid work or transit ridership, and no cached response contains those phrases. The strings 'weekday' and 'day of the week' occur only as covariates in cached findings on asthma, air pollution, temperature and violence. The graph is built mainly from health and social-science abstracts, so the expected result of the live lookup is that it holds no finding on this edge.

claims.literature_gap: Two extended web searches found no peer-reviewed study that measures a Tuesday-Thursday plateau and a Monday/Friday deficit in fare-collection counts after 2020 and compares it with the same counts before 2020. The peer-reviewed evidence is on travel diaries (Motte-Baumvol et al.) and on total weekday loss (Light et al.). The day-of-week pattern in ridership is asserted in agency statements and trade reports.

prediction.definitions: For each retained week w and weekday d, R[w,d] is the sum of `ridership` over the 65 CBD complexes. The index is I[w,d] = R[w,d] / mean(R[w,Tue], R[w,Wed], R[w,Thu]). Deficit(d) = 1 - mean over weeks of I[w,d]. MF deficit = (Deficit(Mon) + Deficit(Fri)) / 2. Midweek range = max minus min of the three mean indices for Tue, Wed and Thu. Delta = MF deficit in the recent period minus MF deficit in 2019, in percentage points. Intervals are 95% percentile intervals from 10,000 bootstrap resamples of weeks, drawn separately in each period (seed 20261112).
prediction.magnitude: Recent CBD MF deficit 8% to 14% (Monday 7% to 13%, Friday 8% to 16%). Recent midweek range 1 to 4 points. 2019 CBD MF deficit 2% to 6%, so the gap was smaller before 2020 but not absent. Delta +4 to +10 points.
prediction.support_if: All three hold in the primary analysis: (a) recent MF deficit >= 8%, with its interval's lower bound >= 5%, and Deficit(Mon) >= 5% and Deficit(Fri) >= 5% separately; (b) recent midweek range <= 3 points; (c) Delta >= 4 points with an interval that excludes 0.
prediction.refute_if: Any one holds: (a) recent MF deficit < 4% with its interval's upper bound < 8%; (b) Delta <= 1 point with its interval's upper bound < 4 points; (c) recent midweek range > 6 points.
prediction.otherwise: Neither met gives unsettled (precedence rules 1 and 2). The outcome states which of (a), (b), (c) failed.
prediction.sub_question_absent_before_2020: Scored separately and not part of the verdict: the gap counts as absent before 2020 if the 2019 MF deficit is below 3% and its interval includes values below 2%. The registrant predicts it was not absent (2% to 6%).

plan.access: concord/socrata.py with concord.socrata.DOMAIN set to https://data.ny.gov in the script. The source records therefore carry kind 'nyc-open-data' although the portal is New York State's; the url field shows data.ny.gov.
plan.measure: Sum of the `ridership` column (entries by MetroCard or OMNY) with transit_mode = 'subway'. Entries are a proxy for people present, not a count of pedestrians; exits are not recorded, and fare evasion is not counted.
plan.area: Primary: the 65 station complexes that have a station flagged cbd = true in MTA Subway Stations (39hk-dx4f). In that table every complex is either wholly flagged or wholly unflagged. The flag is the MTA's own definition of the Manhattan central business district (60th Street and south). The join is station_complex_id = complex_id; all 65 matched in both the 2017-2019 and the 2025 datasets.
plan.periods: Recent: 1 November 2025 to 31 October 2026 (the data ran to 5 November 2026 when registered). Baseline: 1 January to 31 December 2019.
plan.unit_and_exclusions: Unit: weekday (Monday to Friday) within a calendar week (Monday to Sunday). A week is dropped if any of its seven days is an observed US federal holiday, if any of its days falls from 24 December to 1 January, or if its five weekdays are not all inside the period. Juneteenth counts as a holiday in 2025 and 2026 only. Every retained week therefore has all five weekdays. Days are calendar days of transit_timestamp. No other day is removed in the primary analysis (storms, school holidays and religious holidays stay in).
plan.model: The ratios defined under prediction.definitions, with week-bootstrap intervals. No regression model.
plan.queries: Server-side aggregation: sum(ridership) grouped by date_trunc_ymd(transit_timestamp) and date_extract_hh(transit_timestamp) for the CBD complex list and for each borough, and by day and station_complex_id for the ranking.
sensitivity: S1 office core: CBD complexes whose mean station coordinates lie within 1.2 km of Grand Central-42 St (40.7527, -73.9772) or of Wall St at Broad St (40.7069, -74.0110).
S2 median across weeks in place of the mean.
S3 drop only the federal holidays themselves and 24 December to 1 January, keeping the rest of those weeks (unbalanced; day means divided by the Tue-Thu day mean).
S4 recent period = calendar 2025 in place of November 2025 to October 2026.
S5 complex-level: the MF deficit computed for each CBD complex, reported as the median and interquartile range across the 65 complexes, and an interval from resampling complexes.
plan.placebo: The same Delta computed for 2019 minus 2018 (both from t69i-h2me, the same exclusions). Hybrid work did not change between those years, so Delta should be near 0. The placebo passes if |Delta| < 1.5 points. If it fails, the primary Delta is reported with that year-to-year variation beside it, and a primary Delta smaller than three times the placebo's absolute value is treated as not met for condition (c).
secondary: Hour bands, by hour of entry: AM peak 06:00-09:59, midday 10:00-15:59, PM peak 16:00-19:59, evening 20:00-23:59. The same deficits and Delta in each band for the CBD. Prediction: the largest Delta is in the PM peak, when office workers enter CBD stations to go home; the Friday evening deficit is under 3% or negative in both periods.

Outer-borough residential contrast: all subway complexes in the Bronx, Brooklyn and Queens, AM peak entries only (residents leaving home). Prediction: Delta is positive but smaller than the CBD PM-peak Delta, between 2 and 6 points.
Trajectory: CBD MF deficit for calendar 2022, 2023 and 2024 from wujg-7c2s (descriptive).

Ranking: the 20 busiest complexes by mean entries per retained weekday in 2019 and in the recent period. Prediction: at least 16 complexes are in both lists, the Spearman correlation of mean weekday entries across all complexes is at least 0.95, and fewer of the top 20 are CBD complexes in the recent period than in 2019 or the same number.
plan.figure: figures/transit/weekday_pattern.png: the day-of-week index for the CBD in 2019 and the recent period with intervals, and the MF deficit by hour band.

alternatives: A Monday/Friday deficit that existed before 2020 for reasons other than remote work (long weekends, compressed schedules, part-time work, school calendars); the 2019 baseline measures it.

Leisure and tourist trips, which are a larger share of CBD entries than in 2019 and are spread differently over the week (more on Friday evenings), can hide or exaggerate the office pattern; the hour bands address this in part.
Holiday-adjacent days and Friday early closing before long weekends remain in the retained weeks only when the holiday falls in another week; the week exclusion removes most of them.
Service changes: from 2023 the MTA ran less service on some lines on Mondays and Fridays, which could lower entries on those days independently of demand.
Congestion pricing since 5 January 2025 raised subway use into the CBD; it applies on every weekday, so it should change levels more than the day-of-week ratios.
Fare evasion and the move from MetroCard to OMNY change what is counted, but there is no known reason for these to differ by weekday.
Weather and one-off events (storms, strikes, the 2026 World Cup matches in June and July) fall on particular weekdays by chance; the week bootstrap and the median check reflect this.
claims.prior_note: All three conditions must hold. The registrant puts about 0.85 on (a), 0.9 on (c) and 0.6 on (b), since SWAA reports suggest Thursday is a common remote day.
claims.seen_before_registration: No ridership value from 5wq4-mkjj, wujg-7c2s or t69i-h2me had been queried by this project: data/cache/socrata held no file for them and no script in analyses/ names them. The project had queried the station table 39hk-dx4f once (commute-fhv-subway-distance, coordinates only). Before registering, this agent read (1) the metadata and column descriptions of the three ridership datasets, (2) the station table with its cbd column, (3) for one day in each of t69i-h2me (15 May 2019) and 5wq4-mkjj (13 May 2026) the distinct station_complex_id, station_complex, borough and transit_mode with a row count, to check the join, and (4) min and max of transit_timestamp in each of the three datasets. No sum or value of the ridership column was read. The registrant knew the MTA's fall 2022 statement cited under literature, and has a general recollection that system-wide Monday ridership was a few percent below midweek before 2020.

outcome.notes:
Subway entries are fare-paid entries at station complexes, a proxy for people present and not a count of pedestrians. Exits are not recorded. The mean Monday deficit in the recent period includes two Mondays, 26 January and 23 February 2026, on which CBD entries were 38% and 20% of that week's midweek mean. The cause was not checked; the size suggests a system-wide disruption such as a storm. With the median over weeks (S2) the recent Monday deficit is 12.9%, the Monday/Friday deficit 12.0% and the change from 2019 7.5 points (6.7 to 8.3). The verdict is the same under S1 to S5. The deficit was 10.4% in 2022, 14.1% in 2023, 13.0% in 2024 and 12.7% in 2025, so it has been stable for three years. Mean CBD entries per retained weekday were 2.34 million in 2019 and 1.76 million in the recent period. Plan deviations, none of which changes a registered definition: the borough-level hourly queries were run only for 2019, 2025 and 2026 because the half-year queries on the 2020-2024 dataset took several minutes each; the 2025 dataset was queried by month and the complex-by-day totals by week, because longer queries timed out. The graph side is empty: no live lookup was possible and the cache holds nothing on this edge.

After the referee (13 Nov 2026): the referee rebuilt every deciding number from the cache and all three conditions hold under four further variants. Two qualifications are added. The size is nearer 7.4 points (6.4 to 8.5) than 8.7 once the weeks of the two disrupted Mondays are dropped by rule, and the Chicago transfer claim took its band from 8.7. Condition (b) passes narrowly: 68% of bootstrap resamples give a midweek range of 3 points or less. What is confirmed is the pattern and not its attribution to hybrid work. The rest of the system also changed by 4.2 points (2.2 to 6.6) and outer-borough AM-peak entries by 9.4, so about half of the CBD change is not specific to the office district; the largest change is in the AM peak (15.2 against 12.5 in the PM), which the office-worker account does not predict for entries inside the CBD; and the MTA's reduction of Monday and Friday service from 2023 is not tested. The two literature entries the registrant marked as unverified (Motte-Baumvol et al. and the SWAA day-of-week shares) should not be quoted as findings.

claims.plan: Treatment: data/derived/turn_restrictions/sites.json, built from NYC DOT VZV Turn Traffic Calming (sm2x-35i7): 1,457 left-turn records merged within 40 m into 1,207 intersections with install dates 2016-2026 (right-turn and bike-island records dropped). Outcome data, read only after this registration: Motor Vehicle Collisions - Crashes (h9gi-nx95) points since 2014 and Vehicles (bm4k-52h4) collision ids with pre_crash 'Making Left Turn' (the brief's 'bk4m-6pyy' is bm4k-52h4). Script: analyses/turn_restrictions/did.py at commit bd2a8d9, run unchanged. Design: stacked cohorts by install quarter 2016Q3-2023Q2; treated windows 24 months before and months 1-24 after the install month; controls are calming sites installed more than 24 months after the cohort ends (not yet treated), same calendar windows. Model: binomial GLM of post/(pre+post) on cohort fixed effects and a treated indicator, which is conditional Poisson; exp(b) is the ratio of ratios; SEs clustered by site; 95% Wald interval. Data through September 2026. Power check (analyses/turn_restrictions/power.py, assumed rates): about 770 treated sites in 23 cohorts; expected SE of log ratio 0.077 for pedestrians injured (z about -1.6 if the predicted midpoint is true, so this test may well end unsettled), 0.049 for left-turn crashes (z about -4.1), 0.046 for the pedestrian ring. Non-deciding checks: 30 m radius; cohorts whose windows avoid March-June 2020; event-time figure. Left-turn bans are not tested: no dated list of bans exists on NYC Open Data, and the 42nd Street changes of 2019 (extensions of time-of-day bans at 6th Ave, 7th Ave and Lexington Ave) are too few and imprecisely dated. Outcome: 'ped_ring' in did.py (secondary 'lt_ring').
alternatives: Regression to the mean: DOT chooses sites after crash clusters (the design compares with sites DOT chose later, which were also chosen for crash history, but those were chosen later and may have had their clusters later)

Differential pandemic and post-pandemic traffic recovery between early-treated and later-treated places
Geocoding error: NYPD crash coordinates snap to intersections or block faces, so a 40 m radius may miss or misassign crashes
Growth of e-bikes and mopeds, whose crashes with pedestrians are not left-turn car crashes

claims.plan: Treatment: data/derived/turn_restrictions/sites.json, built from NYC DOT VZV Turn Traffic Calming (sm2x-35i7): 1,457 left-turn records merged within 40 m into 1,207 intersections with install dates 2016-2026 (right-turn and bike-island records dropped). Outcome data, read only after this registration: Motor Vehicle Collisions - Crashes (h9gi-nx95) points since 2014 and Vehicles (bm4k-52h4) collision ids with pre_crash 'Making Left Turn' (the brief's 'bk4m-6pyy' is bm4k-52h4). Script: analyses/turn_restrictions/did.py at commit bd2a8d9, run unchanged. Design: stacked cohorts by install quarter 2016Q3-2023Q2; treated windows 24 months before and months 1-24 after the install month; controls are calming sites installed more than 24 months after the cohort ends (not yet treated), same calendar windows. Model: binomial GLM of post/(pre+post) on cohort fixed effects and a treated indicator, which is conditional Poisson; exp(b) is the ratio of ratios; SEs clustered by site; 95% Wald interval. Data through September 2026. Power check (analyses/turn_restrictions/power.py, assumed rates): about 770 treated sites in 23 cohorts; expected SE of log ratio 0.077 for pedestrians injured (z about -1.6 if the predicted midpoint is true, so this test may well end unsettled), 0.049 for left-turn crashes (z about -4.1), 0.046 for the pedestrian ring. Non-deciding checks: 30 m radius; cohorts whose windows avoid March-June 2020; event-time figure. Left-turn bans are not tested: no dated list of bans exists on NYC Open Data, and the 42nd Street changes of 2019 (extensions of time-of-day bans at 6th Ave, 7th Ave and Lexington Ave) are too few and imprecisely dated. Outcome: 'ped' in did.py.
alternatives: Regression to the mean: DOT chooses sites after crash clusters (the design compares with sites DOT chose later, which were also chosen for crash history, but those were chosen later and may have had their clusters later)
Co-installed treatments: LPIs, daylighting, street improvement projects at the same intersections and dates
Changes in NYPD crash reporting and pre-crash coding, notably the fall of 'Making Left Turn' records in 2020
Differential pandemic and post-pandemic traffic recovery between early-treated and later-treated places
Geocoding error: NYPD crash coordinates snap to intersections or block faces, so a 40 m radius may miss or misassign crashes
Growth of e-bikes and mopeds, whose crashes with pedestrians are not left-turn car crashes

outcome.prediction_scored: hit: ratio 0.848 (0.779-0.924) lies inside the predicted 0.80-0.97 and the upper bound is below 1.00, so support_if is met by 0.076 on the upper bound. The causal reading is not supported by the exploratory placebo (see notes).
outcome.notes: Exploratory, written after the registered result was seen (analyses/turn_restrictions/did_explore.py): a placebo installation 12 months early gives a ratio of 0.9119 (0.8252-1.0078), so treated sites were already declining relative to later-treated sites before installation. Extending that pre-installation trend gives a trend-adjusted ratio of 1.0279 (0.8207-1.2873). The likely cause is the comparison group: DOT chooses sites after crash clusters, so treated sites are past their peak while later-treated sites in the same calendar months are still approaching theirs. The registered ratio therefore mixes any treatment effect with regression to the mean in opposite directions in the two groups. Checks fixed in did.py: 30 m radius 0.8436; cohorts avoiding March-June 2020 0.827 (0.7367-0.9284). Treated sites: 1,966 pedestrians injured or killed before, 1,706 after.

graph_effect.label: No graph evaluation of turn calming or turn bans. Nearest: traffic-calming measures on local-road intersections, Montreal, collisions IRR 0.31 (0.12-0.86), weak evidence overall (PMID 37288501). Literature outside the graph: NYC DOT uncontrolled before-after, pedestrian injuries -18% (turn calming), left-turn pedestrian and bicyclist injuries -41% (51 left-turn restrictions, 2016 study).

outcome.settle: A design that separates the treatment from regression to the mean: empirical Bayes before-after with a safety performance function, or a comparison group of untreated signalized intersections matched on the crash history DOT used for selection, registered before the data are read. DOT's site-selection lists (which crash years it used) would let the selection window be excluded.
